71923.title: cephadm: fix Grafana cert CN overflow by using generate_cert()
71923.author: joshjan20
71923.body:
GrafanaService.prepare_certificates() generated Grafana's self-signed certificate with mgr_util.create_self_signed_cert('Ceph', host_fqdn), which builds the certificate's X.509 Common Name directly from the host's FQDN with no length check. RFC 5280 limits CN to 64 characters; cloud providers with long auto-assigned FQDNs (e.g. Google Cloud Platform, which embeds the project ID into every VM hostname) routinely exceed this, causing certificate signing to fail:

  [('asn1 encoding routines', '', 'string too long')]

This surfaces as an unexplained failure to deploy Grafana, with no indication that hostname length is the actual cause.

Rather than truncate the CN (losing information), this switches to ssl_certs.generate_cert(host, addr), the same pattern already used a few lines away for Prometheus's certificate. This function puts the (always-short) node IP in the CN and the full FQDN in the SAN instead, avoiding the 64-character limit entirely rather than truncating anything.

The dashboard module's Grafana integration does not validate against a specific root CA; it uses a single boolean flag
(GRAFANA_API_SSL_VERIFY), already set to false whenever cephadm regenerates a self-signed cert (unchanged by this fix). Switching which root CA signs Grafana's certificate therefore has no effect on dashboard-side validation.

Verified with a standalone reproduction of squid's actual ssl_cert_utils.generate_cert(host, addr) logic: the 69-character FQDN from tracker #80277 is preserved in the SAN, while the CN becomes the short node IP, no length overflow.

This does not exist on main or tentacle, both already use this same generate_cert()-based approach via a newer, refactored certificate system (cert_mgr.py); this brings squid's Grafana cert generation in line with that pattern using APIs already present on this branch.

Adds regression tests confirming prepare_certificates() calls generate_cert() (not the old create_self_signed_cert()) with the correct host/addr arguments, for both long and short FQDNs.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/80277

71930.title: mds: avoid a per-inode bufferlist allocation in encode_inodestat()
71930.author: dvanders
71930.body:
`encode_inodestat()` staged the optional-metadata blob in a temporary bufferlist and encoded into it unconditionally, costing a malloc/free per encoded inode. Only directories carry a charmap, and only when one of the `ceph.dir.charmap` / `casesensitive` / `normalization` vxattrs has been set, so the common case paid for a temporary it never used — and a readdir encodes every inode in the directory.

With no charmap the encoding is a constant: compute its length once into a function-local static (the `max_bytes` room check needs the length before the append) and encode the bytes straight into the destination bufferlist. The temporary is now built only when a charmap is actually present.

A second commit drops a redundant parent-chain walk: `encode_inodestat()` already located the snaprealm near the top of the function, so reuse it instead of having `get_subvolume_id()` re-derive it. Cleanup, not a measurable speedup.

### Measurements
  The gain scales with how many inodes a reply encodes, so it is a large-directory readdir optimization:

  | workload | config | result |
  |---|---|---|
  | stat/readdir walk, one 40,000-entry dir, 8 clients | single MDS, libcephfs | 108 → 163 ops/s (**+51%**), readdir p50 355ms → 131ms, mds_lock util 0.84 → 0.69 |
  | readdir-heavy mixed profile, ~24,000-entry dir | 4 active MDS, kernel client | **+31.6%** (sd 0.5, n=3 alternated arms) |
  | single-inode stat (mdtest) | 4 active MDS, kernel client | +1.6% — noise |

  No regression observed on mutation-heavy or low-readdir workloads. Workloads where the client cache absorbs the walk see nothing, because the MDS never runs the code.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/80673

71934.title: mds: bound a readdir page so a large walk does not stall the rank
71934.author: dvanders
71934.body:
The size of a readdir page is chosen entirely by the client, and the MDS encodes
the whole page while holding `mds_lock`. A client that leaves `max_entries`
unset -- libcephfs does -- is handed the entire directory in one page, bounded
only by the 512KB byte cap. On a 40,000 entry directory that is roughly 2ms of
`mds_lock` per page against ~0.04ms for an ordinary request, repeated for as long
as the walk takes, and every other request on the rank waits behind it. This is
the shape behind the familiar complaint that a backup or scan client ruins
interactive latency for everyone else on the filesystem.

Pages are already separate requests, so `mds_lock` is dropped between them.
Bounding a page costs the reading client extra round trips and gives the rank
more points at which to interleave other work.

The first commit adds `mds_max_readdir_entries` and `mds_max_readdir_bytes`,
both defaulting to 0, which keeps the client's request and today's behaviour. A
sweep of the entry cap (mutator measured underneath 8 walkers on a 40,000 entry
directory) puts the knee around 128:

| cap | mutator ops/s | mutator p99 | walker ops/s |
|---|---|---|---|
| none | 752 | 45.3 ms | 134.3 |
| 512 | 767 | 21.7 ms | 129.5 |
| 128 | 1,371 | 7.7 ms | 112.1 |
| 32 | 2,272 | 5.2 ms | 60.5 |
| 16 | 2,856 | 6.2 ms | 33.8 |

The second commit makes the bound conditional, because a fixed cap is paid by
every walker whether or not anyone else is running. Every 16 entries, once the
page has been encoding for `mds_readdir_yield_budget` (default 0.5 ms) and the
oldest message in the dispatch queue has waited as long, the MDS ends the page.
The walker still gets at least the budget per page, others wait at most about
that long behind it, and an idle rank is unaffected.

The dispatch queue is the thing to watch, and `mds_lock` is not: a client request
is handled inline by the dispatch thread while it holds `mds_lock`
(`MDSDaemon::ms_dispatch2`), so requests arriving during a long readdir queue up
in the messenger rather than blocking on the lock. `mds_lock`'s own waiter count
sees only the threads that take it directly -- the tick, the finishers -- and
stays near zero however many clients are waiting. An earlier version keyed off
that count and did nothing at all.

Budget sweep: two clients each list a 100,000 entry directory from a fresh mount
(so nothing comes from the client cache) while a third does create/unlink. 60 s
per point, two rounds with the order reversed, the budget changed at runtime:

| budget | walker entries/s | create/unlink p50 | p99 | p99.9 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| no walkers | - | 0.43 ms | 1.7 ms | 7.3 ms |
| 0 (off) | 87-92k | 0.45-0.47 ms | 5.8-5.9 ms | 17-18 ms |
| 0.25 ms | 73-77k | 0.52 ms | 1.6 ms | 23-28 ms |
| **0.5 ms (default)** | 80k | 0.50-0.51 ms | 1.9 ms | 19-25 ms |
| 1 ms | 83-85k | 0.49 ms | 2.8 ms | 17-20 ms |
| 2 ms | 87k | 0.47 ms | 3.6-3.7 ms | 24-25 ms |

At 0.5 ms the other client's p99 drops 3x, to near what it is with no walkers,
for 8-13% less walker throughput (walk time includes mount and unmount). 1 ms is
the gentler choice (p99 2.8 ms, 4-7% less); 0.25 ms costs 15% for little more.
The p99.9 does not improve at any budget.

### Points for review

- **The conditional bound is active by default** (`mds_readdir_yield_budget=0.5ms`),
  so behaviour changes on upgrade: a large readdir that previously ran to completion
  under one lock acquisition may now be split, but only while other work is queued.
  The intent is that this stops penalising everything else on the rank without an
  operator having to discover the tunable first, but it is the deliberate decision
  in this PR. `mds_readdir_yield_budget=0` restores the previous behaviour.
- A fixed cap has to be chosen ahead of a workload that varies, and the wrong choice
  is expensive: at a cap of 16 the walker drops to a quarter of its throughput.
- `mds_max_readdir_bytes` is implemented but untested; only the entry cap has been
  measured.
- All figures are fro

71937.title: mds: per-inode allocations in snapshot readdir, and a room check that lets the reply exceed max_bytes
71937.author: xiubli
71937.body:
Several related problems in the MDS reply-encoding path, all reached from
readdir / lssnap.

encode_inodestat() needs the stamp and metadata of one snapid and asks
SnapRealm::get_snap_info() for them. That is a range query: to answer a range
of one it still builds a map<snapid_t, const SnapInfo*>, plus a set and two
more maps inside SnapClient on the past_parent_snaps path, once per realm on
the way up the parent chain. It then deep-copies the SnapInfo's metadata map,
encodes it and throws the copy away. A readdir inside a snapshot encodes every
inode in the directory, so all of that is paid per dentry to answer a question
whose inputs -- the realm and the snapid -- are constant for the whole readdir.
handle_client_lssnap() pays it twice: it resolves every SnapInfo before it
starts encoding, then encode_inodestat() resolves each one again.

issue_client_lease() constructs a std::string from the CDentry's mempool string
to fill a LeaseStat it only needs long enough to encode. On an fscrypt-enabled
directory the alternate name is the encrypted full name, so that is a malloc
and a copy per readdir entry; the null-lease path pays it too.

The readdir paths then decide whether one more entry fits by adding
sizeof(LeaseStat) to the dentry name. That is the size of the C++ object -- 48
bytes on x86-64, 32 of them the std::string -- and bears no relation to what
encode_lease() appends, which is 20 bytes plus the alternate name. It
overestimates a lease with no alternate name and underestimates every lease
whose alternate name is longer than 28 bytes; on an fscrypt-enabled directory
that is all of them. When the estimate is short the entry is encoded anyway and
the room left, bytes_left - dnbl.length(), goes negative; handed to
encode_inodestat()'s 'unsigned max_bytes' it becomes ~4G, so the -ENOSPC check
that argument exists to drive never fires and the reply runs past the max_bytes
the client asked for. A remainder of exactly zero is no better, because
encode_inodestat() reads zero as "no limit". Sweeping max_bytes across a
2048-byte range with 24-byte names, 400-byte inodestats and a 255-byte
alternate name, 681 of 2048 sweeps ended with a negative remainder and 684
produced an oversized reply, worst case 627 bytes over. The client still parses
it, so this is a broken contract rather than bad data.

Found while verifying the above: SnapClient::get_snap_info() breaks out of the
committing_tids walk at the first tid that matches, while get_snap_infos()
walks all of them and lets a later transaction supersede an earlier one --
which is what the projected state of the snap table is. A snapid created by one
tid and destroyed by a later one is reported as still present by one and gone
by the other. The break has been there since the function was written.

Measured per encoded inode, on the resolve/encode step in isolation -- these
are not end-to-end readdir numbers:

```
  realm depth 3, snap owned by that realm    25.0 -> 9.9 ns   -60%   1 -> 0 allocs
  realm depth 3, via past_parent_snaps       58.9 -> 15.7 ns  -73%   4 -> 0 allocs
  realm depth 3, SnapInfo has 8 md entries    189 -> 92 ns    -51%   9 -> 0 allocs
  lssnap, per snapshot                       34.3 -> 7.3 ns   -79%   1 -> 0 allocs
  dentry lease, 255-byte alternate name      88.0 -> 83.6 ns   -5%   1 -> 0 allocs
```

Non-snapshot readdir is unaffected: the CEPH_NOSNAP path never built the map.

No encoding changes: no versioned-encoding boundary is touched and the bytes on
the wire are identical, so there is no client compatibility concern.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/80678

71942.title: test: skip Bench/Perf subtests in unittest_bufferlist by default

71946.title: test/encoding: fix false failures in readable.sh
71946.author: Doracly
71946.body:
`src/test/encoding/readable.sh` reports false failures when the shell locale is not C/POSIX, and on builds that cannot see a release tag. Three independent problems, one commit each.

**1. The sort ran under the caller's locale.**

For types `ceph-dencoder` reports as non-deterministic, the script sorts the dumps of an object and its re-encoded self before comparing them. glibc collates distinct punctuation-only lines (the bare `{`, `},`, `]` of a json dump) as equal, and GNU sort is stable, so tied lines keep their input order and the dumps compare unequal:

    $ printf '        {\n        },\n' | LC_ALL=de_DE.UTF-8 sort   # {  then  },
    $ printf '        },\n        {\n' | LC_ALL=de_DE.UTF-8 sort   # },  then  {

Of the 123 corpus objects whose dump order changes after a re-encode, 107 falsely mismatch under `de_DE.UTF-8`, none under `C`. The fix covers only this `sort`; the `sort -V` calls compare versions, where collation cannot tie.

**2. `diff` is fatal under `set -e`.**

On a mismatch the script shows the difference with `diff`, which exits non-zero and, under `set -e`, kills the background job before it writes its result file. The summary then reports `result file for job N is missing` instead of the diff, and the type's remaining objects go untested.

**3. A non-release decoder version is compared as if it were one.**

Without a reachable release tag the decoder reports an abbreviated git hash, which `sort -V` orders by its leading characters. A digit-prefixed hash lands among the archives:

    $ printf '%s\n' 0.94.2-207-g88e7ee7 4cb6da8e11 9.0.2-1116-g7811c77 | sort -V
    0.94.2-207-g88e7ee7
    4cb6da8e11
    9.0.2-1116-g7811c77

so an 18.2.0 object marked forward incompat at 19.2.0-404-g78ddc7f9027 is tested instead of skipped, and fails. Such a build is newer than every archive, so it is now compared as `zzzzz`.

None of this is a regression: the `diff` call dates to 625a89d4cb6 (2012), the result-file scheme to 8b6be11a360 (2016).

Verified on x86-64 Linux with `LANG=de_DE.UTF-8`, clang debug build reporting `4cb6da8e11`: `ctest -R readable` → `passed 29286 tests.`

71959.title: mds/osdc: avoid Objecter balanced-budget deadlocks under metadata load
71959.author: edwinzrodriguez
71959.body:
## Summary
- After `Objecter::set_balanced_budget()` (tracker #66578), `_throttle_op` can block the caller until OSD replies free budget. Those replies are delivered on `ms_dispatch`, which must take `mds_lock` first. Holding `mds_lock` (or another mutex that `ms_dispatch`/trim depends on) across a throttled Objecter submit wedges the MDS under SpecStorage2020-class metadata load.
- Drop `Journaler::lock` around Objecter submits that can throttle; make `get_layout_period()` lock-free after `set_layout`.
- Drop `mds_lock` around Objecter submits on the log-trim table/sessionmap/OFT path and on dir/inode fetch/store/backtrace; defer overlapping table/sessionmap saves.
- Keep balanced-budget throttling, but move hot Objecter submits off `ms_dispatch` / `mds-rank-fin` onto a dedicated `objecter_finisher` (`mds-obj-fin`) via `queue_objecter()`. Also defer `MDLog::flush`/`write_head` so they never block under `mds_lock`.
- Fix PurgeQueue: its `SafeTimer` shares `PurgeQueue::lock` with `safe_callbacks=true`, so delayed `journaler.flush()` held that lock across the Objecter throttle while cache trim held `mds_lock` in `push()` — permanent deadlock. Use `safe_callbacks=false` and drop the lock around Journaler append/flush/write_head.
## Commits
1. `osdc/Journaler: do not hold lock across Objecter throttle` (Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/80667)
2. `mds: do not hold mds_lock across Objecter throttle on trim path`
3. `mds: do not hold mds_lock across Objecter throttle on dir/inode I/O`
4. `mds: submit Objecter ops on dedicated finisher under balanced budget`
5. `mds: do not hold PurgeQueue lock across Objecter throttle`
## Test plan
- [ ] `unittest_journaler_lock` — `get_layout_period()` does not take `Journaler::lock`
- [ ] `unittest_mds_table_save_unlock` — unlock window + defer overlapping `MDSTable::save`
- [ ] Build/run `bin/ceph-mds` with the series applied
- [ ] SpecStorage2020 SWBUILD (or equivalent metadata hammer) against a single active MDS with `mds_cache_memory_limit` stressed; confirm no `ms_dispatch` / asok / beacon wedge from Objecter throttle × lock cycles

71960.title: mds: fix prealloc_inos overlap crash on recovery
71960.author: joscollin
71960.body:
* **The Issue:** An ungraceful MDS crash during metadata-heavy workloads can cause a state divergence where the `SessionMap` persists its state to OMAP before the `InoTable` flushes its corresponding event update to the MDLog journal.
Upon recovery, the MDS loads mismatched timeline states (future OMAP vs. past MDLog) and attempts to re-allocate already assigned inodes to clients, triggering a fatal `interval_set` overlap assertion (`ceph_assert(p->first > start+len)`).
* **The Fix:** Reconciles the state dynamically during the boot sequence by iterating through loaded OMAP sessions at the end of `SessionMap::_load_finish` (and legacy) and deducting any `prealloc_inos` from the `InoTable` free pool.
* **QA/Testing:** A Teuthology regression test is explicitly omitted to avoid flaky CI results. The race condition spans a microsecond window that cannot be deterministically caught via external Python scripts without introducing highly bespoke C++ fault injection killpoints.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/80693

71962.title: mds: pipeline dirfrag OMAP fetches with buffered fallback
71962.author: LiShengG
71962.body:
Large dirfrags require multiple OMAP reads. Currently, the MDS buffers all
batches before decoding dentries, serializing I/O and decoding while retaining
the entire encoded dirfrag in memory.

Submit the next OMAP read before decoding the current batch so I/O and
decoding can overlap without buffering the entire encoded directory.
Pipelining is enabled by default through `mds_dir_fetch_pipelined`, with the
buffered implementation retained as a runtime fallback. The mode is latched
per fetch so configuration changes do not disrupt an in-flight scan.

This PR is independent of #71745; the snap-purge persistence fix remains separate. For pipelined fetching, snap_purged_thru advances only after the full scan completes, using the target and eligibility condition captured at initialization.

**End-to-end latency** (cold cache, kernel client; with the default `mds_bal_split_size`, a 100k-entry directory is split into fragments, so the 64-fragment row is the default-configuration case)

| Workload | Runs/group | A: main | B: Disabled | C: Enabled | C vs. A | C vs. B |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 100k entries, 64 fragments | 30 | 1448\.9 ms | 1434\.7 ms | 1327\.8 ms | −8.4% | −7.5% |
| 4 clients × separate 100k-entry directories | 6 | 10841\.7 ms | 10661\.3 ms | 8019\.7 ms | **−26.0%** | **−24.8%** |
| 100k entries with concurrent statx requests | 6 | 1305\.1 ms | 1314\.9 ms | 1054\.5 ms | −19.2% | −19.8% |
| 100k entries, single fragment | 30 | 1408\.2 ms | 1380\.8 ms | 1160\.7 ms | **−17.6%** | **−15.9%** |
| 100k entries, batch size 128 | 6 | 1476\.2 ms | 1469\.7 ms | 1125\.9 ms | −23.7% | −23.4% |
| 10k entries, single fragment | 30 | 120\.4 ms | 124\.6 ms | 113\.5 ms | −5.7% | −8.9% |

**Memory usage** (MiB)

| Workload | Metric | Runs/group | A: main | B: Disabled | C: Enabled | C vs. A |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 100k entries, 64 fragments | Peak MDS RSS | 30 | 388\.3 | 388\.6 | 388\.6 | \+0.1% |
| 100k entries, single fragment | Peak MDS RSS | 30 | 417\.2 | 417\.2 | 387\.4 | −7.1% |
| 100k entries, single fragment | Peak OMAP buffer | 12 | 51\.212 | 51\.212 | 0\.524 | −99.0% |
| 4 clients × separate 100k-entry directories | Peak MDS RSS | 6 | 1542\.5 | 1528\.0 | 1381\.5 | −10.4% |

These numbers were measured on the previous revision of this PR, before the
rebase and split. The batch read and decode path is the same; what changed
since then is error handling and when `snap_purged_thru` advances. RSS was sampled every
10 ms; OMAP buffer is the logical key/value bytes held by a single fetch
callback. Rows with 6 runs are preliminary.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/80600

71965.title: cmake,crimson,librbd,rgw: enable -Wconditional-uninitialized for clang
71965.author: Doracly
71965.body:
Enables clang's `-Wconditional-uninitialized` and fixes everything it
flagged across the tree, in 24 files.

The warning fires where a variable is read on some path that never
assigned it. Most instances are false positives in the sense that the
unset path is unreachable, but the compiler cannot prove it: the
assignment and the read are guarded by conditions that are correlated in
practice but not syntactically linked. Those are fixed with a default
value (or, twice, by removing a redundant branch), and each commit
message records the invariant that makes the default unreachable.

Four findings were real:

* **librbd** — `DeepCopyRequest` passed an uninitialized value to
  `finish()` when `exclusive_lock` was null, because
  `ExclusiveLock::start_op()` writes its out-param only on the path where
  it is actually called. If the indeterminate value happened to be `0`,
  a deep copy reported success after logging "lost exclusive lock".
  Now `-ERESTART`, matching how `Operations.cc` handles the same case.
  Tracker: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/80702

* **tools/osdmaptool** — `--test-map-pgs-dump-all --test-random` printed
  three uninitialized ints: only the dump-all branch assigns them,
  but `--test-random` takes precedence. The combination is now rejected,
  with a CLI test.
  Tracker: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/80703

* **crimson/os/seastore** — `LogManager::omap_iterate()` returned an
  uninitialized value when no key matched, e.g. an upper-bound seek past
  the last key; the scrub omap scan asserts on it. Now `NEXT`, as the
  btree leaf `iterate()` returns. Present since v21.0.0, so it needs an
  umbrella backport.
  Tracker: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/81647

* **rgw** — (find_hdr_cksum()): with no matching header, the "no checksum"
  return used cksum_type, which still held the last type tried (xxhash128).
  The only current effect is a wrong header name in a level-10 log line,
  so it's filed as cleanup with no tracker.

Supporting changes:

* `compressor/zlib` and `erasure-code/jerasure` compile vendored isa-l and
  gf-complete C sources directly, so they get Ceph's warning flags.
  `igzip.c` and, on arm64, `gf_w4_neon.c`/`gf_w8_neon.c` trip false
  positives; the warning is suppressed for those vendored sources rather
  than patching the submodules. Seastar is exempted the same way.

* `-Wno-deprecated-register` is dropped in its own commit. `register` has
  been ill-formed since C++17 and clang reports it as `-Wregister`, an
  error, so the suppression could never have any effect.

The flag is added as a plain warning, not `-Werror=`. `run-make.sh`
already builds C++ with `-Werror` (`CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_DEBUG`), so CI treats
it as an error without breaking release or developer builds on a clang
version that finds new instances. The flag has existed since clang 3.0,
so no version guard is needed.

It is enabled per language with `COMPILE_LANG_AND_ID`, so C sources are
covered too (`src/crush/mapper.c` was one of the places it fired), and a
gcc C compiler paired with clang++ never sees it.

One commit per component, with the build-system commits last and the
cmake change that enables the warning at the end, so every intermediate
commit still builds.

71966.title: mgr/dashboard: resolve OSD host through nested CRUSH buckets
71966.author: vobruba-martin
71966.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/80683

## Summary

The Dashboard OSD list assumes that OSDs are direct children of `host` CRUSH buckets.

This breaks valid CRUSH hierarchies that contain one or more intermediate bucket levels, for example:

```text
root
└── host
    └── diskgroup
        └── osd
```

In such a hierarchy, the Dashboard backend does not populate the OSD's `host` field because it only checks direct children of each host.

The missing `host` field subsequently causes the OSD details Devices tab to fail when the frontend evaluates:

```text
selection?.host.name
```

with:

```text
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')
```

## Fix

This PR changes host resolution in the OSD list API to recursively walk descendants of each `host` bucket.

Negative child IDs are treated as CRUSH buckets and traversed until OSD leaves are reached. The implementation does not depend on a specific intermediate bucket type such as `diskgroup`.

Live validation was also performed on a Ceph 20.2.4 cluster using a real custom `diskgroup` CRUSH hierarchy. After applying the backend change to the active manager:

- affected OSDs reported the correct enclosing host;
- the OSD Devices detail rendered successfully;
- the previous JS console exception disappeared.

The frontend is additionally made null-safe by changing:

```text
[hostname]="selection?.host.name"
```

to:

```text
[hostname]="selection?.host?.name"
```

71979.title: extblkdev/fcm: add FCM dedup log perf counters
71979.author: David-Skel
71979.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/80744

## Problem
The `fcm` (Flash Core Module) extblkdev plugin currently queries NVMe log page `0xCA` to report physical and logical capacity and compression utilization numbers up to Ceph perf counters. 

However, IBM FCM drives also provide hardware-level deduplication statistics on NVMe log page `0xE0` (`NAS`, `NML`, `NLO`, `SPU`). Ceph currently does not query or expose these deduplication metrics, preventing visibility into hardware dedup efficiency via `ceph daemon osd.X perf dump` or Prometheus monitoring.

## Fix
1. Extend `ExtBlkDevFcm::fcm_dev` with `query_dedup_log()` to issue an NVMe admin passthrough command (`NVME_IOCTL_ADMIN_CMD`) fetching log page `0xE0`.
2. Add `get_fcm_dedup_core()` and `get_fcm_dedup()` to retrieve and cache dedup metrics across underlying devices using the same 15-second cache window as the utilization query, with graceful fallback on firmware where log page `0xE0` is not supported.
3. Register 4 new perf counters under the `extblkdev` group:
   - `dev_dedup_nas`: active deduplicated slots (NAS)
   - `dev_dedup_nml`: mapped LBAs (NML)
   - `dev_dedup_nlo`: LBAs overwritten (monotonic counter, NLO)
   - `dev_dedup_spu`: NAND bytes used by dedup engine (SPU)
4. Update `get_state()` to populate these counters during regular metric collection.

Signed-off-by: David Skelton <David.Skelton2@ibm.com>
Assisted-by: IBM-Bob-2.1.0

71992.title: osd: back off clients on a laggy PG
71992.author: dvanders
71992.body:
A laggy PG can serve neither reads nor writes until its lease is renewed.  Without a backoff its ops accumulate in waiting_for_readable while still holding osd_client_message_size_cap budget, and once that throttle is full the OSD stops reading from every client connection -- so one laggy PG makes all of the other PGs on that OSD unreachable as well.  Backing off hands the op back to the client instead, which keeps the rest of the OSD serving while the affected PG waits for its lease.

Related-to: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/79893

71998.title: msg/async: stop allocating scratch buffers on every event loop pass
71998.author: xiubli
71998.body:
EventCenter::process_events() allocated a std::vector<FiredFileEvent> and a std::deque<EventCallbackRef> on every iteration, only to free them before returning.  Hoist both into EventCenter and reuse them.

The external event queue becomes a std::vector, because a deque frees its nodes as it drains and would not keep its capacity.  fired_events is cleared before each event_wait(), since the Poll and Select drivers push_back() into it rather than resize() it.

Instructions per process_events() call, from a microbenchmark driving a real EventCenter ("idle" is the control):

        workload        pre     post    delta   change
        idle            355      352       -3   -0.85%
        external       2930     2528     -402  -13.72%
        fdevents       1482     1372     -110   -7.42%
        mixed          4059     3550     -509  -12.54%
        mixed-64      13799    12682    -1117   -8.09%

Allocations per call:

        workload        pre   post    pre bytes   post bytes
        idle           0.00   0.00          0.0          0.0
        external       2.00   0.00        576.0          0.0
        fdevents       1.00   0.00        128.0          0.0
        mixed          3.00   0.00        704.0          0.0
        mixed-64       4.00   0.00       1600.0          0.0

No functional change.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/80775

72020.title: ceph-crash: authenticate the startup ping as the crash entity
72020.author: benh57
72020.body:
## What

`main()` resolves the identity to authenticate as into `auth_names`, honouring `--name`, and then throws it away for the startup ping:

```python
if args.name:
    auth_names = [args.name]

log.info("pinging cluster to exercise our key")
pr = subprocess.Popen(args=['timeout', '30', 'ceph', '-s'])   # no -n
```

The ping therefore always runs as the default `client.admin`. Under cephadm that keyring does not exist inside the crash container, so every crash daemon logs an authentication failure on every start:

```
INFO:ceph-crash:pinging cluster to exercise our key
monclient(hunting): handle_auth_bad_method server allowed_methods [2] and I support [1]
monclient: authenticate NOTE: no keyring found; disabled cephx authentication
[errno 13] RADOS permission denied (error connecting to the cluster)
INFO:ceph-crash:monitoring path /var/lib/ceph/crash, delay 600s
```

Crash collection is unaffected: `post_crash()` already iterates `auth_names` with `-n`. So the ping has never exercised the key it claims to test.

## Why it is worth fixing rather than ignoring

This has been dismissed as benign log noise, and on Reef it is. On Tentacle the cephx `aes` -> `aes256k` migration changes the message to `allowed_methods [2] and I support [1]`, which is indistinguishable from a failed `ceph auth rotate`. On a 20.2.4 cluster mid key-rotation it sent us investigating a non-problem during an unrelated incident.

## Verification

Observed on ceph 20.2.4 (tentacle), cephadm-deployed crash daemon. The corrected invocation works with `profile crash` caps, so the ping is a valid test of the key once it is told which key to use:

```
$ docker exec ceph-<fsid>-crash-<host> \
    ceph -n client.crash.<host> -k /etc/ceph/ceph.client.crash.<host>.keyring -s
  cluster:
    id:     <fsid>
    health: HEALTH_WARN
  [...]                                    # exit 0
```

Iterating `auth_names` rather than taking `[0]` mirrors `post_crash()` and keeps working on hosts whose entity is plain `client.crash`.

## Related

https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/64102 - same symptom, reported against 18.2.1 and framed as a keyring-location question; it does not identify the missing `-n`. Also seen downstream as rook/rook#16199.

72021.title: msg/async: reset lossless connections that stop acknowledging messages
72021.author: dvanders
72021.body:
A TCP connection can stop moving data while both ends keep it open, for example when a kernel bug deadlocks its receive path. The messenger only notices when `ms_connection_idle_timeout` (900s) fires. On a lossless connection, every message until then, such as OSD sub-ops and PG leases, is stuck. Lossy connections, such as clients' sessions with OSDs, can stall the same way, but they keep no record of unacknowledged messages and a reset drops what they carry, so detecting that is left to the client.

Add ms_connection_stall_timeout (default 0, off). When set, a connection whose peer has acknowledged none of its outstanding messages for that long is faulted, so it reconnects and resends them. This follows ProtocolV2's sent list, so it depends on the peer's acks rather than on socket activity. Both ends check their own sent list from the connection tick, which then runs every half stall timeout instead of every idle timeout. Resets are counted in msgr_connection_stall_timeouts.

Add ms_inject_blackhole_lossless, which freezes one lossless OSD connection without closing it, and a standalone test that such a connection is reset.

72036.title: mds: fix backend dirfrag prefetch throttle leak, refetch loop and a lookup hang
72036.author: xiubli
72036.body:
Follow-up to #69832 (`mds_dir_prefetch_backend`).

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/80828

### Problems

1. **Throttle slot leak on fetch failure.** A background full fetch sets
   `STATE_BACKEND_FETCH` and takes a `mds_dir_prefetch_backend_max` slot, but
   only the success path in `_omap_fetched()` released them. A failed fetch
   (missing dirfrag object, corrupt fnode header) went through `go_bad()`,
   which leaked the slot. With the default max of 1, a single failure
   disabled backend prefetch for the whole rank until restart.

2. **Refetch loop under cache pressure.** `backend_hit_count` stopped counting
   at the threshold and was never reset. Once trimming dropped a dirfrag back
   to incomplete, the next keyed miss relaunched a full background fetch, so
   the threshold no longer had any effect. Under cache pressure this became a
   loop: the fetch fills the cache, trimming evicts some of it, and the next
   miss reads the whole dirfrag again.

3. **Prefetch ignores cache pressure.** The background fetch ran even when
   `cache_toofull()`, where everything it loads is trimmed straight back out.

4. **Lookup hang on a failed keyed fetch.** With `mds_dir_prefetch=false`, a
   keyed fetch parks the request on `waiting_on_dentry`, but `go_bad()` only
   finished `WAIT_COMPLETE`. If the dirfrag object is missing, the lookup
   hangs forever as a slow request. This is independent of the backend
   prefetch and also affects `main` with `mds_dir_prefetch=false` alone.

### Changes

- `go_bad()`: release `STATE_BACKEND_FETCH` and the throttle slot. Do this,
  and clear `STATE_FETCHING`, only when the failed fetch was a full one. A
  keyed fetch can fail while a background full fetch is still in flight.
- `mark_complete()`: reset `backend_hit_count`.
- `CDir::fetch()`: skip the background fetch while `cache_toofull()`.
- `go_bad()`: also wake dentry waiters. The retried request stops at the
  damaged dirfrag in `path_traverse()` and gets `-EIO`.
- New functional test `qa/tasks/cephfs/test_dir_prefetch.py`, added to
  `fs:functional`. A second client holds a file open in each directory under
  test, so the dirfrag stays cached while `cache drop` trims its other
  dentries.
  - `test_hit_count_reset_after_trim`
  - `test_no_prefetch_when_cache_too_full`
  - `test_fetch_failure`

### Testing

Run with `vstart_runner.py` against a local vstart cluster:

| | without the MDS fixes | with the MDS fixes |
|---|---|---|
| `test_fetch_failure` | FAIL: lookup in the damaged dirfrag hung | ok |
| `test_hit_count_reset_after_trim` | FAIL: background fetch launched before 4 hits | ok |
| `test_no_prefetch_when_cache_too_full` | FAIL: background fetch launched while the cache is too full | ok |

Only `mds_dir_prefetch=false` with `mds_dir_prefetch_backend=true` is
affected, apart from (4). The default (`mds_dir_prefetch=true`) is unaffected.

72039.title: mds: keep large directory walks from thrashing the cache and churning caps
72039.author: xiubli
72039.body:
A client walking a large tree with du or find can push the MDS cache over
its limit and slow everyone else down. A client whose cache is smaller than
the directory it walks also makes the MDS add and release a cap for every
entry it reads. This series fixes the ways it does that; all of them are
already present in main.

- mds: drop the path locks while a readdir is cap-throttled
  The cap acquisition throttle was checked after rdlock_path_pin_ref(),
  and the request was retried every 0.5s while still holding the snaplock
  rdlocks on the directory and its ancestors. So for as long as the client
  stayed throttled, a rename of the directory it reads, or of any
  ancestor, was blocked. The throttle is now checked before the path
  traversal, and the request's locks and auth pins are dropped before the
  retry. Same change for snapdiff.

- mds: splice fetched omap batches instead of copying them
  C_IO_Dir_OMAP_FetchedMore now joins the batches with map::merge()

- mds: only midtouch the dentries a readdir returns
  A scan returns each dentry once. Touching every one to the top of the
  LRU pushed other clients' working sets out. Now they only go to the
  middle; a later lookup still moves a dentry to the top.

- mds: keep a dirfrag complete while a readdir walks it
  Trimming any dentry of a dirfrag makes it incomplete, and readdir then
  has to fetch the whole dirfrag again. The entries a walk has not reached
  yet are the first to be trimmed. So under pressure a walk could fetch
  the same large dirfrag over and over. The MDS now remembers when a
  readdir last sent a page of a dirfrag that was not its last. For
  mds_readdir_keep_complete_interval (default 10s) after that, trimming
  for cache pressure skips that dirfrag, as long as the cache is still
  within mds_cache_memory_limit. Explicit trims (cache drop) are not
  affected. The remote-dentry path marks the dirfrag this way too,
  instead of touching every one of its dentries. New counters:
  mds.dir_readdir_refetch, mds.dir_trim_spared.

- mds: optionally issue no new caps from readdir over the cache limit
  New option mds_readdir_withhold_caps_over_limit, off by default. While
  the cache is over its limit, readdir still sends the entries and their
  leases, but no caps on inodes the client does not already hold, so
  those inodes can still be trimmed. The cost is an extra getattr if the
  client then stats one of them, which is why it is opt-in.

- qa/cephfs: exercise readdir under cache pressure
  New fs:functional task, test_readdir_cache_pressure.

- mds: issue no new caps from readdir to a session that does not keep them
  A libcephfs or ceph-fuse client with the default client_cache_size
  (16384) that lists a directory of a few hundred thousand entries trims
  the inodes of one reply while it reads the next and releases their caps
  one by one. For every entry the MDS adds a cap, encodes it, and later
  looks the inode up again to remove it, all under mds_lock; with 12 such
  walkers this took about 30% of the dispatcher's time. New option
  mds_readdir_withhold_caps_churn_ratio (default 4): once readdir has sent
  a session at least mds_session_cap_acquisition_throttle entries in the
  decay window and more than this many times the caps it holds, its
  replies carry the entries and leases but no new caps. Caps the MDS
  recalled from the session count as held, so a client that gave caps
  back on request is not mistaken for one that cannot keep them. A client
  counter: mds_server.readdir_churn_withhold.

- qa/cephfs: test readdir withholding caps from a session that churns them
  test_withhold_caps_churn and test_withhold_caps_churn_recalled.

Performance of the last change, mdbench with 1 to 12 libcephfs clients on
one shared directory (50000 entries per client for backup-walk, 20000 for
ai-training), two interleaved runs per build, pooled latency, at 12
clients:

  |

72051.title: mds: cut the per-entry cost of encoding readdir replies
72051.author: xiubli
72051.body:
readdir spends most of its MDS time writing replies, not in metadata
logic.  `encode_inodestat()` makes about 20 small bufferlist appends per
inode, and each costs about 90 instructions: the `buffer.cc` helpers it
calls are exported from libceph-common, so under `-fPIC` GCC never
inlines them.

This series:

- encodes an inodestat in 4 contiguous appends instead of about 20;
- builds `buffer.cc` with `-fno-semantic-interposition`, and has
  `list::append()` copy into the carriage directly;
- removes several smaller per-entry costs: a `strlen()`, a layout copy,
  repeated lease checks, out-of-line cap shifts, and `exp(0)` in
  `DecayCounter`.

The bytes on the wire are unchanged.

## Results

Measured with fresh clients reading fully cached 20000-entry
directories:

```
| Metric                                 | Before | After  | Change | Unit            |
|----------------------------------------|-------:|-------:|-------:|-----------------|
| MDS instructions per entry (callgrind) |   5906 |   3642 | -38.3% | instructions    |
| MDS CPU per 10k entries (mean, 6 runs) |  19.93 |  18.70 |  -6.2% | ms              |
| MDS CPU per 10k entries (std dev)      |   0.09 |   0.15 |      - | ms              |
| ms_dispatch thread CPU                 |    562 |    515 |  -8.4% | ticks (per run) |
```

The saving is in the dispatch thread, which serves requests under
`mds_lock`.  Throughput was client-bound in this test and did not
change.

These numbers are from a tentacle-based build, measured with one extra
tentacle-only commit that is not in this PR (about 2% of the
instructions saved).

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/80838

72052.title: umbrella: qa/suites: run cephfs-mirror in foreground under valgrind
72052.author: karthik-us1
72052.body:
Without --foreground, cephfs-mirror daemonizes (Prefork). Teuthology's valgrind wrapper uses --trace-children=no, so memcheck only follows the short-lived parent and never instruments the real worker. After restart_mirror_daemon() → daemon.start(), the new worker can exit while asok still returns Connection refused, and archived valgrind XML is from the parent rather than the mirror process under test.

Set run_in_foreground: True so cephfs-mirror stays one process under memcheck across start/restart.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/77622

(backport tracker: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/80761)
(cherry picked from commit 4a490ff1eed5c3dd547c9afcf9db4879b3d313d0)

72053.title: common/options: reject unknown auth methods
72053.author: tchaikov
72053.body:
The `auth_*_required` options accept any string, and `AuthRegistry` drops the names it does not know. A user who took the new `aes256k` key type for an auth method ran

```
ceph config set global auth_client_required aes256k
```

and after that, every new client failed with

```
monclient: No supported authentication method found! Is the keyring missing?
[errno 2] RADOS object not found (error connecting to the cluster)
```

A bad `auth_cluster_required` does the same to daemons once they restart.

In this changeset, we add a validator that accepts `cephx`, `none` and `gss`.

72066.title: os/bluestore: Fix merge_blob()
72066.author: aclamk
72066.body:
`merge_blob()` uses `move_data()` that moves csum data in granularity of csum chunk size.
So, it must be prepared to handle the case when allocations in pextents that are individually not multiply of csum size, but in total they are.
This has not been the case and `merge_blob()` asserted on `(len % (1 << csum_chunk_order)) == 0`.
For example pextents 4K + 8K + 16K + 20K + 12K = 64K would cause assertion for csum size=32K, while it should be processed.

The fix is to make `merge_blob()` take multiple pextents together and process them with one call to `move_data()`.
This way it is completely isolated from lengths of individual allocations for as long as the sum is multiply of csum chunk size.

Work is based on unittest from https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/71811 by Ming Lei.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/72848

72070.title: osd: release per-object ECOmapJournal nodes once they are empty
72070.author: aainscow
72070.body:
Rolling an omap entry forward through the unprocessed path erased it from the object's list but left the now-empty list under the object's key in entries; the processed paths likewise left empty per-object maps in key_map and removed_ranges_map. Those nodes were only released by a later omap read of the same object or by clear_all() at the next interval change, so a workload that writes omap to many distinct objects grows the journal by a node per object for the life of the interval.

Erase the per-object key once nothing is left under it.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/80858

Some of the methods in class ECOmapJournal were returning references to an object's entry list. As an object can now have no entry in the map of entries, these methods no longer make sense. Therefore, these methods have been removed and their call sites in the unit tests have been modified to use other methods. Some tests were explicitly testing these methods, so they have been removed.

72071.title: test/osd: Add test for ec idle check
72071.author: aainscow
72071.body:
Depends on #72069 and #72070 This branch contains those commits until they merge; only the last commit is new here. It is test-only and is not intended for backport.

This PR adds an assert_idle() method to each optimized-EC class that owns per-op or per-object state: ECExtentCache, ReadPipeline, RMWPipeline, RecoveryBackend and ECOmapJournal. ECBackend::assert_idle() aggregates them, and it's reachable through ECSwitch. Each method is a list of ceph_assert() calls on its own class's containers, so a failure names the container and gives a backtrace. An IDLE-STATE CONTRACT comment in each owning class records the rule that state which grows with I/O must be released when the I/O completes. Bounded per-shard bookkeeping and caches are exempt, with the reason stated.

PGBackendTestFixture::TearDown() now asserts that every shard's backend is idle, for every test. Without #<PR1>, every write test fails on RMWPipeline::oid_to_version. Without #<PR2>, the new omap tests fail on ECOmapJournal::entries.
