72916.title: crimson/osd: spread primary PGs evenly across cores
72916.author: Matan-B
72916.body:
New PGs were assigned based only on total PG count, which could lead to primaries accumulating on a subset of cores.
Since primary PGs handle client write execution, replication operations, and responses, this created noticeable load imbalance. In a 4K randwrite workload with 4 reactors, the busiest cores handled roughly 1.6× more primary writes than the least busy ones.

With this PR, PGs for which the OSD is primary are placed on the core with the fewest primary PG, while other PGs continue to follow the existing placement policy.

Per-core primary counts are also kept up to date as PG roles change, ensuring new PG placements are made using the current primary distribution.

This provides a more even spread of primary workload across reactors and helps reduce core hotspots without moving already mapped PGs between cores.

72917.title: doc/cephadm: fix the OSD, host management and operations pages
72917.author: eameh-LF
72917.body:
A follow-up to #72731, #72733 and #72734, with corrections to three cephadm pages: OSD Service, Host Management and Cephadm Operations. Each page keeps its sections and their order, and no label or section link breaks.

What changed:

- OSD sizes: the exact `size` example is now `3.64T`, written as `ceph-volume` reports the size. `10T` matched no 10 TB drive. The page also says that a range takes only whole numbers: `9.1T:15T` is accepted, but no OSDs are created from it.
- OSD page: the `libstoragemgmt` warning now comes before the command that turns on the enhanced device scan. The `ceph-volume inventory` example under Filters runs in `cephadm shell`, and the HDD model in two hardware lists and one spec is `HDD-123-foo`, not `SSD-123-foo`.
- Host management: the `ceph orch host maintenance exit` synopsis and text now show that `--offline` needs `--force`. The Sudo Hardening section now has a label, so that the operations page can link to it.
- Operations: the key rotation section now names `ceph orch rotate-key` as well as `ceph orch daemon rotate-key`, and says that in releases before Squid 19.2.6 and Tentacle 20.2.4 these commands can take daemons such as NFS and NVMe-oF down. The page also says that cephadm refuses to stop the whole `mgr`, `mon` or `osd` service.
- Operations: the page now says that `cluster-start` starts the admin host first, and waits up to five minutes for the placement groups to become `active+clean`. The keyring list names both copies of the keyring, and the journald note gives the Podman version, 2.1.0.

The commit messages list each correction.

72918.title: doc/cephadm: fix the monitoring, gateway, OAuth2 proxy and certificate pages
72918.author: eameh-LF
72918.body:
A follow-up to #72736 and #72737, with corrections to four cephadm pages: Monitoring Services, Management Gateway, OAuth2 Proxy and Certificate Management. Each page keeps its sections and their order, and no label or section link breaks.

What changed:

- Monitoring setup: bootstrap deploys `ceph-exporter` on every host, but the setup steps left it out. By default, a cluster set up with them had no daemon performance counters in Prometheus. The page now names `ceph-exporter` in the stack, deploys it in the first step and removes it with the other services. The `ceph orch ls` paragraph now follows the deploy steps, not the Grafana URL command.
- Monitoring reference: the custom image options now include `container_image_alloy`, for Umbrella 21 and later releases, and the lists of file templates name `services/alloy` and `services/alloy.j2`. The page now says that only the active Manager serves metrics, and that standby Managers listen on the same port but return none. The mailing list URL under Default Images is now a link.
- Gateway: the credentials link now opens Enabling Security for the Monitoring Stack, not the top of Monitoring Services. It uses a new label on that section. The Prometheus module page already used that label, so its link works too, and the strict build has one warning fewer. The cipher warning no longer says "at this moment".
- OAuth2 proxy: the page now says that the login covers access through the gateway only. By default, Grafana still allows anonymous read-only access on its own port. `ceph orch apply mgmt-gateway` is now a step only for a cluster without a gateway, as it replaces an existing gateway specification with the defaults. The page also says that cephadm does not turn Dashboard SSO back on, and that `ceph dashboard sso enable oauth2` is refused until an `oauth2-proxy` daemon is running.
- Certificates: the health check section no longer contradicts itself. It now says that cephadm raises no health check for cephadm-signed certificates while automated rotation is on, and only a warning for a user-provided certificate near expiry. The page also says that a spec with only one of `ssl_cert` and `ssl_key` is rejected, and the notes under `cert rm` and `key rm` are now note boxes.

The commit messages list each correction.

Preview: https://ceph--72918.org.readthedocs.build/en/72918/cephadm/services/monitoring/, https://ceph--72918.org.readthedocs.build/en/72918/cephadm/services/mgmt-gateway/, https://ceph--72918.org.readthedocs.build/en/72918/cephadm/services/oauth2-proxy/ and https://ceph--72918.org.readthedocs.build/en/72918/cephadm/certmgr/

Review notes:

- Four open PRs against main also change the monitoring page: #72672, #69914, #67229 and my own #72869. This PR adds no conflict to any open PR that changes these pages. To keep clear of #72672, which adds Pushgateway entries close to the Promtail ones, the Alloy image option follows the Loki one, and the Alloy templates follow the Alertmanager ones.
- My draft #72863 rewrites the same link on the Prometheus module page, because the label was missing. If this PR merges first, that change is no longer needed.
- Not in this PR: the Dashboard page gives `ceph orch apply mgmt-gateway --enable_auth=true --placement=<ceph-node-02>` as a step for single sign-on. That command replaces the gateway specification too, so the page needs a change of its own.

72943.title: neorados: drop unused cls_lock_client link
72943.author: djgalloway
72943.body:
Since #68593 (osd: include cleanup) merged on 2026-10-16, every ceph-dev-pipeline **noble / x86_64 / debug** build has failed to link `bin/neorados`:

```
undefined reference to `librados::v14_2_0::ObjectOperation::ObjectOperation()'
undefined reference to `librados::v14_2_0::IoCtx::operate(...)'
collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status
make[3]: *** [src/tools/CMakeFiles/neorados.dir/build.make:133: bin/neorados] Error 1
```

This happens on main and on every branch based on it. Example: https://jenkins.ceph.com/job/ceph-dev-pipeline/10059/ (main: #9949 onward; last good was #9929 at a4692027).

### Cause

`libneorados` links `cls_lock_client`, but nothing in neorados uses it. In a Debug build (`-Og`) with Ubuntu's default `-flto=auto -ffat-lto-objects`, Boost program_options needs `std::string::operator[]`. The linker takes it from a weak copy in `cls_lock_client.cc.o`, and the rest of that object needs librados, which `bin/neorados` does not link.

### Fix

- Drop `cls_lock_client` from `libneorados`.
- Link `cls_lock_client` directly into `ceph_test_librbd` and `ceph_test_rbd_mirror`. They were the only targets getting it through libneorados, and they need it for `rbd_internal`'s `rados::cls::lock` calls. This matches how they already link `cls_rbd_client` and `cls_journal_client`, and how the other targets that link `rbd_internal` (`librbd`, `rbd-mirror`, `unittest_librbd`, `unittest_rbd_mirror`) already link `cls_lock_client`.

Credit to @mmgaggle (Kyle Bader), who diagnosed this and carried the fix as CI-only commits on his `wip-kbader-s3rdma-*` branches ([e9fddc02](https://github.com/ceph/ceph-ci/commit/e9fddc02c2f110f959e3de46b01364891db902f3), [c88dbd7d](https://github.com/ceph/ceph-ci/commit/c88dbd7d8f44fb4269ba88928344383950a858ee)). With those commits, the full matrix passes, noble debug included (ceph-dev-pipeline #10053, #10054, #10069). His version linked `cls_lock_client` into `rbd_internal` instead. Following review, it now goes on the two test targets, so `rbd_internal` is unchanged.

72945.title: rgw: guard a delete's head removal on the ID tag it read
72945.author: AliMasarweh
72945.body:
Continuation to PR https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/72100


55f5b762c67 ("fix conditional Delete and MultiDelete") replaced the delete's call to prepare_atomic_modification(removal_op=true), which added a cmpxattr on the ID tag, with check_preconditions, which adds nothing to the op. A delete that races an overwrite now removes the new head, then sends the manifest it read, the old one, to GC. The new object's tail, or a completion's parts, is never collected.

Guard the removal with append_atomic_test again. DeleteObject already answers the lost race's -ECANCELED with success; answer it the same way in multi-object delete, which reported it as an error before 55f5b762c67 as well.

The workunit case test_delete_racing_put in https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/72096 fails on main (the PutObject's tail remains after GC) and passes with this change on a vstart cluster.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/80898

With the removal guarded, a delete can lose the race to a write that replaced the head. DeleteObject answers that with success, which is right for an unconditional delete. A conditional one (If-Match, If-Match-Size, If-Match-Last-Modified-Time, If-Unmodified-Since) cannot claim its condition held, so the second commit answers its lost race with 409 ConditionalRequestConflict, in DeleteObject and in multi-object delete, and adds that error (https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/80906). The guard also closes a conditional delete deleting an object that fails its If-Match; the workunit case test_cond_delete_racing_put in https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/72096 fails on main and passes with this change.

Versioned buckets
In a bucket whose versioning is suspended, a DeleteObject of the null version logs the removal of the null instance, and whoever applies the olh log removes its head. If a PutObject wrote the key's head and linked a new null version in between, that removal took the new version's head: the version stayed current and lost its data. A new commit makes apply_olh_log cancel a pending removal when a later entry links the same instance as a version, with "null" and the empty instance treated as the same key.

Validated on vstart with the injection points of https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/72096: the workunit case test_suspended_delete_null_racing_put fails without the new commit and passes with it.

Not covered here:

when the guarded removal inside apply_olh_log loses a race, the error is treated as a race with another applier, and the rewritten head stays until the log is applied again;
a conditional DeleteObject with versionId=null checks its condition apart from the unlink, which needs a cls condition on unlink_instance, like the one https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/72118 adds to link_olh.

72952.title: rgw/multisite: sync compressed objects without recompressing them
72952.author: kchheda3
72952.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/81733

Today data sync decompresses a compressed object on the source and the destination
recompresses it with its own settings. When both zones use the same compression type,
that wastes CPU on both sides and sends the uncompressed size over the network. With
this change the object is sent as stored when it already uses the type the destination
would pick. Replicas still follow the destination zone's compression settings.

How it works:
- The destination adds `rgwx-skip-decompress=<class>:<type>,...` to the sync GET. It
  doesn't know the object's storage class until the response arrives, while the source
  does, so it sends the type of every storage class in the destination bucket's placement
  target that has a fixed type, and the source looks up the object's class. `:<type>`
  covers objects without a storage class (the bucket's default class). When a sync policy
  pins the destination class, the object's class doesn't matter, so only `*:<type>` is sent.
- The source sends the object as stored, with `Rgwx-Decompress-Skipped: true`, only if
  the object's class and type match an entry and the request has no Range or partNumber.
  Otherwise it decompresses as before.
- The destination keeps the compression attr and checks it, along with the received
  length. If the class the destination finally resolves uses a different type, it fails
  with an internal error, and sync fetches that object again decompressed.
- Encrypted objects are unchanged (already sent as stored).

Compatibility: an older source ignores the param, so the destination recompresses as
today; an older destination never sends it. `rgw_sync_obj_skip_decompress` (default true)
turns it off. `rgw_sync_obj_etag_verify` doesn't verify objects sent compressed, as with
encrypted objects.

Depends on #72608 and #72508; only the last three commits are new.

72958.title: qa/tasks/mgr/dashboard: write non-zero data in test_copy
72958.author: djgalloway
72958.body:
`tasks.mgr.dashboard.test_rbd.RbdTest.test_copy` fails intermittently in the dashboard API tests ([tracker #68544](https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/68544), open since 2024-10; most recently on [ceph-pr-pipeline 5952](https://jenkins.ceph.com/job/ceph-pr-pipeline/5952/)) with:

```
  File "/ceph/qa/tasks/mgr/dashboard/test_rbd.py", line 791, in test_copy
    self._validate_image(img_copy, ... disk_usage=img['disk_usage'])
AssertionError: 0 != 67108864
```

**Cause:** the test fills the source image with `rbd bench --io-type write --io-total 5M`, and rbd bench's default `--pattern-byte rand` fills its single write buffer with one byte, `memset(bp.c_str(), rand() & 0xff, io_size)` (`src/tools/rbd/action/Bench.cc`, seeded from `time()`). So in about 1 run of 256 every byte written is `0x00`. The source still accounts the written objects (64 MiB), but librbd's copy skips all-zero extents (`if (m_bl->is_zero()) ... return;` in `src/librbd/internal.cc`), so the copy is correctly sparse and reports `disk_usage` 0.

This is not a timing race, so waiting for the copy's usage to converge (#68904, auto-closed unreviewed) would only turn the failure into a `TestTimeoutError` 30 s later.

**Fix:** `--pattern-byte 1`, so the data is never all zeros. The other `rbd bench` calls in `test_rbd.py` (`test_disk_usage`, the rollback test) only check the image they wrote to, which accounts zero-filled writes too, so they're unaffected.

**Backports:** `--pattern-byte` (13a59272967) is on tentacle and umbrella, so this applies there as-is. squid doesn't have it and has the same 1-in-256 behaviour, so a squid backport would need another way to write non-zero data.

72962.title: crimson/net: read the IOHandler shard without touching shard_states
72962.author: tchaikov
72962.body:
The IOHandler is not sharded: each connection has a single instance, shared by the messenger core, its I/O core and every core that sends to it. `send()` and `send_keepalive()` can run on any of them, and they look up the connection's shard with `get_shard_id()`, which goes through the `shard_states` pointer. Only the I/O core is supposed to touch `shard_states`, and it swaps the pointer in `to_new_sid()` and `set_accepted_sid()`, so a sender on another core can find it null or already freed.

The osd.1 log of the failed thrash job shows exactly that: shard 0 accepts a connection from osd.2 and hands it to core 1 with `dispatch_accept(1)`. While core 1 is in `to_new_sid()`, shard 0 gets the same connection back from `send_to_osd()` ("connect to existing"), sends to it, and crashes in `IOHandler::send()`.

So keep the shard id in an atomic, and let `get_shard_id()` read that instead. Senders already recheck the shard after `submit_to()`, so a stale id is fine. In `to_new_sid()`, the new id is set after `io_crosscore.reset_wait()`, since senders on the new core start using `io_crosscore` as soon as they see it.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/75658

72964.title: osd: scale uncached memory limits with a small osd_memory_target
72964.author: dvanders
72964.body:
Follow-up to the review of #72884: rather than adding a second cache, this makes small `osd_memory_target` values work by shrinking what the cache autotuner can't.

The autotuner keeps an OSD near its target by shrinking its caches, but several other consumers are bounded by limits sized for the default 4 GiB, and nothing shrinks them: the RocksDB WAL (and with it the memtables, `max_total_wal_size` = 1 GiB), in-flight client message bytes (`osd_client_message_size_cap` = 500 MiB) and the PG log (300k entries per OSD, 3000 dups per PG). At a 1 GiB target, the caches go to their floor and these still outgrow the budget: under a 1 GiB-per-OSD cgroup limit, OSDs were OOM-killed during 4K random reads, with the PG log alone at 188 MiB.

Below 4 GiB, those limits are multiplied by `osd_memory_target / 4 GiB` while they are at their defaults (the WAL by its square root, which keeps write tail latency unchanged). A value set explicitly is used as is, so operators who already tuned a limit get exactly what they set. At or above 4 GiB nothing changes.

### Results
vstart, 6 OSDs at 256 PGs each, rbd pool at size 3, fio rbd engine, three runs per configuration, caches dropped before each read test:

| | 1 GiB, this PR | 1 GiB, without it | 4 GiB (default) |
|---|---|---|---|
| peak RSS per OSD | **986 MiB** | 1330 MiB | 2097 MiB |
| 4M write, 64 in flight | 752 MiB/s | 760 MiB/s | 763 MiB/s |
| 4K random write | 6884 IOPS | 6787 IOPS | 6817 IOPS |
| ↳ p99 / p99.9 | 8.9 / 16.6 ms | 8.9 / 16.9 ms | 8.9 / 16.9 ms |
| 4K random read, cold | 38276 IOPS | 37513 IOPS | 37773 IOPS |
| 4K read, 3 GiB hot set, warm | 38881 IOPS | 38613 IOPS | 53955 IOPS |
| recovery (one OSD out, in) | 389 s | 392 s | 394 s |

So a 1 GiB OSD stays under 1 GiB at no measurable cost against the same target without this change. The remaining difference to 4 GiB is the hot-set read, which comes from the data cache (onode hit rate was 100% in both); that's what #72884 and @ming1's elastic-target idea are about, and it's out of scope here.

Linear WAL scaling (256 MiB at 1 GiB) cut peak RSS to 794 MiB but raised 4K random write p99.9 latency by 25% (20.7 vs 16.9 ms), from more frequent memtable flushes; hence the square root.

### What it saves

Running OSDs at 1.5 GiB (HDD) / 2 GiB (flash) instead of 4 / 6 GiB, together with #73018 and #73273, in a sizing model with November 2026 US street prices (DDR5 RDIMM about $35/GB):

| Cluster | RAM per server | 5-year saving |
|---|---|---|
| 3 PB object store, 60-bay HDD servers | 288 -> 128 GB | ~$57k (~5% of TCO) |
| 500 TB RBD, 24x consumer NVMe per server | 192 -> 64 GB | ~$92k (~10%) |
| 500 TB RBD, 10x enterprise TLC per server | 96 -> 64 GB | ~$24k (~2%) |

Read latency in these sizings changes by under 5%: at this scale each OSD's hot data is much larger than its cache either way, so the smaller target mostly costs onode hits. Workloads with a small hot set (VM images, database indexes) would feel it more; that is what #72884 and #73018 address.

72965.title: cephadm: bind host rootfs with rslave propagation
72965.author: vshankar
72965.body:
OSD and node-exporter containers recursively bind mount the host's / at /rootfs using the default (rprivate) propagation. Every mount that exists on the host when such a container starts gets copied into the container's mount namespace and host umounts never propagatex to it.

`fusermount -u` detaches the host's copy, but the fuse connection stays alive until the container stops, so ceph-fuse never sees the unmount and never exits. This is hit in fs:upgrade suites where the upgrade redeploys OSDs and node-exporter after ceph-fuse has mounted.

Manual debugging (scanning /proc/*/mountinfo for the fuse device right after fusermount -u) confirmed this: the mount was gone from the host mount table but the fuse connection was still alive, and the mount namespaces of the redeployed osd.{0,1,2} and node-exporter containers still held the ceph-fuse mount at /rootfs/<mntpt> with private propagation.

  mnt:[4026533286] pid=101758 comm=podman-init cmdline=/run/podman-init -- /usr/bin/ceph-osd -n osd.2 -f --setuser ceph --setgroup ceph --default-log-to-file=false --default-log-to-journald=true --default-log-to-stderr=false --osd-objectstore=bluestore
  1301 1229 0:43 / /rootfs/home/ubuntu/cephtest/mnt.0 rw,nosuid,nodev,relatime - fuse.ceph-fuse ceph-fuse rw,user_id=0,group_id=0,allow_other

With that hint, a tiny LLM query pointed to check rslave vs. rprivate flags for kernel mount propogation types and that led me to check the cephadm source and finally the aha moment.

Use rslave (as ceph-volume already does) so host (u)mounts propagate into the containers.

Assisted-by: Gemini
Fixes: http://tracker.ceph.com/issues/64502

72973.title: crimson/net: defer msgr2 acks, bounded by time and size
72973.author: ronen-fr
72973.body:
On lossless (OSD-OSD) connections, crimson writes a standalone ack frame for
almost every received message, even though every outgoing message already
carries the ack in its header (`ack_seq`). On replicated writes, close to half
of the socket writes carry only an ack.

This PR is based on, and includes until they merge:
- fad2b6d584 "crimson/net: don't write an ack frame for every received message"
  from #72685 (Matan): acks ride on outgoing messages, and an ack frame is
  written only once 64 messages are unacked.
- The messenger metrics from #72580 (de0d3ca9defd, 5d0cff184e17).

On top of these, it adds:
- **Bounds on deferred acks.** An ack frame becomes due when no message carried
  the ack within `crimson_msgr_ack_delay` (5ms), or when
  `crimson_msgr_ack_max_pending_msgs` (64) messages or
  `crimson_msgr_ack_max_pending_bytes` (4MiB) of payload are unacked. Without
  the time bound, once traffic stops the peer keeps up to 63 delivered
  messages, for as long as the connection stays idle.
  `crimson_msgr_ack_delay=0` restores the ack-per-message behavior.
- **Acks owed across a reconnect.** An ack still owed when the connection
  reopens (after a fault, possibly on another reactor) is written right away.
- **Counters.** `msgr_ack_frames_sent`, `msgr_ack_frames_received`,
  `msgr_acks_forced_by_timer`, `msgr_acks_forced_by_limit`.
- **Tests.** `test_v2_lossless_connected_fault2` injects faults on ack frames,
  so it now runs with a delay of 0. A new test, `test_v2_lossless_deferred_ack`,
  checks that an outgoing message carries the ack and that the message limit
  forces an ack frame.
- **perf_crimson_msgr.** The tool used only lossy connections, which never
  ack. It now has:
  - `--msgr-policy lossless`, for OSD-OSD-like connections;
  - `--server-reply-delay-us`, to model a replica's commit latency;
  - `--ceph-option name=value`, to set config options;
  - a report of each side's messenger counters.

Early results: perf_crimson_msgr, lossless, 1 connection, depth 64, 4K
messages, loopback, single runs:

| server reply delay | ack delay 0 (old behavior)          | default (5ms / 64)        |
|--------------------|-------------------------------------|---------------------------|
| 0                  | 63.8K IOPS, ~50% of writes ack-only | 81.2K IOPS, 0 ack frames  |
| 500us              | 57.8K IOPS, ~51% ack-only           | 67.5K IOPS, 8 ack frames  |

These measure the messenger alone. Cluster numbers (3 OSDs, CyanStore, ack
delay 0 vs. default) will follow.

Related-to: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/80545

72974.title: mgr/dashboard: allow the user to edit non default rgw entities
72974.author: aaSharma14
72974.body:
https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b64fff05-ef87-400a-aa6a-06524bc779e5




**Description**

This PR fixes RGW multisite management for non-default realms, zonegroups, zones, and storage classes.

**Root cause**

1. radosgw-admin finds zones and zonegroups by name across the whole cluster, but it only uses the realm for period commits.
2. With no zonegroup given, it falls back to the default zonegroup.
3. So many dashboard operations quietly hit the default entities or failed for non-default ones.

**Backend**

1. Realm and zonegroup passed through: every radosgw-admin call for zones, zonegroups and placement targets now carries the realm and zonegroup. This covers zone delete, add and remove zone, listing and deleting placement targets, and looking up placement by ID.
2. Realm lookup: there is a new lookup of the realm from a zonegroup, and the existing zone-to-realm lookup now logs errors instead of swallowing them.
3. Storage classes in non-default zonegroups: adding, editing or placing a storage class on a zone now names the zonegroup. This fixes the error "storage class 'X' is not defined in zonegroup 'default-placement' placement target".
4. Storage-class API errors: the storage-class POST and PUT calls raised a TypeError because the realm name was required, and that is fixed.

**Frontend**

1. Edit forms: the realm, zonegroup and zone forms now handle non-default entities and drop the default-only restrictions.
2. Storage-class screens: the service and list pass the zonegroup on delete and when loading placement targets.

72975.title: crimson: send replication from each reactor's cluster lane
72975.author: knrt10
72975.body:
Every `send_to_osd()` went through the one cluster messenger on reactor 0, so repops and repop replies were all sent from there.

Each reactor now has its own cluster. `messenger. send_to_osd()` uses that lane, so the send happens on the reactor that generated the message. The published cluster messenger is unchanged: peers still dial the osdmap address, and incoming ops are dispatched as before. A lane listens on its own port and is used for the connections it opened. No osdmap or placement change.

Lane handshakes still authenticate through the MonClient on reactor 0. The auth steps run there and copy the session key back. That hop is only during the handshake.

A repop reply is sent on the connection the repop arrived on, as Classic does. The primary reads that reply on its lane. 

On the replica, the reply is still a cross-core send when the socket's reactor is not the PG's.
When a peer goes down, mark_down_all_ports() closes every session with that peer's type, IP, and nonce, on any port, so its lanes are marked down too.


Part of: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/80545

72977.title: osdc, osd, mon: fix split and replica reads for pools in a pool migration
72977.author: aainscow
72977.body:
Stacked on https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/69112 (pool migration, at 566b09e1de6): only the last ten commits are new.

Reads that do not go to the primary of a pool in a migration can return wrong or stale data:

- `SplitOp::create()` plans a split or direct read on the pool the op is addressed to (`base_oloc`), but
  `_calc_target()` then routes an op on a migrating pool to the other pool of the migration. An op on the
  target, which takes the pool's name, goes back to the source for PGs that have not migrated. An op on the
  source's id goes to the target for PGs that have migrated, and for every PG once the migration has
  finished. When the two pools have different layouts, the read returns wrong data or aborts the client.
  The fix: plan the read for the pool `_calc_target()` routes it to, with that pool's layout.
- A source OSD redirects a direct read of a migrated object, and the Objecter resent it to the same shard;
  a second redirect failed `ceph_assert(found)`. The fix: such a read takes the `-EAGAIN` path of a direct
  read whose PG changes, and is redriven to the primary.
- An OSD of a source PG treats an object as migrated once it applies the object's delete, and the primary
  starts redirecting clients at once. A client can then write the object in the target while a replica
  whose delete has not arrived serves the old copy to balanced and localized reads, and to split reads
  that do not ask for the version. The fix: the primary redirects only once the delete has committed on
  every shard, and holds ops on the object until then; a replica or shard bounces a read of a migrated
  object to the primary with `-EAGAIN`. Because of this, reads routed to the source can be split too.

And `prepare_new_pool()` applies `--enable_ec_optimizations` after choosing the stripe unit and deciding on
split reads, so a pool created or migrated with it gets the 4K stripe unit of an unoptimized pool and no
`split_reads` flag. The fix: apply it before those decisions, as `osd_pool_default_flag_ec_optimizations` is.

The first version of this PR sent every read of a migrating pool to the primary. This version keeps split
and direct reads during a migration.

Tests: unit tests for the SplitOp planning and the redirect, a standalone test that reads each object from a
delayed replica as soon as it is written in the target (`qa/standalone/osd/osd-pool-migration-replica-read.sh`),
and a thrash-erasure-code workload in which `ceph_test_rados` reads with `balance_reads` while its pool
migrates between EC k=2 m=1 and k=4 m=2 (`ceph_test_rados --migration-erasure-code-profile`, rados task
`migration_erasure_code_profile`; it runs with the pool-migration facet enabled).

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/81981

Tested: full build including tests (gcc, Debug) and the unit-test suite (211 of 211 pass); clang 19 finds
nothing new in the changed code. The 6 new or changed tests in `unittest_split_ops_ut` fail without the SplitOp and
Objecter fixes. `osd-pool-migration-replica-read.sh` fails on #69112 (5 of 8 objects read stale) and passes with
the fix, and the mon-only `TEST_enable_ec_optimizations` passes. On a cluster, with one source OSD's messages from
other OSDs delayed by `ms_inject_delay_*` (up to 8 s) and a client writing each object as soon as the primary
logged its delete: no stale reads in about 777,000 localized, balanced and versionless EC split reads. An EC k=2 m=1 pool migrating to k=4 m=2, read by 8 clients by name and by the source's id: 292,800 reads all
correct, 194,400 of them split or direct, in unmigrated, migrating and migrated PGs (the run stopped at 87%
migrated; a unit test covers reads by the source's id after completion).

72981.title: mgr: limit in-flight commands per module with EAGAIN
72981.author: NitzanMordhai
72981.body:
Picks up #60194 (closed as stale), reworked per the review there and the tracker discussion.

  Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/62712

  ## Problem
  A module's queued commands keep their client message throttle slot (`mgr_client_messages`) until they reply. If a module is stuck (e.g. volumes blocked on an MDS), its backlog fills the throttle and the mgr stops reading
  commands from all clients, including other modules and native mgr commands (`pg dump`, `osd perf`).
 
  ## Change
  - New per-module option `mgr/<module>/max_command_queue_length`, default 0 (off).
  - `DaemonServer` counts commands queued or running per module and replies `-EAGAIN` instead of queueing once the limit is reached.
  - The limit is read in C++ on each command, so `ceph config set` takes effect even while the module's thread is stuck.
  - New perf counters in `mgr_module_<name>`: `cmd_in_flight` and `cmd_eagain` (exported by ceph-exporter).

  ## Review points from #60194
  | Comment | Now |
  |---|---| 
  | One global counter/limit shared by all modules (@tchaikov) | Counter lives on each `ActivePyModule`, limit is per module option |
  | No MgrMap/mon command, use a module option (@batrick) | Option registered in `mgr_module.py`, no mon change |
  | Thread safety (@batrick) | Atomic counter; admission already serialized by `DaemonServer::lock` |
  | Count in `Finisher` / use finisher queue length (@batrick, @kotreshhr) | The module finisher also runs `notify`/`config_notify`, so its length would reject commands on a healthy but busy module. Commands only are counted |
  | Add counts to perf dump (@batrick) | `cmd_in_flight`, `cmd_eagain` |
  | Python setter via `_config_notify` | Removed: it runs on the module's own thread, so it can't apply a new limit while the module is stuck |
  | Counter can leak on error paths | Decremented by a guard captured in the queued context; verified on success, module error, handler exception and failed-module (`EIO`) paths |
  | Per module for other users, e.g. audit logging (@dparmar18) | Any module can opt in, or declare its own default in `MODULE_OPTIONS` |
  | Sensible default? (@vshankar) | 0 here, see below |

  ## Testing 
  vstart, `mgr_client_messages=16`, 20 concurrent commands to a stuck module (rc 124 = killed after 10s):

  | | limit 0 (today) | limit 4 |
  |---|---|---|
  | selftest blocked by a 30s `eval` sleep: `balancer status` / `pg dump` / `osd perf` | hang (124) | 0.4s |
  | volumes with MDS frozen (`kill -STOP`), `fs subvolume create`: same probes | hang (124) | 0.5s |
  | stuck module `cmd_in_flight` | 16 (whole throttle) | 4, rest get `EAGAIN` |
 
  New qa test: `tasks.mgr.test_module_selftest.TestModuleSelftest.test_command_queue_limit`.

72988.title: qa/tasks/mgr/dashboard: write non-zero data in test_copy
72988.author: djgalloway
72988.body:
`tasks.mgr.dashboard.test_rbd.RbdTest.test_copy` fails intermittently in the dashboard API tests ([tracker #68544](https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/68544), open since 2024-10; most recently on [ceph-pr-pipeline 5952](https://jenkins.ceph.com/job/ceph-pr-pipeline/5952/)) with:

```
  File "/ceph/qa/tasks/mgr/dashboard/test_rbd.py", line 791, in test_copy
    self._validate_image(img_copy, ... disk_usage=img['disk_usage'])
AssertionError: 0 != 67108864
```

**Cause:** the test fills the source image with `rbd bench --io-type write --io-total 5M`, and rbd bench's default `--pattern-byte rand` fills its single write buffer with one byte, `memset(bp.c_str(), rand() & 0xff, io_size)` (`src/tools/rbd/action/Bench.cc`, seeded from `time()`). So in about 1 run of 256 every byte written is `0x00`. The source still accounts the written objects (64 MiB), but librbd's copy skips all-zero extents (`if (m_bl->is_zero()) ... return;` in `src/librbd/internal.cc`), so the copy is correctly sparse and reports `disk_usage` 0.

This is not a timing race, so waiting for the copy's usage to converge (#68904, auto-closed unreviewed) would only turn the failure into a `TestTimeoutError` 30 s later.

**Fix:** `--pattern-byte 1`, so the data is never all zeros. The other `rbd bench` calls in `test_rbd.py` (`test_disk_usage`, the rollback test) only check the image they wrote to, which accounts zero-filled writes too, so they're unaffected.

**Backports:** `--pattern-byte` (13a59272967) is on tentacle and umbrella, so this applies there as-is. squid doesn't have it and has the same 1-in-256 behaviour, so a squid backport would need another way to write non-zero data.

Checklist
- [x] Tracker (select at least one)
  - [x] References tracker ticket
  - [ ] Very recent bug; references commit where it was introduced
  - [ ] New feature (ticket optional)
  - [ ] Doc update (no ticket needed)
  - [ ] Code cleanup (no ticket needed)
- [ ] Component impact
  - [ ] Affects Dashboard, opened tracker ticket
  - [ ] Affects Orchestrator, opened tracker ticket
  - [x] No impact that needs to be tracked
- [ ] Documentation (select at least one)
  - [ ] Updates relevant documentation
  - [x] No doc update is appropriate
- [ ] Tests (select at least one)
  - [ ] Includes [unit test(s)](https://docs.ceph.com/en/latest/dev/developer_guide/tests-unit-tests/)
  - [x] Includes [integration test(s)](https://docs.ceph.com/en/latest/dev/developer_guide/testing_integration_tests/)

72993.title: rgw/rados: fix DeleteObjectTagging resetting object mtime to epoch
72993.author: mheler
72993.body:
set_obj_attrs() increments the object mtime by 1 ns so multisite can detect the change. However, it takes the starting mtime from the RadosObject. DeleteObjectTagging does not read the object first, so that mtime is zero. As a result, the update sets the mtime to 1970 on both the head object and its bucket index entry.

This regressed in f5f6194c07b40c50913e956e06aaa3709d4d53aa , Main and Tentacle stopped exhibiting the issue for DeleteObjectTagging after 94016c7786f29f3061a181c132abd4069337f5c9 which began reading the object first. The D4N and NFS setattr/xattr paths are still affected on all branches.

set_attrs() already reads the head object, so increment its actual mtime by 1 ns there. This preserves the multisite change notification without resetting the mtime to 1970.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/81980

72995.title: mgr/PyOSDMap: efficient implementation in OSDMap.get_pools / get_pool…
72995.author: Harshit-AI3018
72995.body:
Previously, `OSDMap.get_pools()`, `get_pools_by_name()`, `get_ec_profile()`, and `get_require_osd_release()` called `self._dump()`. This triggered a full OSDMap dump through `PyFormatter` that serialized all OSD records, PG temps, xinfo, and CRUSH state before discarding everything except pool/profile data.

On large clusters with hundreds or thousands of OSDs, this caused high latency, memory churn, and GIL contention during periodic ticks of `pg_autoscaler`, `balancer`, and `dashboard`.

This PR introduces targeted C-level accessors in `BasePyOSDMap`:
- `_dump_pools()`: Serializes only pool records using `OSDMap::dump_pool()`, avoiding full cluster state serialization while keeping 100% schema compatibility.
- `_get_ec_profile()`: Fetches a single erasure code profile dictionary directly by name.
- `_get_require_osd_release()`: Directly retrieves the release string.

In addition, `OSDMap.get_pools()` and `get_pools_by_name()` now lazily cache the resulting pool dictionaries per `OSDMap` instance. Because an `OSDMap` instance represents an immutable epoch snapshot, repeated accesses within the same epoch are $O(1)$ operations that avoid crossing the C++/Python boundary.

Fallback to `_dump()` is preserved to maintain compatibility with test harnesses and mocks.

73007.title: blk/kernel: collect the wakeup read in _aio_stop() on FreeBSD
73007.author: wjwithagen
73007.body:
Depends on #71449; only the last commit (blk/kernel: collect the wakeup read in _aio_stop()) is new, the first two belong to #71449.

_aio_stop() submits a 4096 byte read to wake the aio thread and then joins it.  The thread leaves its loop as soon as it sees aio_stop, so it can exit before it has collected that read.

FreeBSD keeps a finished aio job until aio_return() is called for it and finds it by the address of its aiocb.  The leftover job stays in the kernel after wakeup_ctx, and with it the aio_t, has been freed. he next aio_t allocated at that address gets the result of the leftover job (4096) instead of its own, and its own result is handed to the request after that.  This shows up as the abort in _aio_thread(): "unexpected aio return value: does not match length".

Wait for the wakeup read to finish (bounded to 10 seconds) and aio_return() it before the aio_t is released.  Only the HAVE_POSIXAIO path changes; libaio is not affected.

Follow-up to #71449.

Signed-off-by: Willem Jan Withagen <wjw@digiware.nl>

73008.title: mgr/dashboard: order CRUSH map viewer like `ceph osd tree`
73008.author: vobruba-martin
73008.body:
The CRUSH map viewer sorted bucket children with Array.prototype.sort() as strings. With 10 or more OSDs per host this shows osd.10 before osd.2 and buckets are ordered by the string form of their negative ids, so the tree looks random.

The `nodes` list returned by the backend is already in the same order as `ceph osd tree`: buckets by name before devices, devices by device class and then numerically by id. The `children` lists in it are reversed, so order the children by their position in `nodes` instead of re-sorting them on the client.

The roots from crush.find_roots() are already ordered by id like the CLI. Keep that order (the viewer used to reverse it) and only skip the shadow roots, which are not part of `nodes`.

Also stop mutating the API response.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/68752

73018.title: os/bluestore: weight buffer cache shard limits by occupancy
73018.author: ming1
73018.body:
`_resize_shards()` gives every buffer cache shard the same limit, but PGs map to shards by `pg seed % shards`, so the loaded shards trim on every insert while the light ones never fill: the data cache stops well below its commit (574 of 816 MiB on one OSD, 85 % hit rate on a hot set that fits).

This PR splits the data cache budget in proportion to what each shard holds (floor 1/8 of the even share, option `bluestore_cache_data_shard_weighted`, default true), and changes what the data cache asks the autotuner for: by age only the fraction an even split would have held, the rest at `LAST`, so the commit grows only into memory no cache claimed by age and never drains the onode or RocksDB caches.

**Carries the one commit of #73570** (`common/PriorityCache: credit grants made at the last priority`) as its first commit, so it can merge before or after that PR; the tuner fix is needed here because without it a request served at `LAST` is taken from the pool but credited to no cache, the data cache would come out below the even split.

## Measurements

Hot-set test of the tracker: 4-OSD vstart, `osd_memory_target` 2 GiB, `osd_memory_base` 256 MiB, meta/kv ratios 0.30, 128 PGs, 3 GiB hot region of an RBD image, 4K random reads, 120 s pass, two reps.

2026-11-06, two reps each, same binary tree, stock vs this branch. IOPS and p99 are rep 1 / rep 2; the cache columns are from the end of rep 1 (rep 2 differs by at most 1 MiB in held and by 8 MiB in osd.0's commit, 816):

| | IOPS | p99 ms | data committed, MiB (4 OSDs) | data held, MiB | disk reads per pass, MiB |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| stock | 58.0k / 49.2k | 4.6 / 5.2 | 688 / 768 / 712 / 816 | 375 / 512 / 419 / 590 | 1708–3708 |
| this PR | 108.9k / 109.6k | 1.0 / 1.0 | 808 / 944 / 944 / 1048 | 568 / 776 / 780 / 948 | 5–338 |

The four held values of the PR sum to 3072 MiB, the whole hot region split by primaries. The commit above held is the data cache's ratio share of memory no cache asked for, plus the 64 MiB chunk headroom; the accounting identity pool − reserve = Σ grants holds to the byte on every OSD.

## The drain concern from Adam's 2026-11-03 review

Point 2 of the review: a cache whose shards fill their commit asks for more at every balance, gets it back by ratio, fills that too, and "asymptotically ... drain[s] other caches from space". This version closes the loop by construction: by age the data cache asks for what an even split would have held, the same as today, so it cannot get back more than it chipped in; only the surplus is asked at `LAST`, served after every cache's binned content and only from memory nobody claimed by age.

Measured where a drain would show, a pool with nothing spare (2026-11-06, this branch): 4 OSDs, `osd_memory_target` 1 GiB (pool 614 MiB, fully claimed by age bins in every phase), 606k 4 KiB objects under a stat storm plus 4K random reads of a sparse 4 GiB image; option on at runtime, then off; 6-minute phases, means over the last 120 s (MiB, 4 OSDs):

| | data committed | data held | onode cache | kv | kv_onode | onodes | buffer hit % |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| off | 106 / 96 / 124 / 124 | 13 / 21 / 23 / 58 | 158 / 170 / 147 / 148 | 171 / 160 / 180 / 148 | 172 / 180 / 156 / 184 | 46k / 63k / 33k / 61k | 2–3 |
| on | 132 / 117 / 168 / 149 | 118 / 106 / 151 / 139 | 160 / 157 / 136 / 137 | 148 / 152 / 148 / 141 | 168 / 179 / 152 / 181 | 68k / 89k / 41k / 73k | 6–23 |
| off again | 92 / 84 / 120 / 124 | 12 / 18 / 22 / 58 | 184 / 196 / 156 / 168 | 160 / 152 / 172 / 148 | 172 / 172 / 156 / 168 | 69k / 90k / 41k / 78k | 2–3 |

- **No ratchet.** osd.0's commit after switch-on: 104 → 124 → 144 at +9 s, then 140, 136, 132 for the rest of the phase. The review's model predicts monotonic growth.
- **The shards fill the commit** (held 13–58 → 106–151) for a commit 21 to 44 MiB larger.
- **The other caches keep their content.** Onode cache −11 to +2 MiB with onode counts rising; kv and kv_onode within 32 MiB and far from capacity (RocksDB b

73021.title: msg/async/rdma: demote to_dead beacon error log to debug
73021.author: taaahaaa
73021.body:
When tearing down RDMA QueuePairs, `Infiniband::QueuePair::to_dead()` transitions the QP to `IBV_QPS_ERR` and posts a dummy beacon send work request (`BEACON_WRID`) to drain remaining work completions.

On verbs providers like Mellanox mlx5, calling `ibv_post_send()` on a QP that has already transitioned to `IBV_QPS_ERR` fails with `EAGAIN` (errno 11, "Resource temporarily unavailable").

`RDMADispatcher::schedule_qp_destroy()` already handles a non-zero return from `to_dead()` by destroying the QP directly. Logging this expected condition with `lderr(cct)` (-1) pollutes stderr with false error messages on every ephemeral client disconnection (e.g. `ceph -s` or any rados client command).

73024.title: rgw: support Keystone write-only S3 credentials
73024.author: xek
73024.body:
## Summary

Adds opt-in support for OpenStack Keystone scoped S3 signing-key exchange in RGW (`rgw_keystone_s3_auth_mode = signing_key`).

In `signing_key` mode, the gateway exchanges SigV4 request proofs for date- and service-scoped derived keys via `POST /v3/s3tokens/signing_key`, avoiding permanent root secret retrieval and network exposure. SigV2 requests undergo per-request identity validation via `POST /v3/s3tokens/validate`. Derived keys are held in a bounded process-local LRU cache bounded by identity expiration and local TTL; there is no fallback to raw secret retrieval.

## References

- Keystone spec: https://review.opendev.org/c/openstack/keystone-specs/+/1011634
- Related Keystone server-side change (WIP): https://review.opendev.org/c/openstack/keystone/+/1012017

## Testing

- Native suite on this change: 91/91 tests and 2/2 ctest pass, including the new signing-key exchange and credential-validation tests.
- Functionally validated against a live Keystone + RGW deployment: baseline (5) and advanced (8) credential scenarios pass.

Opening as draft for early review.

73029.title: mgr/cephadm: fix host maintenance when the CRUSH host bucket is not named after the host
73029.author: vobruba-martin
73029.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82029

## Problem

When a host is placed into maintenance, cephadm sets the `noout` flag on the host's CRUSH bucket. The bucket name was derived from the hostname known to cephadm (the short hostname) instead of being looked up in the CRUSH map. If the bucket is named differently (renamed bucket, custom `crush_location`, bucket named after the FQDN, host added under a different name), the monitor rejects `osd set-group` with EINVAL and maintenance fails with `Unable to set the osds on <host> to noout (rc=-22)`.

Worse, `noout` was set only after `cephadm host-maintenance enter` had already stopped all daemons on the host. The error was raised before the host was marked as being in maintenance, so the host was left with all daemons stopped while `ceph orch host maintenance exit` refused with `Host <host> is not in maintenance mode`.

## Changes

1. **mgr/cephadm: set noout before stopping daemons for maintenance**

   `noout` is now set right after the ok-to-stop checks, before the NVMe-oF gateways are disabled and the daemons are stopped. If anything afterwards fails, `noout` is unset again. A failure to set `noout` now leaves the host untouched.

2. **mgr/cephadm: look up CRUSH buckets when setting noout for maintenance**

   - The host buckets holding the host's OSDs are looked up in `osd_map_tree` instead of deriving the name from the hostname. A bucket is used only if all OSDs in its subtree, including nested buckets, belong to this host. OSDs not covered by such a bucket are flagged individually as `osd.N`.
   - Targets that already have `noout` (e.g. set by an admin) are skipped. The targets maintenance flagged are recorded in the host's inventory entry with their CRUSH ids and, for buckets, the OSDs below them. The rollback and exit unset exactly these.
   - On exit a bucket is only unset if it still has the same OSDs. Otherwise, or if the CRUSH map is not available, the flag is left set and reported in the exit output and the mgr log.
   - Hosts that entered maintenance with an older version (no record) are handled as before.

## Notes for reviewers

- The OSD check on exit is strict: moving OSDs between two buckets that were both flagged by the same maintenance also leaves both flags set and reports them.
- An OSD moved out of a flagged bucket during maintenance loses its `noout` protection at that moment. This is not new; exit reports it afterwards.
- If an admin sets noout during maintenance on a target that maintenance has already flagged (e.g. to keep it afterwards), it is removed on exit: the flag was already set, so the admin’s command changes nothing that could be detected.

73033.author: kotreshhr
73033.body:
Avoid flaky metrics cache hit assert in mirror status test.

keys entries by time window (int(monotonic() / ttl)), not by "N seconds
since the last fill", so two quick calls can still miss if they cross a window edge.

Example with ttl=3s: a call at monotonic 8.9 uses token 2 and caches the
result; a call 0.2s later at 9.1 uses token 3, misses, and reloads omap.
The mirror tick may have refreshed metrics_updated_at in between, so
assertEqual(res1, res2) fails even though the gap is well under the TTL.

73037.title: src/common/options: add descriptions to mgr messenger throttle options
73037.author: anthonyeleven
73037.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82055

Add a `desc` and a `long_desc` to the eight messenger throttle options in `src/common/options/mgr.yaml.in` that had neither: `mgr_client_bytes`, `mgr_client_messages`, `mgr_osd_bytes`, `mgr_osd_messages`, `mgr_mds_bytes`, `mgr_mds_messages`, `mgr_mon_bytes` and `mgr_mon_messages`. Without them, `ceph config help` and the generated option docs said nothing.

What the text says, and where it comes from:
- `DaemonServer` gives each peer type one byte throttle and one message throttle through `set_policy_throttlers`, so every connection of that type shares them. Client covers the ceph CLI and daemons that connect as clients, such as RGW.
- A connection takes 1 message and the message's size before reading it off the network, in `ProtocolV2::throttle_message` and `throttle_bytes`, and gives both back when the `Message` is destroyed or its op is unregistered.
- When `get_or_fail` fails, the connection stops reading and retries every `ms_client_throttle_retry_time_interval`, so the senders back up.
- The active Manager's `throttle-mgr_<type>_<bytes|messages>` perf counters show it: `val` at or near `max`, and `get_or_fail_fail` rising.
- A limit of 0 means no limit, and a single message larger than the byte limit is still read.
- The throttles are built in the `DaemonServer` constructor and nothing tracks these keys, so a change takes effect when a Manager next becomes active, after a restart or failover.
- Each byte and message pair links to the other, and the byte options link to `mgr_dispatch_throttle_bytes`, whose `long_desc` says to size it against them.

73044.title: osd/OSDMap: don't copy the map to compute a read balance score
73044.author: anthonyeleven
73044.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82062

`OSDMap::calc_read_balance_score` made a `deepish_copy_from` of the whole OSDMap and scored the copy, and `get_pgs_by_osd`, which the score calls for every pool, made another copy to map the pool's PGs. Nothing changes either copy: every call made on them is const, and `deepish_copy_from` doesn't copy the CRUSH map anyway. This uses the map itself in both and drops the OSDMap argument from `calc_rbs_fair` and `calc_rbs_size_optimal`, which only read it.

`OSDMap::dump` scores every replicated pool, so each dump copied the map twice per replicated pool, including every `pg_upmap_items` entry. The mgr dumps `osd_map` under the GIL whenever a Python module asks for it, and the mons do the same for `osd dump` and `osd pool ls detail`.

Measured with `osdmaptool --dump json` on one host, using the map of a Reef cluster with 1,018 OSDs, 134 replicated pools and 10,108 `pg_upmap_items` entries:

| Build | Dump time |
|---|---|
| main | 2.52 s |
| main with this change | 2.05 s |

The output is byte-identical. Each copy took about 1.7 ms, twice per replicated pool. Most of the remaining time is spent mapping every PG of every replicated pool for the scores. #73045 leaves the scores out of the mgr's `osd_map` getter. The prometheus module reads `osd_map` twice per collection, and on that cluster the mgr stops dispatching messages for about 7 s each time.

73045.title: mgr: leave read balance scores out of the osd_map getter
73045.author: anthonyeleven
73045.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82063

`OSDMap::dump` computes a read balance score for every replicated pool, and each score maps every PG of the pool. The mgr's `osd_map` getter dumps the map under the GIL whenever a Python module asks for it, so every module stalls while the scores are computed.

On a Reef 18.2.8 cluster with 1,018 OSDs, 134 replicated pools and 10,108 `pg_upmap_items` entries, `osdmaptool --dump json` of the same map takes 2.55 s with Reef and 0.09 s with Quincy, which has no read balance score. The prometheus module reads `osd_map` twice per collection there, and the mgr stops dispatching messages for about 7 s each time. rbd_support reads it twice a minute.

No module needs the scores from `osd_map`:
- The balancer, the only module that uses them, gets them from `get_osdmap().dump()`, which still includes them.
- `ceph osd dump` and `ceph osd pool ls detail` are served by the mons and are unchanged.
- The dashboard passes every pool field through `/api/pool`, including `read_balance`. Neither its UI nor its OpenAPI spec uses it, so the field just stops appearing there.

This adds a `with_read_balance` argument to `OSDMap::dump`, true by default, and to `dump_pool`. Only the `osd_map` getter passes false, so every other dump keeps the scores, including the mons' `osd dump` and `report`, `osdmaptool --dump`, ceph-dencoder, ceph-objectstore-tool, and the mgr's `OSDMap.dump()`, which the balancer's read modes read them from. #73044 makes the scores cheaper for the callers that still want them.

#72754 complements this. It has pg_autoscaler and the balancer read the `osd_map` getter instead of building their own dump with `OSDMap.dump()`, and this PR takes the scores out of that getter. With both, the balancer's `upmap` mode plans from the getter's dump, which doesn't need the scores. The `read` and `upmap-read` modes still plan from `osdmap.dump()`, which has them.

The new `DumpWithReadBalance` test in `TestOSDMap.cc` dumps the map with the default, with `with_read_balance` true and with it false. It checks that the replicated pool has a `read_balance` section in the first two dumps and not in the third, and that the EC pool never has one.

73046.title: mon/OSDMonitor: defer purged snaps scrub stamps to the next real map change
73046.author: anthonyeleven
73046.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82064

Each OSD scrubs its purged snaps every `osd_scrub_min_interval`, plus up to `osd_scrub_interval_randomize_ratio` of that, and reports when it last did in every beacon. `prepare_beacon` proposed a new OSDMap epoch every time the stamp moved, so a cluster made one epoch per OSD per scrub interval, about every 30 hours with the defaults.

Nothing reads the stamp: `osd_xinfo_t::last_purged_snaps_scrub` is only encoded, decoded and printed by `osd dump`. The epochs still cost what any epoch costs. Every OSD and client receives and applies the incremental, the mons store it and later trim it, and the mgr rebuilds `osd_map` for its Python modules, which takes seconds under the GIL on large clusters. On main each epoch also empties MgrMapCache.

Why we want this: on a Reef 18.2.8 cluster with 1,018 OSDs, days with no data movement and no OSD up or down changes have 790 to 920 epochs. Comparing 133 consecutive epochs field by field, everything that wasn't backfill was a single OSD's `last_purged_snaps_scrub` changing. 1,018 OSDs every 1.25 days on average is about 815 epochs a day, and on that cluster each one makes the mgr's Python modules stall for 2.5 s or more.

This records the stamp in the pending incremental without proposing, so it goes out with the next real map change. The OSD resends it in every beacon in case that incremental is lost, for example across a mon election.

Since Python 3.14 multiprocessing defaults to forkserver on Linux and spawns its helpers with sys.executable, so creating the ThreadPool in the cephadm module fails with BrokenPipeError and the module does not load.

Pass the byte string to PyConfig_SetBytesString() instead.

73053.title: rgw: fix aws:PrincipalType for request identities
73053.author: vxtls
73053.body:
RGW currently reports `aws:PrincipalType` as `User` for every request. A public bucket policy that explicitly denies anonymous reads under a restricted prefix therefore fails to match those requests.

Derive the condition value from the authenticated identity: `Anonymous` for anonymous requests, `Account` for account roots, `AssumedRole` for role sessions, and `User` for other identities accepted by authentication. Preserve the distinction between the authenticated OIDC caller of `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` and its issued role session, and retain user/account classification for `GetSessionToken`. Replace previous PrincipalType entries when rebuilding the environment.

Add unit and S3 endpoint regression coverage for identity mapping, repeated environment construction, explicit Deny, negative conditions, IfExists, access outside the restricted prefix, signed/presigned requests, invalid credentials, IAM accounts and STS credentials. Update the bucket policy documentation.

Reproduction: allow public `s3:GetObject` on a bucket, then add an explicit Deny for `deleted/*` conditioned on `aws:PrincipalType` being `Anonymous`. An unsigned GET under that prefix should return 403, while a signed user GET and public reads outside that prefix should remain allowed.

Validation: build succeeded; all 68 IAM policy unit tests passed, including 21 PrincipalType regression tests.
S3/STS integration tests have not been run.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82061

73066.title: mds: do not ship null dentries with an exported dirfrag
73066.author: xiubli
73066.body:
A dirfrag keeps a null dentry for every name unlinked from it, and an export ships all of them. When a deleted tree spread by `ceph.dir.pin.distributed` empties, every MDS hands its subtrees back to the parent's MDS through `export_empty_import()`, and that MDS's cache jumps by millions of dentries (rank 0 went from 1.9M to 9.4M dentries in about a minute at the end of IO500 mdtest-easy-delete with 7 active MDS). An export pin moved after a delete ships them too, and the importer hands the empty dirfrag straight back with all of them.

This change:
- keeps an emptied dirfrag in `export_empty_import()` while it is dirty; the rmdir that usually follows drops the null dentries without a commit;
- drops the clean, unreferenced null dentries of each dirfrag in `encode_export_dir()`, as `trim_dentry()` would;
- drops them in batches before the export when a dirfrag has more than `mds_null_dentry_drop_batch` (new option, default 10000), letting go of `mds_lock` between batches.

Moving the export pin of a directory with 1000000 committed null dentries between 2 active MDS, while a create/unlink loop runs on each; ops and latency in the 120 s after the move, 2 runs each:

|                    | main        | this change |
|--------------------|-------------|-------------|
| ops                | 567k / 558k | 818k / 847k |
| p50 (us)           | 103 / 102   | 111 / 108   |
| p99 (us)           | 1176 / 1166 | 1175 / 1110 |
| p99.9 (ms)         | 51 / 52     | 10.5 / 9.2  |
| p99.99 (ms)        | 372 / 359   | 224 / 239   |
| max (s)            | 13.3 / 10.4 | 5.1 / 2.6   |
| longest export (s) | 11.3 / 10.4 | 2.7 / 1.0   |
| dentries exported  | 2.0M / 2.0M | 5 / 1       |

Reproducer and more numbers in the tracker.

Tested with vstart_runner: test_exports, test_strays, test_fragment, test_multimds_misc, test_snapshots, test_failover, test_forward_scrub, test_scrub_checks, test_journal_repair, test_dump_tree, test_misc; no new failures compared to main.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82078

73067.title: debian: build with ninja
73067.author: tchaikov
73067.body:
Since #66066 (0665ed1391a), every RGW executable and library statically links `librgw_lancedb.a` through `rgw_common`. All of these links wait for the cargo build and then start together. With Ubuntu's default LTO and `make -jN`, nothing limits how many run at once, so the jammy and noble package builds run out of memory. In ceph-dev-pipeline build 10219, 31 LTO links were running on a host with 255 GiB of RAM when the OOM killer killed `ld`. See https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82052.

This PR builds the Debian packages with `cmake+ninja`, so the job pools in `LimitJobs`, which are sized by the host's memory, limit the links too. With LTO enabled, each link is budgeted 6000 MiB instead of 4500 MiB. The RGW targets and `ceph-osd` are already in the heavy link pool, which has half as many jobs, so they get about 12000 MiB each. On a host with 255 GiB of RAM, that allows 43 regular and 21 heavy links at once.

Ninja has no jobserver, though, and without one `-flto=auto` runs an LTRANS job per CPU thread in every link. The first noble build with Ninja (build 10226) still ran out of memory: 21 heavy links were running 1485 LTRANS jobs between them, about 12.4 GiB per link. So the last commit passes `-flto=N` to the linker, where N is the number of CPU threads divided by the size of the heavy link pool. On a 192-thread builder, N is 9.

Peak PSS of each link's whole process tree, from two full local builds (`-g -O2 -flto=auto -ffat-lto-objects`, 32 threads, 3 heavy link jobs, so N = 10):

| target | link pool | `-flto=auto` | LTRANS jobs | `-flto=10` | LTRANS jobs |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `crimson-osd` | heavy | 8.8 GiB | 29 | 5.5 GiB | 0 (peak in WPA) |
| `radosgw` | heavy | 8.0 GiB | 32 | 5.6 GiB | 9 |
| `denc-mod-rgw.so` | heavy | 7.4 GiB | 29 | 5.5 GiB | 9 |
| `radosgw-admin` | heavy | 7.2 GiB | 26 | 5.2 GiB | 8 |
| `librgw.so` | heavy | 7.2 GiB | 28 | 5.8 GiB | 9 |
| `ceph-osd` | heavy | 4.4 GiB | 27 | 2.3 GiB | 9 |
| **whole build** | | **2697 s** | | **2708 s** | |

With the cap, the heaviest link fits in the 6000 MiB budget, and 21 heavy links would need about 126 GiB. Each LTRANS job costs about 120 MiB, so without the cap a link grows with the size of the host. All 76 targets that link `librgw_lancedb.a` are in the heavy pool, so the RGW links don't need a pool of their own.

RGW should still link `rgw_lancedb` only into the targets that serve s3vectors. This PR doesn't change that. It only keeps the package build within the host's memory when many links become ready at once.

We could disable LTO instead, but I'd rather keep the performance it gives us.

The OOMs in #40097 happened before Ninja had these job pools, which were added in 897fd990bfc.

73072.title: crimson/os/seastore: prevent duplicate journal batch flushes
73072.author: myoungwon
73072.body:
When the journal I/O depth reaches FULL, RecordSubmitter waits for an outstanding I/O to complete before flushing the pending batch.

When an outstanding I/O completes, decrement_io_with_flush() is called to release an I/O slot and flush the pending batch if RecordSubmitter was FULL.
In decrement_io_with_flush(), flush_current_batch() is called before wait_unfull_flush_promise is resolved and reset. Note that flushing the batch may trigger another I/O completion callback, re-entering decrement_io_with_flush() before the promise is reset.

Since wait_unfull_flush_promise is still present, the reentrant call attempts to flush the current batch again, even though the first flush has already submitted its records and replaced the current batch with an empty one.

This can result in encode_records() being called with an empty record group, causing the metadata length assertion to fail:

ceph_assert(bl.length() == record_group.size.get_raw_mdlength());

To prevent this, move wait_unfull_flush_promise to a local variable and reset the optional before calling flush_current_batch().


Signed-off-by: Myoungwon Oh <ohmyoungwon@gmail.com>

73076.author: anthonyeleven

When `ceph orch host maintenance enter` fails its ok-to-stop checks, the error always ends with `Note: Warnings can be bypassed with the --force flag`. 73079.title: rgw/sts: select JWKS keys by token kid before signature verification
73079.author: next0262
73079.body:
Tracker: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82089 (Enhancement)

`WebTokenEngine::validate_signature()` tries the provider's JWKS keys in order until one verifies the JWT. It reads each JWK's `kid` for logging but does not use the token's `kid` to select the verification key.

Use the token's `kid` to select matching keys before verification. This follows the key-selection model described in [OIDC Core §10.1.1](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html#RotateSigKeys), where old and new signing keys can coexist during rotation. All eligible signing keys sharing the matching identifier are tried. If none verifies the token, validation fails. The existing all-key fallback is retained when the token has no `kid` or the JWKS has no eligible signing key with a matching identifier.

The helper selects candidates in one traversal of the parsed JWKS. The existing verification loop uses those objects directly, without serializing and reparsing individual keys. The OIDC documentation describes matching-key validation and the fallback behavior.

Testing: sixteen key-selection unit tests passed locally on Ubuntu 24.04 ARM64 / GCC 13.3 using a separate CMake harness with existing Ceph common, Boost and GoogleTest libraries. Also compiled `rgw_rest_sts.cc` to an object file. Full RGW linking and STS integration tests have not been run locally. RGW teuthology QA is pending review.


A local RS256/RSA-2048 microbenchmark with eight signing keys and the matching key last reduced verification attempts from eight to one: bare n/e took 536 → 172 µs, and x5c took 4.11 → 1.03 ms. These are medians of seven batches of 200 validations in an ARM64 VM, including JWT/JWKS parsing but excluding network, thumbprint checks and logging; they are not end-to-end STS timings. [Method, build details, source and full results](https://github.com/next0262/ceph/tree/212b17082cf8bc396b09f6b4e6989b7f1f8c8f4b/benchmarks/rgw-sts-kid).

73081.title: mon/OSDMonitor: unstick osdmap trim after PG merge
73081.author: anthonyeleven
73081.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82094

#48212 made `LastEpochClean::Lec::report` truncate `epoch_by_pg` to the pool's new `pg_num`, but the cached `floor` is kept. The floor is recomputed only when the reporting PG's previous value equals it, so when the PG that held the floor was merged away nothing moves it again, and osdmap trimming stops until the leader mon restarts. This takes the floor from the remaining PGs when the list shrinks. It also brings `next_missing` back inside the list, so that PGs added by a later split are waited for instead of being counted as already reported.

Why we want this: on a Reef 18.2.8 cluster with 30 CephFS file systems, after seven pools were shrunk the mons kept about 52,600 osdmaps for almost nine days. During that time a layout change through a kernel mount that had been idle for months made the mon send that client about 47,500 maps, roughly 30 GB. While the mon built and queued them it stopped answering its other sessions for about 20 seconds. The MDS daemons whose sessions were on that mon passed `mds_beacon_grace`, and 7 file systems failed over. The stuck trim is why the backlog was that large.

Testing:
- New `unittest_mon_last_epoch_clean`: both tests pass with the change, and both fail without it, 10 instead of 60 for the merged floor and 21 instead of 0 for the split that follows a merge.

73082.title: librbd: relax exclusive lock requirement for image-meta set/rm
73082.author: idryomov

73083.title: mds: bound should_split_fast() without scanning the null dentries
73083.author: xiubli
73083.body:
While a split of a dirfrag is pending, every hit_dir() on it calls should_split_fast().  When the dirfrag holds more than the fast limit (mds_bal_split_size * mds_bal_fragment_fast_factor) of linked and null dentries together but no more than that in its fragstat, it counts the linked dentries one by one, under mds_lock.

A big directory that is being emptied gets there: when its dirfrags shrink below mds_bal_merge_size they merge into one that still holds some thousand files and every null dentry left by the unlinks.  In an IO500 mdtest-hard-delete with 16 tasks the merged dirfrag had 12831 files, so a split was queued, and 1.93 million null dentries.  Each lookup and unlink in the directory then held mds_lock for about 270 ms to scan them; the finisher thread got the lock only between two of them, so journal completions waited up to 62 seconds and the client requests behind them piled up: the slowest tasks finished 100 to 150 seconds after the others.

Return false straight away while the dirfrag is already being split or merged: can_fragment() refuses another fragment operation until that one is done.  That is also the worst case, since the freeze waits for every auth pin on the dirfrag to drop, and each request dropping one went through the scan.  Another run caught the merged dirfrag in that state with 2627 nested auth pins, each completion taking 260 ms.

Otherwise, a dentry whose projected linkage differs from its current one is xlocked, and so auth pinned, by the request changing it, and that pin counts in dir_auth_pins.  The effective size is therefore within dir_auth_pins of the linked dentries; only scan when the fast limit lies in that range.  Should a projected linkage ever come without a pin, the fast split is only delayed until the normal one.

73084.title: mds: optionally give no writeable range until the client asks for one
73084.author: xiubli
73084.body:
An open with `CEPH_FILE_MODE_WR` gives the client a writeable range right away: `Server::handle_client_open()` calls `check_inode_max_size()`, which takes the filelock wrlock (possibly revoking other clients' file caps) and journals an inode update with the new `client_ranges`. When the client releases Fw on close, the range drops to 0, which is another journaled update. Many applications open read-write and never write; mdtest did that in its read phase until hpc/ior#557.

This PR adds `mds_defer_open_client_range` (default **off**). With it, an open for write still issues the caps but no range, and a client gets a range only when its cap message asks for a max_size above the range it has. Only the client asking gets a new range: `check_inode_max_size()` no longer hands ranges to every Fw holder on the inode. `_do_cap_update()` no longer grows max_size ahead of the writes for a client without a range. Otherwise, the journaled update would just move from the open to the close. The kernel client and libcephfs already wait for the MDS before writing past max_size and resend the request after a reconnect or a cap import, so no client change is needed.

The first commit is a separate fix found while measuring this: since 52918175f01, `issue_new_caps()` flushes the journal when the opener wants caps whose lock is busy, and that includes the rdlocks the open request holds itself. So every write-mode open of an existing file by name, as the kernel client sends it, forced a journal flush.

### Measurements

Setup:
- One bare-metal host, 3 NVMe OSDs, 1 MDS with a 32 GiB cache, pinned to 4 cores.
- Kernel client: the Fedora 7.2.9 in-tree module.
- tuned `latency-performance`.
- Fresh cluster per run; 3 runs per arm, interleaved; numbers are medians.

| arm | build | option |
|---|---|---|
| base | main + the fix for [82083](https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82083) | n/a |
| off | this PR + the fix for 82083 | `mds_defer_open_client_range=false` |
| on | this PR + the fix for 82083 | `mds_defer_open_client_range=true` |

All arms carry the fix for tracker 82083 (`should_split_fast()` scanning every null dentry under mds_lock), which is a separate PR. Without it, hard-delete can stall for tens of seconds while `should_split_fast()` rescans about 1.9M null dentries of a merged dirfrag, and those stalls hide the effect of this change.

#### IO500 (16 processes, standard mode; score, median [min–max] of 3)

| mdtest-easy-write | 6.720 | 6.790 | 6.833 |

73090.title: mds: compute ephemeral split floor before requeuing pins
73090.author: vshankar
73090.body:
When max_mds changes, MDCache::handle_mdsmap() requeues every ephemerally pinned directory before recomputing the minimum split depth (export_ephemeral_dist_frag_bits) for the new max_mds. queue_export_pin() therefore checks a rank's dirfrags against the old depth and only queues the directory if one of them now hashes to another rank. On ranks where none does, the dirfrags are never split to the new depth, leaving part of a distributed pinned directory coarsely fragmented after max_mds is increased and limiting how evenly it is spread across the ranks.

Compute the split depth before requeuing.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82102
