73204.title: blk/spdk: restrict PCI device selection to PCIe transports
73204.author: next0262
73204.body:
https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82234

Replaces #63527, which was automatically closed as stale and cannot currently be reopened.

`spdk_pci_addr_parse()` accepts some IPv4 addresses, including `127.0.0.1`. When used with a TCP target, this sets `local_pci_device` and causes `spdk_nvme_probe()` to receive `NULL` instead of the TCP transport ID. OSD startup then fails to find the target.

Only parse PCI addresses for PCIe transports. The documented TCP example also needs `adrfam:IPv4`.

The original reproducer used three local SPDK NVMe-oF TCP targets and failed during OSD mkfs before the fix. OSD startup succeeded with the fix in the original 2025 run.

```
../src/vstart.sh --debug --new -x --localhost --bluestore \
--bluestore-spdk "trtype:tcp adrfam:IPv4 traddr:127.0.0.1 trsvcid:4420 subnqn:nqn.2019-02.io.spdk:cnode0,\
trtype:tcp adrfam:IPv4 traddr:127.0.0.1 trsvcid:4420 subnqn:nqn.2019-02.io.spdk:cnode1,\
trtype:tcp adrfam:IPv4 traddr:127.0.0.1 trsvcid:4420 subnqn:nqn.2019-02.io.spdk:cnode2"
```

Updated against current main, retaining the SPDK version guards and the corrected environment initialization order.

For this update, a standalone C++ check used the bundled SPDK address parser and the selection block extracted from NVMEDevice.cc. Eight transport/address cases passed for both the old and new SPDK option-name branches. The same check fails with the unpatched code. This is a focused check with stubbed environment/probe interfaces; a full Ceph/SPDK build and a fresh OSD startup test have not been run.

73205.title: rgw: evaluate If-Match before If-Modified-Since on GET
73205.author: RaminNietzsche
73205.body:
## Summary

RFC 9110 [13.2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-13.2.2) evaluates `If-Match` before `If-Modified-Since`. RGW checked date preconditions first in `Object::Read::prepare`, so GetObject with a failing `If-Match` and a future `If-Modified-Since` was answered **304** instead of **412**.

- Swap the entity-tag and date precondition blocks in the RADOS and POSIX read prepare paths. Guards that skip `If-Modified-Since` when `If-None-Match` is present (and `If-Unmodified-Since` when `If-Match` is present) are unchanged.
- s3-tests: `test_get_object_ifmatch_failed_with_ifmodifiedsince` (412) and `test_get_object_ifmatch_good_with_ifmodifiedsince_future` (304 when ETag matches).

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82233  
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/19965

Probe script (case `T4 If-Match fails + If-Modified-Since future`): https://gist.github.com/RaminNietzsche/818ad8dd6b8d8093560183cd09d2b169

## Testing

On a single-host vstart cluster built from this branch (tree at `5ab2b0ddb70` + this commit):

| Request | main | this branch |
|---------|------|-------------|
| `If-Match: "ABCORZ"` + `If-Modified-Since: 2100-01-01` | 304 | 412 PreconditionFailed |
| `If-Match: <etag>` + `If-Modified-Since: 2100-01-01` | (304) | 304 |

s3-tests: `-k "test_get_object_ifmatch_failed_with_ifmodifiedsince or test_get_object_ifmatch_good_with_ifmodifiedsince_future"` — 2 passed.

73207.title: qa: tolerate concurrent distro logrotate run
73207.author: djgalloway
73207.body:
The ceph task's log rotater runs `logrotate /etc/logrotate.d/ceph-test.conf` every 30 seconds on every host. The distro's own daily `logrotate.service` includes `/etc/logrotate.d` too, so when it runs during a job it rotates and compresses the same ceph logs under the default state file. If the task's run starts while that lock is held, logrotate exits 3 with `state file /var/lib/logrotate/logrotate.status is already locked`. The rotater only tolerated the "renaming temp state file" message, so the greenlet died and the error was re-raised from `Rotater.end()` at teardown, failing jobs whose tests had passed.

Two triggers were seen on trial nodes:
- the 00:00 UTC daily run (all the Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 failures cluster between 00:00:11 and 00:01:41)
- a `Persistent=true` catch-up run on Rocky 10.2 hosts, whose image ships a stale `/var/lib/systemd/timers/stamp-logrotate.timer` (dated 2026-08-19), so the timer fires 3–60 minutes after boot, inside the first job after a reimage. On trial192 the system run held the lock for 71 seconds.

Only configs with a `log-rotate` key (fs/bugs clusters and `qa/clusters/2-node-mgr.yaml`, which rados/mgr symlinks) are exposed. 15 jobs in 676 runs between Oct 15 and Oct 28 hit this.

Skip the round when the lock is held; the system run rotates the same files, so nothing is lost. Exit code and message verified as root on a Rocky 10.2 trial node (logrotate 3.22.0).

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82197

73208.title: [WIP][agent] mgr/cephadm: check hosts in parallel when a spec adds several hosts
73208.author: rkachach
73208.body:
## Problem

Adding hosts with a single spec file (`ceph orch apply -i hosts.yaml`) runs `cephadm check-host` on each host **one after the other**, and the orchestrator module's command thread waits for each one. On a 300-host scale test this apply took **~25 minutes**. Because a mgr module runs its commands one at a time on a single thread, every other `ceph orch` command waited behind it for the whole duration: `ceph orch ls` took 24m48s to return.

`dump_ops_in_flight` on the active mgr showed exactly this: the `orch apply` was running (`flag_point: orchestrator`, age 909s), and every other orch command was queued behind it (`flag_point: queued for module`), with their ages increasing:

| command | age | flag_point |
|---|---|---|
| `orch apply` | 909s | orchestrator |
| `orch host ls` | 898s | queued for module |
| `orch ls` | 890s | queued for module |
| `orch ls` | 204s | queued for module |
| `orch apply` | 69s | queued for module |

`py-spy` showed the thread running the apply waiting on a single host's check:

    _apply (cephadm/module.py) -> _add_host -> _check_valid_addr -> wait_async -> get_result

A slow or unreachable host made it worse: it held up every host after it, for up to `default_cephadm_command_timeout` (900s).

## Change

When the specs passed to `apply()` add **more than one host**:

1. **Resolve** each host's address synchronously, as today.
2. **Check** all of them **concurrently** on cephadm's event loop: at most `mgr/cephadm/max_parallel_host_checks` (default **10**) at a time, each bounded by the usual per-host timeout.
3. **Add** the hosts **one by one, in the original order**, as today. Each `_add_host()` receives its precomputed check result (the resolved address or the error) instead of running the check again.

Only the checks run concurrently. Everything that changes cluster state (inventory, crush buckets, offline hosts, sudo hardening, health checks) stays sequential and unchanged.

The batch has no overall timeout: each check is already bounded by its own `asyncio.wait_for()`, so a large batch is never cut short. The code uses `event_loop.get_result(..., None)` rather than `wait_async()`, because `wait_async()` would apply `default_cephadm_command_timeout` to the whole batch.

### Behaviour kept as before
- Results are returned in spec order, with the same messages.
- `continue_on_error` behaves the same. Without it, the apply stops at the first failing host, in spec order.
- Check failures, DNS failures and timeouts produce the same errors, including the `CEPHADM_HOST_TIMEOUT_ERROR` health warning.
- Re-adding a host with a new address still resets the cached SSH connection before it's checked, and again if the check fails.
- **Single-host specs and `ceph orch host add` don't change**: they never take the parallel path.
- **Hostnames listed more than once** and **invalid specs** are left out of the parallel checks and checked one by one, as before.

### New module option
| option | type | default | min |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mgr/cephadm/max_parallel_host_checks` | int | 10 | 1 |

It sets how many `check-host` calls run at the same time during a bulk host add. A limit is needed so we don't open hundreds of SSH sessions at once. Making it configurable lets admins lower it in environments where many concurrent new SSH connections are a problem, for example hosts reached through a jump host, whose sshd `MaxStartups` (default `10:30:100`) starts dropping connections beyond 10.

## Commits

1. **mgr/cephadm: split host address resolution from check-host.** Pure refactor: `_check_valid_addr()` is split into `_resolve_host_addr()` and an async `_check_host()`. No behaviour change.
2. **mgr/cephadm: check hosts in parallel when a spec adds several hosts.** The change described above, plus the new option.
3. **mgr/cephadm: fix "orch apply --no-overwrite" with hosts not yet added.** An independent, pre-existing bug found by the new tests. With `--n

73210.title: Rgw objects migration headers
73210.author: arttor
73210.body:
## Summary
Issue: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/80329.

The PR adds a new system query param to RGW, `rgwx-mtime`, similar to the
existing `rgwx-version-id`. The goal is to help users migrate their S3 data
into Ceph. Keeping the original object timestamp is important for lifecycle
rules, which work on object age.

The second commit adds RGW regression tests for the new and the existing
system params.

Notes on the implementation:
- Works on PutObject and CompleteMultipartUpload, for system users only.
- The format is `<secs>[.<fraction>]`, the same as the `Rgwx-Mtime` response
  header. A malformed value returns InvalidArgument.
- `parse_rgwx_mtime` moved from `rgw_rest_client.cc` to `rgw_common` and is
  now stricter, so requests and sync responses share one parser.
- For multipart, the mtime is passed on the MultipartUpload object, like
  object lock and checksum settings. No SAL interface or on-disk change.
- Object lock default retention counts from this mtime, the same as
  lifecycle. An explicit retain-until date still wins.
- Multisite (raised on the tracker): sync only applies a remote object if its
  mtime is newer, so an object with an old mtime loses to newer copies.
  cc @mheler 

## Testing
Tested on a vstart cluster: the new workunit, lifecycle expiration and object
lock with old mtimes, and the s3-tests multipart, versioning, object_lock and
lifecycle tests.

73213.title: doc/rados: explain which daemons use the cluster network
73213.author: anthonyeleven
73213.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/58687

The tracker asks whether Monitors and MDSes also use the cluster network to reach OSDs. The diagram in the Network Configuration Reference shows only OSDs on it, and that is correct: `cluster_network` applies only to the osd service, and only ceph-osd picks a cluster address. The diagram's caption, though, says the cluster network offloads heartbeat traffic from the public network. OSDs send heartbeats over both networks, and a ping counts as answered only when replies arrive on both, so heartbeats are not offloaded.

- The caption now says the cluster network is optional and carries OSD replication and recovery traffic.
- A new paragraph after the diagram says which daemons use the cluster network, that OSD heartbeats must succeed on both networks, and that a cluster network failure while the public network still works can make OSDs flap.

73214.title: rgw/s3: honor object lock fields in POST object and validate CopyObject
73214.author: jzhu116-bloomberg
73214.body:
On a bucket with object lock enabled, POST object (browser-based upload) ignores the `x-amz-object-lock-mode`, `x-amz-object-lock-retain-until-date` and `x-amz-object-lock-legal-hold` form fields. The object is stored with only the bucket's default retention, or with no protection at all if the bucket has no default, and the request still returns 204. A client that asks for a retention period or a legal hold gets an object with no or wrong protection silently.

AWS does not document object lock fields for POST object, however, RGW accepts the same values as headers on PutObject, CopyObject and CreateMultipartUpload. This PR changes the POST object behavior to match with what PutObject, CopyObject and CreateMultipartUpload do.

This PR moves the object lock header parsing for PutObject, CopyObject, CreateMultipartUpload and POST object into a shared helper. CopyObject then gets the same InvalidRequest check as PutObject and CreateMultipartUpload when copying to an unlocked bucket with object lock headers.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82248
Signed-off-by: Jane Zhu [jzhu116@bloomberg.net](mailto:jzhu116@bloomberg.net)

73215.title: rgw/iam: emit ResponseMetadata after the Result element
73215.author: BenoitKnecht
73215.body:
`GetRole`, `GetRolePolicy`, `ListRolePolicies`,
`ListAttachedRolePolicies` and `GetAccountSummary` wrote `<ResponseMetadata>` before `<XResult>` inside the `<XResponse>` element. AWS always emits the result first, and SDKs with generated `awsQuery` deserializers (e.g. the Rust `aws-sdk-iam`) require the first child of `<XResponse>` to be `<XResult>`, so these calls fail with:

```
invalid result, expected GetRoleResult got StartEl { ... "ResponseMetadata" ... }
```

`botocore` tolerates either order, which is why the AWS CLI is unaffected.

Move `ResponseMetadata` after the Result section, matching the other IAM handlers.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82250

73216.title: rgw: add radosgw-admin bucket check olh-list
73216.author: k-keshava
73216.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82247

Problem

Racing PUT and DELETE requests on null versions (https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/81603) corrupt the bucket index of versioning-suspended buckets:

- versioned list entries (<key>\0v<epoch>\0i<instance>) that belong to no instance entry, many still flagged CURRENT, so ListObjectVersions reports several versions with IsLatest=true;
- the version marker (the plain <key> entry) overwritten by a suggested update from a bucket listing, or deleted;
- in some cases, the instance entry of the version the OLH points to is missing.

PR #72554 stops new corruption, but no existing command repairs buckets that are already affected. On a vstart cluster, none of these did:

- "bucket check" and "bucket check --fix" only recalculate stats.
- "bucket check --check-objects --fix" sends suggested updates for null versions that target the plain key, overwriting the marker again.
- "bucket check olh --fix" only handles OLH entries with exists=false and pending_removal=true.
- "bucket check unlinked --fix" only handles instance entries with versioned_epoch=0 that are not listable.
- "bucket reshard" copies the corrupted entries to the new shards.
- "object unlink" removes the _:<instance>_<name> key, not list entries.
- S3 DeleteObject with VersionId=null removes one list entry and deletes the marker, leaving the rest.

Changes

New command "radosgw-admin bucket check olh-list [--fix] [--dump-keys]", modelled on "bucket check olh". For each object in a versioned bucket it checks that:

1. Every versioned list entry belongs to an instance entry, as given by that entry's versioned_epoch. Other entries are orphaned and removed.
2. Only the version the OLH points to is CURRENT, in both its list and instance entries. If the OLH does not exist, none are.
3. While the OLH exists, the plain <key> entry is a version marker. An overwritten or missing marker is restored.
4. If the instance entry of the version the OLH points to is missing, the version is still identified: link_olh sets a version's versioned_epoch to the OLH epoch when it becomes current, so the list entry with that epoch is it, and the instance entry is restored from it. If no list entry matches, the object is reported as unresolved and that version's list entries are left alone.

Commits:

- cls/rgw: bucket_check_olh_list (read-only, returns a report) and bucket_fix_olh_list (re-checks and repairs in the same cls call, so a repair is serialized with normal index operations on that shard). An object with a pending index op, or an OLH log entry newer than rgw_pending_bucket_index_op_expiration, is reported as busy and left alone. Older ones are treated as abandoned, so a crashed RGW cannot block repairs forever.
- rgw: the radosgw-admin command. It walks each shard's OLH entries in parallel coroutines (--max-concurrent-ios) and refuses unversioned buckets and non-Normal index layouts. It counts busy and unresolved objects, and fails with a clear error on OSDs without the new cls methods. --dump-keys prints orphaned_list_entries, wrong_current_flags, bad_version_marker, restored_instance and unresolved per object. After --fix it tells users to run "bucket check --fix" to recalculate the stats. Also updates the usage text (help.t), the man page and PendingReleaseNotes.
- test/cls_rgw: 6 tests: healthy objects, orphaned entries plus a wrong CURRENT flag plus an overwritten marker, a missing marker, busy objects, restoring a missing instance entry (a later null PUT then replaces it cleanly), and unresolved objects.
- qa/rgw: test_rgw_bucket_check.py injects orphaned entries and overwritten markers with "radosgw-admin bi put" and checks that olh-list finds and fixes them.

Testing

On a vstart cluster (Ubuntu 24.04 arm64), on this branch rebased onto main at c57633a64a2. There was one rebase conflict: upstream moved the OPT enum into radosgw-admin.h, so BUCKET_CHECK_OLH_LIST was added there.

- Build: cls_rgw, radosgw-admin, the vstart daemons

73220.title: mds: do not merge a small dirfrag that is still hot
73220.author: xiubli
73220.body:
`MDBalancer::maybe_fragment()` splits a dirfrag when it is hot (`pop_me` above `mds_bal_split_rd/wr`), whatever its size, and merges a dirfrag when it is small (`CDir::should_merge()`, below `mds_bal_merge_size`), whatever its load. A small directory that many clients use, such as a shared `__pycache__` or a lock or publish directory, is split because it is hot, its frags are merged because they are small, the merged frag is hot again and is split again, and so on.

Every split and merge freezes the dirfrags. Each cycle, requests in the directory wait for the freeze ("failed to authpin, dir is being fragmented"), and for a few seconds after it the MDS serves a fraction of its normal rate.

A small hot directory is then split at most once, and stays that way until it cools down, when it is merged as before.

### Results

cephfs-mdbench python-env: clients open and read a few dozen shared `.pyc` names in one directory, and publish them by writing a temp file and renaming it onto the name. Default balancer options.

- vstart, 1 or 2 active MDSs, each pinned to 4 cores (2x Xeon 8180M), with the clients on the other NUMA node;
- a memstore OSD, so that the MDS is the bottleneck;
- a fresh cluster per run, 3 runs per build, interleaved, 20 s per client count;
- ops/s is the op count divided by the step length, and latencies are in ms, pooled over the runs;
- "base" is the merge-base, 932a319280e, with the fixes for [tracker 82218](https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82218) ([PR](https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/XXXXX)) and [tracker 79321](https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/79321). python-env otherwise hits the 79321 assert, and the 5 s stalls of 82218 hit both builds at random and hide this issue at low client counts. "fix" adds this PR.

Over a run, the publish directory is split 8 times and merged 6-7 times on base, and split twice and never merged with the fix.

1 active MDS:

| clients | build | ops/s per run | p50 | p90 | p95 | p99 | p99.9 | p99.99 | max |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

73225.title: rgw: restrict SSE-KMS key ids to their tenant or bucket owner
73225.author: vupn0712
73225.body:
## Summary

https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82278

For SSE-KMS, RGW takes the key id straight from the client's
`x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id` header (or the bucket's
`PutBucketEncryption` default) and hands it to whichever KMS backend is
configured, without checking that the key actually belongs to the
caller's tenant or to the bucket owner.

That matters because RGW talks to the KMS backend under one shared,
RGW-wide credential -- a single Vault token, or a single Keystone user
for Barbican -- not the caller's own identity. So if tenant A knows (or
guesses) a key id that belongs to tenant B, nothing stops them from
using it to encrypt their own objects. B's key policy never gets
consulted, because the request RGW sends doesn't carry A's identity at
all.

This adds an off-by-default option, `rgw_crypt_s3_kms_key_scope`
(`none`/`tenant`/`owner`), that makes RGW require the key id to start
with an owner prefix before it'll use it -- the check runs inside RGW,
in `rgw_s3_prepare_encrypt()`, before any KMS backend is contacted, and
also in `RGWPutBucketEncryption::execute()` so a bad default key id gets
rejected when it's set, not just at first use. It covers every write
path (PUT, POST, multipart init, copy destination) since they all go
through the same code before encrypting.

For `owner` scope, tenant and user id get joined with the same
separator you configure (e.g. `tenant.user`) rather than Ceph's usual
`tenant$user` notation, because `$` turns out to be one of several
characters Vault's transit engine rejects in a key name (along with
`/`, `:`, `,`, `~`, and `+` -- only `.`, `-`, and `_` actually work, and
`-` is a bad choice if your key ids are UUIDs since the matching logic
would grab the UUID's own dashes instead of the real boundary).

None of this touches decryption or SSE-S3 -- an object's stored key id
is never re-validated after it's written, and SSE-S3 has its own,
separate key-management path entirely.

### Backend compatibility

I didn't want to just assume this works the same everywhere, so I
actually checked each backend:

- **Vault** -- works. Verified end to end on a real single-node Ceph
  cluster against a real Vault 1.15.6 transit backend (compat=0), with
  two tenants: using your own (correctly prefixed) key works and
  decrypts fine, using the other tenant's key gets 403 AccessDenied, and
  a key id with no recognizable prefix gets rejected too.
- **KMIP** -- also works, though for a less obvious reason: RGW's KMIP
  client does a LOCATE by name before it ever fetches a key, which only
  works if whoever created the key already gave it a real, chosen name
  (see the key-creation example already in `doc/radosgw/kmip.rst`).
  Verified the same two-tenant test against a real PyKMIP 0.10.0 server,
  same outcome as Vault.
- **Barbican** -- doesn't work. Barbican assigns its own UUID to every
  secret when it's created and gives you no way to prefix it yourself,
  so turning this option on with `rgw_crypt_s3_kms_backend = barbican`
  would just deny every SSE-KMS request. Noted with warnings in
  `rgw.yaml.in` and `doc/radosgw/barbican.rst`, which also gets into why
  Barbican needs a different fix altogether: RGW authenticates to it as
  one shared Keystone user for every tenant, so Barbican's own
  per-secret ACLs can't tell RGW's tenants apart either.

## Test plan

- [x] Unit tests in `src/test/rgw/test_rgw_kms.cc` for the prefix-matching
      logic itself (disabled by default, matching prefix, mismatched
      prefix, missing separator, empty expected owner).
- [x] Built the full RPM set and deployed it to a real Ceph cluster;
      manually tested against a real Vault 1.15.6 server and a real
      PyKMIP 0.10.0 server (details above).
- [ ] Haven't submitted an s3-tests case for the cross-tenant-key
      rejection yet.

73226.title: mgr/tests: give the cephfs mock real exception classes
73226.author: tchaikov
73226.body:
Starting with pytest 9.2, monkeypatch.setattr() looks up the value to restore in the target's `__dict__` (pytest-dev/pytest#10644). But Mock stores the attributes it creates on first access in `_mock_children`, not in `__dict__`. So when test_mocked_fs_path_resolver finishes, undo() finds nothing to restore and deletes cephfs.ObjectNotFound, and Mock won't recreate an attribute once it has been deleted. If `test_caching_fs_path_resolver` runs later on the same xdist worker, its `monkeypatch` fails with:
```
  AttributeError: 'Mock' object at cephfs has no attribute 'ObjectNotFound'
```
The smb tests patched these attributes only because the mocked cephfs module had no exception classes that could go in an except clause. Mock the cephfs exceptions the same way the rados ones are mocked, and remove the monkeypatch calls.

73232.title: crush,osd: do not bias upmap remaps towards position 0 (primary / EC shard 0)
73232.author: FredNass
73232.body:
The upmap balancer moves the shard at position 0 (the primary, shard 0 on EC pools) much more often than any other shard. When the balancer has to fill a CRUSH bucket from other buckets, the OSDs of that bucket end up with several times the average number of primaries, even though PG counts look perfectly balanced. In production we saw this on a Reef EC 6+2 pool: ~50 primaries per OSD on two hosts against a pool mean of 10, 94% of them placed by `pg_upmap_items`.

**Cause:** two scans in the upmap code always start at position 0 and keep the first candidate:
- `CrushWrapper::_choose_type_stack()`: when a bucket has overfull leaves but no underfull candidates, the first alternative bucket goes to the lowest eligible position.
- `OSDMap::find_best_remap()`: it keeps the most overfull source OSD with a strict `>`, so the frequent ties go to the lowest position.

**Fix:** seed both scans with `pg.ps()`, so they start at `seed % size` and wrap around. The balancer still does not consider primaries, but remaps are spread evenly over positions, so the primary distribution follows CRUSH. The amount of balancer work and the resulting PG distribution are unchanged. Existing `pg_upmap_items` are not touched, so upgrading causes no data movement.

**Testing:**
- New test `OSDMapTest.calc_pg_upmaps_no_primary_bias`: 20 racks x 2 hosts x 4 OSDs, size-8 EC pool, rack-0 at 1/4 of its weight.
  - Without the fix it fails: 34.6% of remapped shards at position 0, and 19.4 primaries per rack-0 OSD against a mean of 6.4.
  - With the fix: 13.8% at position 0, and 7.5 primaries per rack-0 OSD.
- `unittest_osdmap` and `unittest_crush_wrapper` pass.
- Offline osdmaptool reproduction, 320 OSDs, 3 seeds: primaries per OSD in the under-weighted rack drop from 23-36 to 3-14 (pool mean 8), with identical PG balance. Details in the tracker.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82280

73233.title: mgr/cephadm: migrate user-provided grafana certificates from tentacle
73233.author: rkachach
73233.body:
Tentacle stored per-host grafana certificates in certmgr as grafana_cert and grafana_key. These are now grafana_ssl_cert and grafana_ssl_key, and the certificate used by the service is selected through the spec's certificate_source. The old entries are no longer loaded by the TLSObjectStore, so after upgrading a user-provided grafana certificate is silently replaced by a cephadm-signed one.

Add migration 11 -> 12 which reads the legacy entries straight from the mgr store and copies every valid user-provided cert/key pair to the new names as an editable, user-made pair. A certificate is considered cephadm-generated when it was not marked user-made and its issuer is either the cephadm root CA (tentacle) or the legacy Ceph/cephadm self-signed issuer (squid and earlier); squid custom certificates were carried into the tentacle store without user_made, so the issuer check is needed to classify them correctly. When every host running grafana ends up with a user-provided pair, the grafana spec is switched to certificate_source 'reference'.

Expired, unparsable or key-less certificates are not migrated, and entries already present under the new names are kept. The legacy entries are left in the mgr store.

73234.title: mgr/cephadm: fix certmgr reference certificates for grafana
73234.author: rkachach
73234.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82283

On Umbrella, a user-supplied per-host grafana certificate set with `certmgr` could not be made to work:

- With `certmgr cert set` + `certmgr key set`, the key was removed as soon as grafana reconciled its certificates, so certmgr reported `missing key` and grafana fell back to a self-signed certificate.
- With `certmgr cert-key set --hostname <host>`, the key stayed but the certificate was still not found when the host name in `orch host ls` differs from the host FQDN.
- In both cases, grafana with ssl enabled was deployed with empty cert/key files instead of failing, replacing a working daemon with a broken one.

## Changes

- **`certmgr key set` stores keys as editable, user-made objects**, the same as `cert set` and `cert-key set`. Previously they matched the marking used for inline-saved credentials and were removed by `rm_inline_saved_cert_key_pair()` on reconcile.
- **Per-host `reference` certificates are looked up by orchestrator host name**, falling back to the FQDN so certificates registered under the FQDN (as the docs used to recommend) keep working. Grafana docs updated.
- **Grafana is not deployed without its TLS certificate/key** when ssl is enabled. A new placement fails with `CEPHADM_DAEMON_PLACE_FAIL`; a reconfig/redeploy of an existing daemon is aborted and it keeps its current config.
- **The apply-time warning for per-host `reference` certificates** now recommends `certmgr cert-key set` instead of separate `cert set`/`key set` (it also passed the cert name as `--key-name`).

## Tests

- `test_grafana_reference_per_host` is no longer an expected failure; moved to `TestCertMgrHostScope`, and the dedicated facet and its ignorelist are removed.
- New QA tests:
  - per-host reference cert provisioned with `cert set` + `key set`: grafana serves it, the stored cert/key are unchanged after deploy, and the cert check is clean;
  - grafana applied before its reference cert exists: not deployed, `CEPHADM_DAEMON_PLACE_FAIL` raised, then deployed and cleared once the cert is set (own facet, since the warning is expected);
  - cert registered under the FQDN still served (skipped when FQDN == host name).

## Backport

Umbrella is affected; all commits are intended for backport.

73239.title: log: report failure to open the log file on stderr
73239.author: mkhon
73239.body:
`Log::reopen_log_file()` ignores a failed `open()` of the log file. A daemon that cannot create its log file, for example because `/var/log/ceph` does not exist in a read-only container, then silently loses everything below the `err_to_stderr` level, with no hint why its log is empty.

This prints the error on stderr, the same way a failed `fchown()` of the log file is already reported right below:

```
failed to open log file /var/log/ceph/ceph-osd.0.log: (2) No such file or directory
```

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82296

Nothing is printed when file logging is off: with `log_to_file=false` the log file path is cleared before the reopen, so `open()` is not attempted.

73240.title: DNM: qa_triage: the shared library of what it learned
73240.author: aainscow
73240.body:
jenkins do not test

**Do not merge.** This holds the shared library of [qa_triage](https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/73070), the tool that triages the failed jobs of teuthology runs, on a branch that anyone with write access to ceph/ceph can push to: a pull request lets maintainers push to its branch. It is here so that what the tool learns from everyone's reviews is shared, until the library has a home of its own.

It is everything in `src/script/qa_triage/library/`:

- `problems/`: the records of known problems, one per tracker issue, or per pull request for a problem nobody filed an issue for: where each hangs in the tool's decision tree, and the log checks that confirm it.
- `nodes/`: the questions the decision tree learned, as Python that the tool checks before it runs it, and `wording.yaml`, how the tree's answers read.
- `labels/`: the jobs people settled: what each failure is, as a reviewer said.
- `memory/`: what people answered for each kind of failure, from the RADOS wiki of reviewed runs and the tracker.
- `scripts/`: scripts people wrote to pull debug data out of a job's logs.

To use it, set this in `~/.config/qa_triage/config.yaml`:

```yaml
db: https://github.com/aainscow/ceph.git#wip-qa-triage-db:src/script/qa_triage/library
```

The tool then fetches only this directory of this branch, keeps it up to date, and pushes what is learned back here, once it passes the tool's checks and the person approves it. Each change is a commit on this branch, so it can be reviewed and reverted here.

The CI that runs for ceph pull requests is not for this: "jenkins do not test" above keeps Jenkins off it.

73241.title: include/scope_guard: make scope_guard non-movable
73241.author: tchaikov
73241.body:
The defaulted move constructor left the moved-from guard armed, so a guard that was moved ran its action twice, once from each object. The defaulted move assignment threw away the action the target was holding, and the moved-from guard still ran later. It only compiled for callables that can be assigned, which rules out any lambda with
captures.

No caller moves or assigns a guard, and `make_scope_guard()` doesn't need to move one either: since C++17, both its return statement and "auto g = make_scope_guard(...)" construct the guard in place. So instead of fixing the move constructor, drop it. Deleting the copy constructor and copy assignment also suppresses the implicit move operations, so a guard can be neither copied nor moved.

`make_scope_guard()` didn't compile when given an lvalue: with `F = T&`, the `const F&` and `F&&` constructors end up with the same signature. Decay F, so the guard keeps its own copy of the callable.

While at it, mark the constructors `[[nodiscard]]`, and drop the `in_place_type` overload of `make_scope_guard()`, which nobody calls.

73242.title: rgw/cloud-sync: keep the tenant out of the destination bucket name
73242.author: supriti
73242.body:
get_path() joined the tenant and the bucket name with a '-', so the tenanted bucket proj1/data and an untenanted bucket called proj1-data both expanded to "proj1-data" and overwrote each other at the destination.

Use get_namespaced_name() instead. It joins with a '/', which is never legal in a bucket name, so the tenant stays in the object key and the two cannot collide.

That only holds while something in target_path comes before ${bucket}. get_target() splits the path at the first '/' to get the destination bucket name, so a template starting with ${bucket} would hand it the tenant on its own. Refuse that case and log what to change.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/81925

73246.title: mds: drop stopped ranks from the resolve and rejoin gathers
73246.author: anthonyeleven
73246.body:
When max_mds is reduced and other ranks restart while the top rank is still in up:stopping, a recovering rank can wait forever in up:resolve or up:rejoin for a message from the rank that has since stopped.

resolve_gather and rejoin_gather are seeded from the recovery set, which includes up:stopping ranks. Once such a rank finishes stopping, it never sends its resolve or rejoin, and its late messages are dropped as stale. Nothing removes it from the gathers. handle_mds_map() handles a newly stopped rank only while this rank is clientreplay, active or stopping, and MDCache::set_recovery_set() only replaces the set, even when the set is recalculated after a restart.

Following the review on #38328, set_recovery_set() now drops ranks that left the recovery set from resolve_gather, rejoin_gather and rejoin_ack_gather, and finishes the gather if that was the last outstanding member. handle_mds_map() recalculates the recovery set when it shrinks while this rank is in resolve, reconnect or rejoin. A failed or restarting rank stays in the recovery set, so only ranks that have finished stopping, and so hold no subtrees or cache, are dropped.

Reproduced on 18.2.8 with three active ranks: lower max_mds to 2, fail rank 1, and once a standby has taken it, mark the fs not joinable and fail rank 0. After rank 2 stops and the fs is joinable again, stock ranks 0 and 1 stay in up:rejoin indefinitely, with rank 1's rejoin_gather still holding rank 2. With this change backported, both ranks go active within seconds. A qa test with the same steps is included in test_failover.py; it has not run under teuthology yet.

This supersedes #37701 and #38328. #71644 also edits set_recovery_set(), to add ranks that newly join the recovery set. The two are complementary, and whichever merges second needs a trivial rebase that keeps both loops.

73254.author: aainscow
73254.body:
Stacked on https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/69112 (pool migration, at 3d0fac933b8): only the last seven commits are
new. Each commit fixes one tracker, carries its reproducer and stands alone, so any of them can be taken into #69112.
The fix for https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82290 moved to its own PR, https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/73741.

- https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82291 mgr: `adjust_pgs()` stopped recording pool names when it learned to skip
  nopgchange pools, so the `osd rm-pg-upmap-primary-all` that a merge waits for was never sent and pg_num decreases
  of pools with a pg_upmap_primary entry stalled. The names are recorded again.
- https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82292 osd: the OSD read the source of a client's `copy_from` at the migration target
  the client had addressed, so an object whose PG had not migrated was not found (ENOENT). The source is now read
  from the migration's root, which the OSD's Objecter routes to the pool that has the object.
- https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82293 mon, mgr: a migration no longer sets the target's autoscale mode to off and
  nopgchange on, or forces autoscale on and clears nopgchange when it finishes. Instead the monitor refuses pg_num and
  pgp_num changes to any migrating pool, and the autoscaler skips migrating pools. The source pool keeps the freeze
  as before.
- https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82294 mon: a snap removal is recorded against the migration target of its time.
  After a later migration the monitor no longer found it, so a resent removal was queued again, also for the source
  whose OSDs had already purged the snap, and they aborted in the snap trimmer
  (`interval_set.h: 568: FAILED ceph_assert(false)` in `adjust_purged_snaps`). The monitor now looks in every pool of
  the migration.
- https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82289 osd: a source delete that could not get the object's write lock was retried
  only by recovery, while the object held a recovery slot until its delete completed, so a PG's migration could stall
  for good. The delete is now retried from the op queue when the lock is released. A debug option,

  object a migration deletes from its source.

  migrating since, and the OSD reports a PG only once, so the migration stopped. Reports are now checked against the
  committed osdmap.

The 82293 commit also updates `TEST_osd_pool_create_migrate_from` (osd-pool-create.sh), which checked the old
nopgchange messages. That test cannot pass on #69112 alone; https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/73154 fixes it, and these

and passes with it:

- 82294, osd-pool-migration-snap-remove.sh: without the fix the second removal queued the

73255.title: mon/MonmapMonitor: tell the peon when a forwarded mon_join is ignored
73255.author: aainscow
73255.body:
A monitor that needs to join, or to change its location for `--set-crush-location`, sends a mon_join to the leader rank from a peer's probe reply. When that rank is its own, for example a restarted leader whose peers still follow it, the join goes to the monitor itself and is forwarded to the leader once the monitor is back as a peon. By then the leader has usually applied the join, and `preprocess_join()` dropped it without `no_reply()`, so the peon kept the routed request, resent it after every election and reported SLOW_OPS until it restarted.

`preprocess_join()` now calls `no_reply()` when it drops a join, as the other services do for messages they ignore.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82307

73256.title: mon/MonmapMonitor: make mon set_new_tiebreaker idempotent
73256.author: aainscow
73256.body:
Replacing the stretch mode tiebreaker with a new monitor in the same zone, as Rook does when it fails over the arbiter monitor, succeeded the first time and failed with EINVAL ("... matches mons <old tiebreaker>") when the command ran again, because the old tiebreaker is still in the monmap and is no longer skipped by the location check. The command can run twice without the user repeating it: an election can lose its reply (https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/81930), and clients resend commands after a reconnect. Rook then got an error for a change that had been made, and its failover stopped before removing the old monitor.

`mon set_new_tiebreaker` now replies success without a change when the named monitor is already the tiebreaker, as `mon add disallowed_leader` does for a monitor that is already disallowed.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82308

73264.title: mds: don't ack dirfrag replicas whose inode isn't replicated to the peer
73264.author: anthonyeleven
73264.body:
A surviving (active) MDS can abort in `MDCache::handle_cache_rejoin_ack()` on `ceph_assert(isolated_inodes.empty())` while peer ranks are in up:rejoin. This is tracker 80407, the same assert as 62036 and 50821, and distinct from 80402 and 54840.

The crash starts on the recovering rank. When it processes a surviving peer's strong rejoin for a fragmented directory that it does not have in cache, it invents a single `frag_t()` dirfrag and records the peer as a replica of it. After it fetches the inode, `opened_undef_inode()` → `CInode::force_dirfrags()` splits that dirfrag, and `CDir::split()` copies the replica map onto every leaf, so the peer is now recorded as a replica of leaves it never held. If the peer then trims the directory and sends a cache expire before the recovering rank sends its acks, the expire removes the peer from the inode and from the leaves it actually had, but the remaining leaves keep the stale replica. The 2014 sweep in `handle_cache_expire()` only runs when the named dirfrag is missing, so it doesn't catch this. `rejoin_send_acks()` then acks those leaves to the peer without the inode, the peer builds an unconnected dirfrag that nothing in the ack links, and the assert fires. The deferral from #52648 doesn't help, because it keys on `rejoin_done`, which is null on an active survivor.

A dirfrag replica cannot exist without an inode replica, so acking a dirfrag to a peer we don't record as a replica of its inode is never correct. This drops such stale replicas in `rejoin_send_acks()` instead of acking them, for inodes we are authoritative for. Base inodes, inodes we are not authoritative for (the subtree-root case the in-tree FIXME describes) and subtree-root dirfrags are left alone. Subtree roots are known from the subtree map after replay and are never invented and split, and the walk can reach one before the "peer missed MDentryLink" fix-up has run for its inode. The check doesn't rely on replica nonces, which are unreliable after a split.

The race window is short, so this also adds a dev-only option, `mds_debug_rejoin_ack_delay` (default 0), that defers `rejoin_send_acks()` with a timer while the rank keeps processing messages. The new test in `qa/tasks/cephfs/test_rejoin.py`, run in fs:functional, uses it: a fragmented directory one level below an export-pinned directory, a survivor holding an ordinary replica of its inode and one leaf, no client caps and no subtree root at or below it; fail the auth rank, and drop the survivor's cache once the recovering rank has split the directory. Under vstart_runner it failed 3 of 3 runs without the fix (the survivor aborted on the assert) and passed 3 of 3 with it. It has not run under teuthology yet.

Reproduced on 18.2.8 with three active ranks and the delay backported. Stock crashed the survivor on the assert. With the fix, the recovering rank logged dropping 26 stale leaf replicas instead of acking them, the survivor stayed up, and all ranks went active.

@vshankar @batrick @xiubli

73273.title: osd, os/bluestore, kv: keep read-once data out of the OSD's caches
73273.author: ming1
73273.body:
## Motivation

On dense RGW hosts memory per OSD is a direct cost, and an OSD runs up to
its `osd_memory_target` under RGW small-object writes, deep scrub and
backfill although almost nothing it caches is used again: every onode
touched and every RocksDB block read goes to the front of its cache, and
the tuner, which looks only at recency, hands them the budget. Keeping
read-once data out of the caches halves the peak under RGW writes at the
same throughput, which makes a lower `osd_memory_target` for RGW workloads
possible without hurting performance.

## What changes (v3, 12 commits)

1. `osd`: recovery push reads use `FADVISE_DONTNEED`
   (`RecoveryHandle::cache_dont_need` was never set).
2. `osd`: EC recovery reads use it too, in both EC backends, honouring the
   handle's client-waiting flag; the shards read for a reconstruction are
   sent once, and the sources kept them cached.
3. `os/bluestore`: two preps without behaviour change (`_add()` loses its
   unused `level`; `_touch()` is factored out of `maybe_unpin()`).
4. `os/bluestore`: an onode enters a bounded probation FIFO and is admitted
   to the LRU on its second later use. Probation is bounded by the arrivals
   of the last four age bins (the shard keeps its own ring of arrivals per
   bin) and at least 1024 onodes per shard, so backfill scans are not
   evicted early; over budget the promoted onodes come first, with half of
   probation's share reserved for newcomers so a shifted working set can
   still prove itself. `bluestore_onode_cache_probation_ratio` (0.1;
   0 = old behaviour), changeable at run time. Perf counter
   `onodes_probation`. Unit tests.
5. `kv/rocksdb_cache`: `EvictEntry()`/`LRU_InsertAfter()` factored out
   (also fixes `EraseUnRefEntries()` not decrementing the element count),
   then the same probation for `binned_lru` blocks; probation is not
   binned, so the tuner sees it at its lowest priority.
   `rocksdb_cache_probation_ratio` (0.1; 0 = off), run time. Counter
   `probation`. Unit tests in a new `unittest_binned_lru_cache` that drives
   one shard directly.
6. `os/bluestore`: ghost list. The shard remembers the keys its LRU
   evicted last, as many as its budget, and a miss on one of them goes
   straight back to the LRU, so a hot set squeezed by the tuner grows back
   as it would under a plain LRU; scan residue leaves from probation and is
   not remembered. Unit tests.
7. `doc`: configuration reference section and release note.

Both probations need the age bins to rotate, and only BlueStore's mempool
thread rotates them, so the shards start with probation off and BlueStore
turns it on from that thread; tools that open the store without it, and
the mon's block cache, admit at once as before.

Applies on main, no dependency on open PRs; the `maybe_unpin()` fix
(tracker 82605) and its test are #73664 now. `unittest_bluestore_types`
172/172, `unittest_binned_lru_cache` 16/16.

## Test results

A/B on a 2-OSD vstart cluster on two NVMe drives, `osd_memory_target`
4 GiB, base = main plus #73018, every workload on a cluster created from
scratch for each build (drives discarded first), 120 s per steady phase.
Peak RSS GiB, osd.0 / osd.1:

| Workload | Before | After | Change | Time or throughput, before -> after |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Deep scrub, all PGs | 4.36 / 4.43 | 1.34 / 1.32 | **-69% / -70%** | 319 s -> 319 s |
| Recovery, source / target OSD | 4.04 / 1.99 | 2.27 / 1.59 | **-44%** / -20% | clean after 312 s -> 297 s |
| RGW PUT 4 MiB | 1.55 / 1.54 | 1.54 / 1.54 | -1% / 0% | 1174 -> 1117 MiB/s |
| RGW PUT 4 KiB | 4.51 / 4.48 | 2.01 / 2.00 | **-55% / -55%** | 8395 -> 8437 obj/s |
| RGW GET 4 MiB | 4.33 / 4.32 | 3.77 / 3.44 | -13% / -20% | 2718 -> 2366 MiB/s |
| RGW GET 4 KiB | 3.68 / 4.03 | 3.73 / 3.43 | +1% / -15% | 3092 -> 3092 obj/s |
| RBD write 4 MiB | 1.63 / 1.65 | 1.61 / 1.62 | -1% / -2% | 1164 -> 1275 MiB/s |

73274.title: qa/cephfs: wait for the tick before checking phase tracker lock counters
73274.author: vshankar
73274.body:
test_enabled_under_load reads the mds_lock perf counters as soon as the tracker has seen 100 client requests. Unlike the per-phase counters, which are updated as each phase ends, those counters are only fed by update_lock_stats() from MDSRank::tick(), and enabling the tracker resets them. A busy workload can cross the request threshold well within one mds_tick_interval of the reset, leaving lock_acquisitions at 0 while `dump phase times`, which computes the lock stats on the spot, already reports thousands of acquisitions.

Wait for the first tick to publish the lock stats before asserting on them.

73276.title: crimson/osd: OperationThrottler should not sleep on a future mClock tag
73276.author: mohit84
73276.body:
Reduce admission latency in OperationThrottler by having background_task wait on its condition variable instead of sleeping when the head mClock item is not yet due.When dequeue() returns a future tag background_task runs seastar::sleep() until that time. Ops that arrive meanwhile including immediate ops (RepRequest, LogMissingRequest, etc), which are served before mClock’s classes wait out the whole sleep.

Fix: co_await cv.wait(timeout) in place of the sleep.
     Enqueue, release_throttle() and stop() then wake it
     and dequeue() runs again immediately.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82357

73277.title: mgr/dashboard: draw cd-usage-bar without Carbon Charts
73277.author: vobruba-martin
73277.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82358

`cd-usage-bar` drew every usage bar as a Carbon meter chart (`ibm-meter-chart`). In tables, where one bar is rendered per row, this blocks the browser: on the OSDs page of a cluster with 444 OSDs and 50 rows per page, rendering the table took about 8 seconds.

Each meter chart measures its DOM while it is being built, and the component read the threshold color with `getComputedStyle()`. Every measurement forces a style recalculation of the whole page, and each recalculation gets more expensive as the table grows, so the cost grows quadratically with the number of rows.

This PR draws the usage bar with plain HTML and CSS instead, keeping the look of the meter chart (labels, status colors and indicator, range indicator) and shows the used/available/total values in a Carbon tooltip styled like the meter chart tooltip. The bar needs no layout measurements while the table is rendered. The tooltip measures only when it is opened.

### Measurements

Trace of the OSDs page with 444 OSDs, 50 rows per page:

| | Carbon meter chart | HTML/CSS bar |
|---|---|---|
| Rendering 50 rows | 8089 ms | 1356 ms |
| Forced style recalculations | 950 | 300 |
| of them caused by the usage bars | 650 (~6.2 s) | 0 |

The remaining 300 recalculations come from the Read/Write bytes sparklines, which are out of scope here.

### Other changes in behaviour

- The tooltip opens when hovering anywhere over the bar or its labels. The meter chart showed it only over the used (filled) part, so at 0 % usage the user had to hit a single pixel.
- The meter chart took values and thresholds only once in `ngOnInit()`, so table refreshes and thresholds loaded later (e.g. the OSD nearfull/full ratios) were ignored.
- A usage of 100 % and more is consistently shown as danger (the meter chart drew 100 % in the primary color with a danger icon and no label).
- The bar shrinks with narrow columns instead of painting over the neighbouring cells.
- The status colors no longer depend on the theme custom properties being defined on the element.
- The inputs which only configured the chart (`height`, `totalUnit`, `animations`, `legendEnabled`, `toolbarEnabled`, `tooltipOptions`, `customColorScale`) are dropped; none of them is used.

### Screenshot

Carbon meter chart (left) and the new bar (right):

![usage bar comparison](https://tracker.ceph.com/attachments/download/8694/usage-bar-compare.png)

73286.title: messages/MOSDPGPush: send the pushed data in the data segment
73286.author: ming1
73286.body:
Recovery and backfill targets copy every pushed byte, because `PushOp` data travels in the message payload, which msgr2 does not page align. Send it in the data segment instead: MOSDPGPush v5 (compat 5) for peers with `SERVER_VAMPIRE`; older peers still get v4.

Note: OSDs built from main before this change advertise `SERVER_VAMPIRE` but cannot decode v5; do not mix the two.

Tested on vstart: recovering a 4 MiB object made 64 aligned 64 KiB copies on the target; with this change, none. New unit test: `MOSDPGPush.data_segment` in `unittest_osd_types`.

73287.title: cls/rgw: refresh version listing metadata on index completion
73287.author: viduship
73287.body:
Updating retention can change an object's modification time without updating its version-listing entry in the bucket index. Lifecycle then compares different timestamps and can cancel cloud transition with ECANCELED, even after retention has expired.

Refresh the existing version-listing entry in the same index transaction. Keep the version order and current-version flags unchanged. The CLS regression covers updates to current, noncurrent and null versions, and checks bucket object and byte counts.

Resolves: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82371

Related: #72996 handles the lifecycle Object Lock checks.

73288.title: crimson/osd: fix hanged ops in EC due to incorrect attr_cache
73288.author: shraddhaag
73288.body:
## Issue

This PR fixes 3 hangs due to obc not containing one or the other key in the attr_cache. The following cases are solved here: 

1. When an obc is reloaded from disk, in `attr_cache`, the object info with key `_` and the snapset is not loaded. In `get_write_plan()`, when `object_info_t(attr_cache.at("_"))`  tries to decode `_` key, zero bytes are decoded and it throws `end_of_buffer`. Since nothing is looking for this error, we get `Exceptional future ignored`, and the op hangs forever. 
2. After a snapshot, when an object receives a write, it should first clone the existing head obc. In `translate_transaction()`, the clone is not added to the `obc_map`. When `get_write_plan()` tries to decode the clone, its throws `std::out_of_range`, and the operation hangs forever. 
3. When the client sends a snap rollback request, both the existing head and the snap clone (which is the source for the new head), should be added to the obc_map. But only the head is added, not the snap clone. When `get_write_plan()` tries to decode the new source, it throws `std::out_of_range` and the operation hangs forever. 

## Fix
For each of the above cases, the following fixes have been made: 
1. the object info and the snapset are set when the obc is reloaded from disk. 
2. In the `obc_map`, the clone obc is also added. 
3. In the `obc_map` the source obc (the obc to rollback to) is also added. 

## Testing
QA: 
* https://pulpito-ng.ceph.com/runs/shraddhaag-2026-10-30_07:41:49-crimson-rados:basic-main-distro-debug-trial 
* https://pulpito-ng.ceph.com/runs/shraddhaag-2026-10-30_07:43:17-crimson-rados:thrash-main-distro-debug-trial 
* https://pulpito-ng.ceph.com/runs/shraddhaag-2026-10-30_12:40:43-crimson-rados-main-distro-debug-trial

73290.title: doc/rados: add object size, I/O rate, and omap guidance
73290.author: anthonyeleven
73290.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/20215

The tracker asks for librados guidance on the trade-offs of object size, I/O rate, and omap versus regular data. Introduction to librados has none, so this adds an Object Size, I/O Rate, and Omap section at the end of the page.

- Object size: the `osd_max_object_size` limit and its scrub check, the 4 MiB objects that RBD, CephFS, and RGW use, the `min_alloc_size` cost of very small objects, and EC optimizations removing small-object padding in Tentacle and later.
- I/O rate: writes and default reads go through the primary; `LIBRADOS_OPERATION_BALANCE_READS` and `LOCALIZE_READS` let replicas serve reads, and since Umbrella balanced reads on erasure-coded pools go to the shard holding the data. Links to the read balancer and primary affinity.
- Omap: stored in RocksDB, supported on replicated pools and, since Umbrella, on erasure-coded pools with EC optimizations (#66726); the `LARGE_OMAP_OBJECTS` thresholds.

73292.title: [mgmt-gateway] qa/cephadm: shared base class for cephadm_cases suites
73292.author: rkachach
73292.body:
Move the generic helpers of the certmgr teuthology suite (#72243) into a
shared base class, `CephadmTestCase` in `qa/tasks/cephadm_cases/base.py`,
so the upcoming cephadm service suites (mgmt-gateway first, #72872) build
on the same code instead of carrying another copy.

### Changes

- **qa/cephadm: add a shared base class for cephadm_cases suites**
  `CephadmTestCase(MgrTestCase)` holds what any cephadm integration suite
  needs: running `ceph` commands in `cephadm shell`, waiting for the
  orchestrator and for services, applying specs and confirming they were
  stored, polling and holding conditions, health checks and mgr failover.
  A suite sets `WORKDIR` (recreated on the admin host and mounted in
  `cephadm shell`), copies its helper scripts with `install_file()`, and
  may override `POLL_TRANSIENT` and `check_stored_spec()`. `setUpClass()`
  saves the cephadm root CA to `WORKDIR` so clients can verify what the
  daemons serve.
- **qa/cephadm: build the certmgr tests on the shared base class**
  `CertMgrTestCase` now derives from `CephadmTestCase` and keeps only the
  certmgr-specific parts (test PKI, certificate helpers, module options
  reset at teardown, TLS checks in `check_stored_spec()`). No behaviour
  change: against a recording fake cluster, the old and new classes issue
  the same commands for `apply()` (including both rejection paths),
  `wait_health()`, `wait_service()`, `rm_service()`, the certificate
  helpers and teardown.

Only helpers certmgr uses are added here; the ones needed by the service
suites come with #72872, together with their first user.

### Testing

- `orch:cephadm:certmgr` run: <link>
- flake8 / mypy clean on the changed files

73293.title: [mgmt-gateway] qa/cephadm: add orch/cephadm/services/mgmt-gateway teuthology suite
73293.author: rkachach
73293.body:
Add `orch/cephadm/services/`, meant to hold one teuthology suite per
cephadm service, and `orch/cephadm/services/mgmt-gateway` as its first
suite. It covers mgmt-gateway, oauth2-proxy and `secure_monitoring_stack`
in their different combinations, cephadm's HA setup, and what clients get
when a component goes down.

Depends on #73292 (shared `CephadmTestCase` base class); until it merges
its two commits also show up here.

The tests check what clients actually get from the daemons (status codes,
redirects, TLS and client-certificate behaviour, Prometheus scrape
targets) rather than the config cephadm writes. Requests go through
`probe.py`, run inside `cephadm shell`. The OIDC identity provider is
`oidc_idp.py`, a minimal provider run as a cephadm custom container with
the cluster's own Ceph image, so the suite pulls nothing from outside the
Ceph registries.

### Facets

| Facet | What it covers |
|---|---|
| `gateway` | one gateway, no SSO: mTLS on backends and the internal endpoint, routes and basic auth, `/health`, dashboard standby handling across a mgr failover, credential rotation, `ssl: false` (custom and default port), removal; a backend down, the gateway down |
| `oauth2` | gateway + oauth2-proxy + the test IdP: every route behind the IdP, callback URL, browser login, session across redeploy and mgr failover, dashboard SSO lifecycle; oauth2-proxy down fails closed, a backend down with a session |
| `ha` | cephadm's HA setup: 2 gateways behind a VIP (keepalive-only ingress), 2 of every service behind them; access and URLs through the VIP, keepalived failover, port left free on host addresses, session across oauth2-proxy instances; one instance of each layer down (active gateway, oauth2-proxy, prometheus, alertmanager, grafana, active mgr) unnoticed by a logged-in user |
| `transitions` | plain -> secure -> gateway -> gateway+SSO and back, gateway straight from plain, `secure_monitoring_stack` ignored with a gateway |
| `open-issues` | reproducers for bugs not fixed yet, marked `@unittest.expectedFailure`: green while the bug is there, red ("unexpected success") once fixed, as a reminder to move the test to its facet |

### cephadm bugs found by the suite

Fixed in separate PRs (needed for the `gateway`, `ha` and `transitions`
facets to pass):
- <PR C>: mgmt-gateway records and advertises port 443 with `ssl: false` and no port, while nginx listens on 80
- <PR D>: Prometheus gets `username: None` service discovery credentials when security is turned on before the SD server restarts
- <PR E>: keepalived's health check of a VIP mgmt-gateway fails on every host since #67344, so a dead gateway never loses the VIP

Still open (`open-issues` facet):
- without a VIP, internal URLs (dashboard API hosts, grafana datasource, prometheus discovery) stay on the first gateway even when it is stopped
- after an oauth2 login users land on `/` instead of the requested page (oauth2-proxy allowlist vs. the FQDN/port in the callback)

### Testing

`orch:cephadm:services:mgmt-gateway`, with the three fixes: <link>

    teuthology-suite --suite orch:cephadm:services:mgmt-gateway \
        --ceph <testing-branch> --machine-type <type> \
        --filter-out rocky -k distro

(The quay.ceph.io images are tagged `<sha1>-centos-stream9`: pass
`overrides: cephadm: distro-suffix: centos-stream9` if the default tag is
missing.)

73294.title: squid: src/common/options: add descriptions to mgr messenger throttle options
73294.author: anthonyeleven
73294.body:
backport tracker: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82311

---

backport of https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/73037
parent tracker: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82055

Adds a `desc` and a `long_desc` to the eight mgr messenger throttle options, `mgr_{client,osd,mds,mon}_{bytes,messages}`, which had neither, so `ceph config help` and the generated option docs say what each one limits, what happens when it fills, and how to tell from the perf counters.

One commit, resolved the same way as the tentacle backport #73268, plus one squid-only change. `src/common/options/mgr.yaml.in` conflicted because squid doesn't have `mgr_dispatch_throttle_bytes` (added on main by 948de224df1, which isn't backported), so the change to its `long_desc` and the `see_also` links to it from the four byte options are dropped. Squid still registers the MDS and Monitor message throttles as `mgr_mds_messsages` and `mgr_mon_messsages` (main fixed the spelling in 40033e7b645, #71976, which isn't backported), so the `mgr_mds_messages` and `mgr_mon_messages` descriptions name those perf counters as they're spelled here. Squid also doesn't have `ms_client_throttle_retry_time_interval` (added on main by 94d175908a7, which isn't backported): its ProtocolV2 retries a throttled read after a fixed 1 ms, so the descriptions say "every millisecond" instead of naming that option. 73295.title: osd: let clients with no osd caps get EPERM instead of hanging
73295.author: anthonyeleven
73295.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/23765

A librados or librbd client whose key has only mon caps hangs on its first OSD op instead of getting EPERM.

Since the fix for https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/62382 (#52939 on main, #59307 for reef, #59306 for squid), MonClient honors the return value of `ms_handle_fast_authentication`. For a key with no osd caps at all, `OSD::ms_handle_fast_authentication` returns false, so the OSD rejects the session. The client sees a connection fault, reconnects, and never gets a reply; with `rados_osd_op_timeout` at its default of 0 it waits forever. Before that change the OSD returned 0 ("no action") here, the session stayed up with no grants, and `PrimaryLogPG::do_op` denied each op with EPERM.

Reproduced on Reef 18.2.8: with a key that has only `mon 'allow r'`, `rados -p <pool> ls` and `rbd ls <pool>` block, and the client log shows repeated `AUTH_CONNECTING` and `_fault` on the OSD connection. With `osd 'allow r pool=<other>'` added, both fail at once with `Operation not permitted`.

- Keep the session with an empty `OSDCap` when the key has no osd caps, so each op fails with EPERM. The Manager already accepts a session without caps the same way. Caps that fail to decode or parse are still rejected.
- Add a check to `qa/workunits/rados/test_pool_access.sh` that a key with only mon caps gets `Operation not permitted`, time-boxed so that a hang fails the test.

73296.title: [mgmt-gateway] python-common: default mgmt-gateway port to 80 when ssl is off
73296.author: rkachach
73296.body:
With `ssl: false` and no `port`, nginx listens on 80
(`external_server.conf.j2` uses `spec.port or 80`), but
`MgmtGatewaySpec.get_port_start()` returned 443 whatever the ssl setting.
cephadm records, port-checks and opens in the firewall the port from
`get_port_start()`, and builds the gateway's external URL from it. So it
advertised `http://<host>:443` (used e.g. for the oauth2-proxy redirect URL
and the dashboard links) while nothing listened there, and opened the
wrong firewall port.

Default to 443 with ssl and 80 without, the same rule as the template.

Found by the new `orch/cephadm/services/mgmt-gateway` teuthology suite
(#72872, gateway facet, `test_ssl_disabled_default_port`), which passes with
this fix.

73297.title: mgr/cephadm: give prometheus valid service discovery credentials
73297.author: rkachach
73297.body:
When security gets enabled at runtime (`secure_monitoring_stack` set, or
the first mgmt-gateway deployed) on a mgr that started without it,
Prometheus can end up with no scrape targets at all.

The service discovery server only sets its basic-auth credentials
(`enable_auth()`) when it restarts with security on, and that restart is
asynchronous: `config_update()` just signals the http server thread. In
the same serve loop pass, `_check_daemons()` redeploys prometheus for the
new security setting, and its config read the credentials straight from
the `ServiceDiscovery` attributes. Before the restart they are still
`None`, so `prometheus.yml` got `username: None` / `password: None`. Every
discovery request was then rejected once the server restarted with auth,
and nothing reconfigured prometheus again, since the credentials are not
one of its dependencies.

Add `ServiceDiscovery.get_credentials()`, which returns the credentials
clients must use, loading them from the mgr store (or creating them
there) when the server has not set them yet, and use it when generating
the prometheus config. `enable_auth()` loads the same stored credentials,
so both sides agree whatever the order.

Found by the new `orch/cephadm/services/mgmt-gateway` teuthology suite
(#72872, transitions facet: `test_full_cycle` saw no prometheus targets
after enabling `secure_monitoring_stack`); the facet passes with this fix.

73310.title: rgw/sts: use the jwks_uri host and port for thumbprint verification
73310.author: next0262
73310.body:
## Problem

With `rgw_enable_jwks_url_verification = true`, `verify_oidc_thumbprint()` opens its own TLS connection to the JWKS endpoint and compares the last certificate of the chain with the thumbprints registered on the OIDC provider. There are two defects in how it reaches the endpoint.

1. The host is taken from `jwks_uri` by stripping only the scheme and the path. An explicit port stays attached, so `https://host:6443/openid/v1/jwks` becomes `host:6443` and `gethostbyname("host:6443")` fails. Even `https://host:443/...` fails this way, as reported in the tracker.
2. The connection port is hard-coded to 443, so a provider on another port is unreachable even if the host resolves.

### Concrete case — Kubernetes service account tokens

A Kubernetes cluster can be registered as the provider for `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`, allowing pods to authenticate to RGW with projected service account tokens. The kube-apiserver issues those tokens and can serve discovery and JWKS directly on its HTTPS port, which defaults to 6443. For example, the discovery document could contain the following fields.

```sh
curl -sk https://kube-apiserver:6443/.well-known/openid-configuration
```

```json
{
  "issuer": "https://kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local",
  "jwks_uri": "https://kube-apiserver:6443/openid/v1/jwks"
}
```

For this setup, `jwks_uri` carries an explicit `:6443`. With endpoint verification enabled and thumbprints registered, `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` fails at the thumbprint check because RGW tries to resolve `kube-apiserver:6443` as a hostname.

The JWKS download itself (`RGWHTTPTransceiver`, curl) handles the port correctly. The failure is in the separate certificate check. Users connecting directly to a provider on a non-default port cannot enable that check and may have to leave `rgw_enable_jwks_url_verification` off, which is its default value.

## Fix

- Add `rgw::parse_url_host_port()` next to the existing Boost.URL helpers in `rgw_url.cc` and use it in `verify_oidc_thumbprint()`, with a default port of 443. A `jwks_uri` that does not parse now fails verification with a log message instead of proceeding to DNS lookup.
- Resolve the host with `getaddrinfo()` instead of the IPv4-only `gethostbyname()`, trying each returned address so IPv6 literals and AAAA records work too.
- Drop `get_top_level_domain_from_host()`, which has no other caller.

Behaviour for a `jwks_uri` without an explicit port, served on 443, is unchanged.

## Tests

`unittest_rgw_url` gains six cases for the new parser covering the default port, an explicit port, explicit 443, an IPv6 literal with a port, userinfo and invalid inputs. All 20 tests pass. Also compiled `rgw_rest_sts.cc` with the existing build dependencies.

The connection and thumbprint functions were exercised standalone against a local TLS server on ports 443 and 6443 over IPv4 and IPv6. Matching and non-matching thumbprints, a closed port and an unparsable URL behaved as expected. The pre-patch code fails the same setup with `gethostbyname failed for host: localhost:6443`. The local build has `WITH_RADOSGW=OFF`, so the full `rgw_common` build still needs CI.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/74001

73312.title: doc/cephfs: describe when other clients see changes
73312.author: anthonyeleven
73312.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/24642

The tracker asks what CephFS guarantees about when a change made on one mount becomes visible on another mount, in what order, and whether files, directories, kernel clients, and FUSE clients differ. `doc/cephfs/posix.rst` says CephFS keeps strong cache coherency across clients but answers none of that, so this adds a "Visibility to other clients" section after "Bottom line".

- Namespace changes: other clients see a change only after the MDS has journaled it. After an early reply, `set_xlocks_done()` leaves the xlocks readable only by the requesting client (`LOCK_XLOCKDONE` can_read is `XCL` in `src/mds/locks.c`), and lease and `Fs` revocation happens before the change.
- `wsync`, ceph-fuse, and libcephfs return only after the MDS has made the change. libcephfs never sends async creates (`src/client/Client.cc`, the delegated_inos comment in `Client::verify_reply_trace`).
- `nowsync`, the kernel default since 5.16: only create (`try_prep_async_create`, which needs `Fx` and `Dc` on the directory) and unlink (`get_caps_for_async_unlink`, which needs `Fx` and `Du`, and not rmdir) go async. `fsync(2)` on the directory waits for them on both the kernel client (`flush_mdlog_and_wait_inode_unsafe_requests` over `i_unsafe_dirops`) and ceph-fuse (`Client::_fsync` over `unsafe_ops`). Since 19.1.0, though, the MDS never grants `Dc` or `Du`, so on Squid and later these wait for the MDS too (https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82472); a note in the section says so.
- File data: the filelock `LOCK_MIX` state grants `Fr`, `Fw`, and `Fl` but not `Fc` or `Fb`, so while clients on several hosts have a file open for writing every read and write goes to the OSDs, and the move out of `LOCK_EXCL` makes the writer flush its buffered data first.
- Exceptions: shared writable mmap, already listed above, and LazyIO. @xiubli's #69754 adds a LazyIO bullet to the divergence list in the same file. The two changes touch different parts of the file and don't conflict.

@vshankar @xiubli, could you confirm these guarantees, in particular these two points:

1. With `wsync`, an observer on another host never sees a later namespace change from one process before an earlier one, including across directories on different MDS ranks.
2. With `nowsync`, an observer may not yet see an async create or unlink whose call has already returned. The text says it "might", and also that it might see a later change in another directory first.

73313.title: [managment-gateway] mgr/cephadm: fix keepalived health check of a VIP mgmt-gateway
73313.author: rkachach
73313.body:
Since the fix for https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/74929 (#67344), an SSL
mgmt-gateway with a `virtual_ip` listens on `<vip>:<port>` only, so other
services can use that port on the host's other addresses. keepalived's
check was not adapted: it still probed `https://<host addr>:<port>/health`,
which nothing answers. The check failed on every gateway host, so all
priorities dropped by the same 20 (100/90 -> 80/70) and the VIP holder kept
the VIP when its gateway died; only keepalived or the host itself going
down moved it.

- Give nginx a second server, in that mode only, listening on
  `127.0.0.1:<port>` and serving `/health` only (404 otherwise). It binds a
  specific address, so the port stays free elsewhere as 74929 requires,
  and it is not reachable from outside the host.
- Make keepalived check the gateway on `127.0.0.1`, with the gateway's
  scheme (the check used https even with `ssl: false`, where nginx serves
  plain HTTP). keepalived and nginx both use the host network.
- Use `curl -fs --connect-timeout 2 --max-time 3` for the gateway and
  haproxy checks: without `-f` curl exits 0 on HTTP errors, and a check
  must not hang.

The template change only renders with ssl and a `virtual_ip`; without a
`virtual_ip` the nginx configuration is byte-identical to before.

Found by the new `orch/cephadm/services/mgmt-gateway` teuthology suite
(#72872). Verified on a cluster: keepalived's check passes on both gateway
hosts, and stopping the gateway on the VIP holder moves the VIP to the
other host within ~12s (ha facet, `test_active_gateway_down`).

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/<id>

### Testing
- `test_keepalived_checks_mgmt_gateway_on_loopback` (`test_mgmt_gateway.py`, ssl on/off): keepalived check and the loopback `/health` server
- `test_ingress.py`: haproxy check expectations updated for the new curl flags

73314.title: qa/valgrind: suppress librgw_lancedb static-init leaks by object
73314.author: djgalloway
73314.body:
Since https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/73063 lancedb is built as a Rust cdylib and shipped as `librgw_lancedb.so.1`. rustc hides the crate's internal symbols in a cdylib and the package build strips `.symtab`, so valgrind only sees `obj:` frames for that library and the existing `fun:*opendal*register_default_operator_registry*` suppression no longer matches. Every rgw valgrind job then fails on 13 `Leak_PossiblyLost` records allocated from the library's ELF constructors (`call_init` / `_dl_init`), e.g. [this run](https://qa-proxy.ceph.com/teuthology/anuchaithra-2026-10-29_04:19:23-rgw-wip-anrao4-testing-2026-10-28-0758-main-distro-default-trial/689436/remote/trial097/log/valgrind/).

This adds a second suppression keyed on `obj:*/librgw_lancedb.so*` plus `fun:call_init*`, scoped to the same static-init path the original rule covered. The original rule is kept for builds with symbols.

Verified by replaying valgrind's suppression matching rules over the XML log from the failing job: all 13 errors match the new rule.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82395

73316.title: os/bluestore: declare intrusive_ptr hooks ahead of their use
73316.author: wjwithagen
73316.body:
BlueStore_fwd.h forward-declares Blob, Onode, SharedBlob and OpSequencer together with their boost::intrusive_ptr typedefs, and code such as Extent and TransContext uses those *Ref types in inline constructors before the types are complete. Their refcounting hooks are either hidden friends (Blob, Onode, SharedBlob) or come from RefCountedObject (OpSequencer); neither is found before the type is complete, so clang fails with

  error: use of undeclared identifier 'intrusive_ptr_release'

Declare the hooks in namespace bluestore next to each typedef. The friend definitions stay as they are and now define these declarations; OpSequencer gets inline definitions right after the class.
