73428.title: doc/radosgw: document migration from LDAP authentication to STS
73428.author: anthonyeleven
73428.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/63683

63683 asks for a strategy for migrating from the LDAP auth engine to STS, so that the LDAP engine can be deprecated. This adds a section at the end of the LDAP authentication page.

The first part says how a role session differs from an LDAP user:
- Only IAM policies grant it access.
- RGW creates a shadow user `<tenant>$oidc$<sub>` for it, and that user owns what the session creates.
- `ListBuckets` needs `s3:ListAllMyBuckets` and lists only the shadow user's buckets.

The second part is a procedure:
- Set up an OIDC identity provider backed by the same directory.
- Enable STS alongside LDAP.
- Register the OIDC provider and its thumbprint.
- Create a role per LDAP user, with a trust policy on `app_id` and `preferred_username`.
- Move clients one at a time.
- Optionally, run `bucket link` and `bucket chown` to the shadow user.
- Disable LDAP last.

It also adds `--ttype=ldap` to `radosgw-token --encode`. Without it the command prints nothing and exits with EINVAL.

I ran the procedure on a Reef 18.2.8 lab cluster with Keycloak 26.0.7, LDAP user federation to OpenLDAP, and the AWS CLI:
- Two LDAP users each created a bucket with a `radosgw-token` key. RGW created them as `type=ldap` users with no keys, and each owned their bucket.
- With an audience mapper on the client, the Keycloak token had `aud` `["rgw", "account"]`. A trust policy on `app_id` and `preferred_username` let alice assume her role and refused bob with AccessDenied.
- alice's role session read and wrote her LDAP-owned bucket through the role's permission policy alone, and got AccessDenied on bob's bucket.
- A bucket that the session created, and the object that it wrote into alice's bucket, were owned by `$oidc$<sub>`, where `sub` is Keycloak's ID for alice.
- `ListBuckets` was denied until the role allowed `s3:ListAllMyBuckets`. It then listed only the shadow user's bucket. alice's bucket showed up too after `bucket link` and `bucket chown` moved it to the shadow user.
- With `rgw_s3_auth_use_ldap` false, LDAP tokens got AccessDenied, and new role sessions kept working.
- The thumbprint pipeline in the section gave the thumbprint of the realm's signing certificate.
- bob's refused `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` still left a shadow user for him, because the shadow user is created before the trust policy is checked.

Two statements come from reading main, not from the lab:
- ACL grants never apply to role sessions (`RoleApplier` in `rgw_auth.h`).
- A role's permission policies cover only buckets in the role's tenant (`rgw_auth.cc`).

Reef wants a 16-character `rgw_sts_key`. Main, tentacle, and squid take the base64 key from `ceph-authtool --gen-print-key` that the section uses.

It cherry-picks cleanly to umbrella, tentacle, and squid.

@cbodley, is this the migration path you had in mind for deprecating the LDAP engine? @pritha-srivastava and @cagamps, would you review the STS parts?

Description:

Editing an NVMe-oF gateway group and adding a gateway node showed "Gateway group updated successfully", but reopening the group still listed only the original nodes. This includes groups with mTLS enabled.

73434.title: osd: prioritize backfills that free space on full OSDs
73434.author: FredNass
73434.body:
> [!NOTE]
> **Superseded by #70136.** That PR scores backfills by how much space they relieve, on both the primary and the backfill targets, and takes target headroom into account. In the same simulation, on the same seeds, it drains full OSDs as fast as this PR and makes clearly better rebalance progress. Combining the two adds nothing and would interact badly. Comparison: https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/70136#issuecomment-6798366225. The description below is kept for reference.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82597

## What this PR does

When an OSD exceeds the backfillfull (or full) ratio, the backfills that would
free space on it get no special treatment. These are the backfills of PGs
remapped away from it, whose outgoing or stray copies are only removed once the
PG goes clean. They queue behind unrelated rebalancing work in the FIFO backfill
reservation queues. Meanwhile the full OSD rejects incoming backfills
(`backfill_toofull`) and keeps filling with client writes until it reaches
`full_ratio` and client writes are blocked.

This PR boosts the backfill reservation priority of a PG when completing its
backfill will free space on a backfillfull or full OSD:

- **OSDs to be drained:** acting-set members that are not in the up set (the
  outgoing copies kept through pg_temp until backfill completes), plus stray
  peers. Both are only removed once the PG goes clean.
- **Flags:** both `CEPH_OSD_BACKFILLFULL` and `CEPH_OSD_FULL` are checked.
  `OSD::send_full_update()` reports exclusive flags, so a full OSD does not
  carry the backfillfull flag.
- **New option** `osd_backfill_drain_full_priority_boost`, default 21, 0
  disables it, runtime-changeable. The boost is additive and clamped by
  `get_max_prio_for_base()`, so a boosted clean backfill (base 100) never
  outranks a degraded one (base 140).
- **Why 21:** the pool `recovery_priority` setting shifts backfill priorities
  over 20 points. Among backfills of the same degradation level, one that
  drains a full OSD goes first whatever the pool priorities.
- **Raise-only hook:** fullness flags usually change while PGs already sit in
  `backfill_wait`. `Active::react(const AdvMap&)` raises the local reservation
  priority in place when an OSD to be drained becomes backfillfull or full,
  through `AsyncReserver::update_priority()`, the path `set_force_backfill()`
  already uses. The hook never lowers a priority: a PG keeps its boost until it
  next requests a reservation. This avoids preemption churn around the
  threshold, and keeps draining an OSD that would otherwise refill and cross it
  again.

This follows the idea of `get_delete_priority()`, which already boosts PG
deletion when the local OSD is running out of space.

## Complementary with #70985

#70985 (mgr/balancer: balance when degraded if some PGs are backfill_toofull)
and this PR act on two different levers. Together they free full OSDs fastest
and keep client I/O freezes as short as possible:

- **#70985** lets the upmap balancer run while PGs are `backfill_toofull`. It
  changes *where* the data goes, moving PGs off overfull OSDs.
- **This PR** decides *in which order* the OSDs serve the resulting backfills.
  The ones that drain a full OSD go first, including those the balancer just
  created.

Each one alone leaves a gap, which the other fills:

- **#70985 alone:** the balancer's moves wait behind the rest of the rebalance
  in the reservation queues, so full OSDs stay full for 28-45 h (median) after
  a 10% expansion.
- **This PR alone:** full OSDs drain in 1-2 h, but the PR cannot change the
  target mapping. Under heavy ingest the drained OSDs refill from incoming PGs
  and client writes, and cross the threshold again.

Simulated on a near-full cluster, median of 10 paired seeds:

| Client writes blocked (h), critical case | main | main + #70985 | this PR | this PR + #70985 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1%/day ingest | 3.3 | 3.0 | 0.2 | 0.2 |
| 2%/day ingest | 11.5 | 3.3 | 0.2 | 0.2 |
| 4%/day ingest

73435.title: rgw: apply bucket default encryption to CopyObject
73435.author: vupn0712
73435.body:
## Summary

https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82706

CopyObject skips `get_encryption_defaults()` entirely, so copying an object into a bucket that has default encryption configured (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS), without passing explicit SSE headers, just stores the copy unencrypted. PutObject, PostObject and CreateMultipartUpload already honor the bucket default here -- CopyObject is the odd one out. AWS S3 encrypts the copy with the destination bucket's default in this situation, so this is a real behavior gap, not a missing nice-to-have.

Fix is small: call `get_encryption_defaults()` from `RGWCopyObj_ObjStore_S3::get_params()` for local copies, the same way the other write paths already do. Explicit SSE headers on the copy request still win over the bucket default, same precedence as everywhere else. Copies from a remote zone are untouched.

## Test plan

- [x] Added s3-tests (`test_sse_s3_default_copy_*`, `test_sse_kms_default_copy_*`) for both SSE-S3 and SSE-KMS bucket defaults, at 1KB and 8MB, checking both the response headers and that the copied content comes back correct.
- [ ] CI

73443.title: rgw: add GET /admin/account?stats and radosgw-admin account list --stats
73443.author: BenoitKnecht
73443.body:
Account quotas can already be read and set through the admin API (`GET /admin/account`, `PUT /admin/account?quota`), but account storage usage was only available through `radosgw-admin account stats`, one account at a time. This PR makes it available in the admin API, and in bulk for all accounts through `radosgw-admin account list --stats`.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82608

## Motivation

There is currently no practical way to monitor account usage against account quotas: nothing exports account (or user/bucket) quota or usage as metrics, and collecting it means running `account info` and `account stats` for every account.

The goal is a follow-up PR adding a collector to the mgr prometheus module, which would periodically run `radosgw-admin account list --stats` and export metrics such as `ceph_rgw_account_used_bytes`, `ceph_rgw_account_quota_max_bytes` and `ceph_rgw_account_stats_last_synced_timestamp_seconds`, so that clusters can alert on accounts approaching their quota without running an external exporter. These are cluster-wide values, so the mgr is a better fit than radosgw perf counters, which would be duplicated on every radosgw and only cover accounts with recent traffic. The mgr already runs `radosgw-admin` for account operations (e.g. the dashboard's `RgwAccounts`), which avoids having to manage admin API credentials in the prometheus module.

This PR adds the RGW side needed for that collector, and the equivalent admin API call for external tools.

## Changes

### `GET /admin/account?stats`

```
GET /admin/account?stats&id=RGW00000000000000001[&sync-stats=true]
```

- Accepts `id`, or `name` with an optional `tenant`, like `GET /admin/account`.
- Requires the `accounts=read` cap.
- Returns the same output as `radosgw-admin account stats`, since both use `rgw::account::stats()`:
  ```json
  {"stats": {"size": 13, "size_actual": 4096, "size_utilized": 0, "size_kb": 1,
             "size_kb_actual": 4, "size_kb_utilized": 0, "num_objects": 1},
   "last_synced": "2026-11-03T09:55:20.621604Z",
   "last_updated": "2026-11-03T09:55:20.615309Z"}
  ```
- `sync-stats=true` recalculates the stats from all of the account's buckets first, like `--sync-stats`. `--reset-stats` isn't exposed, since a GET shouldn't modify state.
- `stats` is matched as a regular query parameter rather than registered as an admin sub-resource. `RGWHTTPArgs` only records one admin sub-resource per request, and the user and bucket APIs already accept `stats=true` as a regular parameter, so registering it globally could prevent e.g. `GET /admin/bucket?stats=true&policy` from being recognized.

### `radosgw-admin account list --stats`

- Lists each account's info (including `quota` and `bucket_quota`) along with its stats, `last_synced` and `last_updated`:
  ```json
  [{"info": {"id": "RGW00000000000000011", "name": "acct-a", "quota": {"enabled": true, "max_size": 10737418240, ...}, ...},
    "stats": {"size": 5, "size_actual": 4096, "num_objects": 1, ...},
    "last_synced": "...", "last_updated": "..."}]
  ```
- `--max-entries` and `--marker` work as for the plain listing, with the entries in an `accounts` array instead of `keys`.
- The stats aren't synced, so each account only costs a read of the account object and of its stats header. Accounts removed while the listing is in progress are skipped.
- The per-account dump lives in `rgw::account::dump_info_and_stats()`, so a bulk admin API call could reuse it later.
- Without `--stats`, the output is unchanged.

### Freshness of the stats

Neither call syncs the stats by default. Changes to an account's buckets are added to its stats every `rgw_user_quota_bucket_sync_interval` (3 minutes by default), and the stats are fully recalculated every `rgw_user_quota_sync_interval` (1 day). The docs describe this, and `last_updated`/`last_synced` show how recent the stats are.

## Testing

- `qa/tasks/radosgw_admin_rest.py`: stats of an empty account; stats synced after an account-root user write

73444.title: pybind/mgr/mirroring: cleanup redundant exception raise in set_mirror…
73444.author: dparmar18
73444.body:
…_info()

In set_mirror_info() (src/pybind/mgr/mirroring/fs/snapshot_mirror.py), when setxattr('/', 'ceph.mirror.info', ..., XATTR_CREATE) on the remote file system fails with EEXIST, the existing claim is read with get_mirror_info() inside a try block whose except MirrorException raises MirrorException(-errno.EEXIST, 'already an active peer'). That handler catches every MirrorException raised in the block:

- the get_mirror_info() errors invalid ceph.mirror.info value format (EINVAL) and error fetching ceph.mirror.info xattr (errno of the failed getxattr).

All three are reported as Error EEXIST: already an active peer.

Fix: remove the inner try/except MirrorException so that the mismatch error and the get_mirror_info() errors reach the caller unchanged. The raise for the mismatch stays. Also fix the typo "mirrorred".

can be inspected without py-spy or gdb in the container. The commands
run on the admin socket thread rather than a module finisher, so they
work on standby mgrs and while a module's command queue is stuck.

handle_py_debug() takes the GIL on a new thread state in the main
interpreter without holding the registry lock, which could deadlock
against a module thread that holds the GIL. An atomic flag makes calls
that arrive before Python is initialized return EAGAIN.

Dump every Python thread, tagged with its module:

client would time out, repeat the command to collect the result. Output

73455.title: rgw: ensure multipart complete happens before lease expiration
73455.author: cbodley
73455.body:
the CompleteMultipartUpload and AbortMultipartUpload requests take a cls lock on the multipart meta object for mutual exclusion. however, these are timed locks that expire to accomodate for crash recovery. continuing to process the operation after this lock expiration can lead to data loss

so we must prevent CompleteMultipartUpload from writing its target head object after its lock has expired. because the lock is held on a different rados object, we can't guard the head object write with assert_locked() to guarantee mutual exclusion

what we can do is prevent the osd from applying this write after the osd's lock expiration time. barring significant skew between the osd clocks, this strategy can preserve the mutual exclusion provided by cls_lock

this uses the new librados assert_time_range() operationto guard the head object writes issued by multipart complete. failed checks return ETIME which maps to the default 500 InternalError response

because this relies on a new librados operation that won't be present on older osds, we may see EOPNOTSUPP errors there. radosgw handles these errors by retrying the write without this assert_time_range() guard, so this fix only takes effect once the cluster is fully upgraded

---
includes commits from 3 dependent pull requests:
- https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/73599
- https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/73596
- https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/73586

73458.title: common/crc32c_aarch64: use 2032 byte blocks in the PMULL path
73458.author: dvanders
73458.body:
**Draft, for feedback.** It helps large buffers a lot on Neoverse-N1, but it is not ready while N1's cache-resident sizes are slower.

The aarch64 PMULL path crcs 1024-byte blocks as three independent `crc32cx` streams and merges them with two carry-less multiplies. The merge sits on the dependency chain into the next block, and three streams already saturate `crc32cx`, so the merge is the main overhead left. This uses 2032-byte blocks (the same layout with twice the stream length), which halves that overhead. The merge constants were computed two ways (from `x^(8n-33) mod P`, and by solving pmull/crc32cx over GF(2)); both agree with each other and with the existing 1024-byte constants. The software prefetches are scaled to the new block size.

GB/s with Ceph's flags (`-O2 -march=armv8-a+crc+crypto`); up to 64 KiB from cache, larger from DRAM:

| bytes | Apple M5 Max, clang 21 | Neoverse-N1, clang 18 | Neoverse-N1, gcc 13 |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 512 | 15.8 → 15.8 | 13.2 → 10.2 | 10.6 → 10.6 |
| 1024 | 36.0 → 35.9 | 18.2 → 20.1 | 18.2 → 20.2 |
| 4096 | 33.6 → 35.1 | 19.2 → 17.8 | 19.1 → 17.5 |
| 65536 | 32.2 → 33.6 | 19.6 → 18.9 | 19.4 → 18.8 |
| 1 MiB | 29.4 → 32.1 | 10.7 → 14.4 | 10.1 → 14.3 |
| 24 MiB | 29.7 → 31.7 | 10.8 → 14.4 | 10.0 → 14.2 |

Large buffers gain 7–8% on M5 and 33–42% on N1. On N1, 4–64 KiB loses 3–8% with both compilers, and 512 bytes loses 23% with clang. The N1 numbers are single runs.

I also tried dropping the prefetches altogether. That helps M5 (+6% on large buffers), but takes N1 down to 8 GB/s on DRAM-sized buffers, so the prefetches are what feed N1's DRAM stream. They cost 5–13% on N1's cache-resident sizes, though, so the direction seems to be fewer or later prefetches rather than none.

**Feedback wanted:**
- Has anyone tuned crc32c on other aarch64 cores (Graviton, Grace, Ampere One)? Numbers from there would show whether the N1 loss is general.
- Would per-size dispatch (keep 1024-byte blocks below some size) be acceptable, or should one loop be tuned for both?

Testing: checked against a bytewise `__crc32cb` reference for every length 0..10000 at all 8 alignments with 5 seeds, for data and NULL buffers, on both cores. Adds a unit test (`BlockBoundaries`) covering every length across several blocks at every alignment against `ceph_crc32c_sctp`.

73459.title: msg/async: crc large rx data segments as they arrive
73459.author: dvanders
73459.body:
**Draft, for feedback on the approach.** Not ready: see the open problems below.

In crc mode, a msgr2 receiver checks each segment's crc32c in the epilogue, in one pass over the whole segment after all of it has been read. That pass runs on the connection's only worker, which reads nothing from the socket meanwhile: ~0.8 ms for a 24 MiB segment on Apple M5, ~2 ms on Neoverse-N1. If the socket receive buffer is smaller than what arrives in that time, it fills, the sender's `sendmsg()` blocks, and the connection stalls once per large message. crc32c itself isn't slow (~30 GB/s on M5); the cost is the stall. On a single connection with 24 MiB objects, macOS loses 2.7x to data crc, 4 MiB objects 1.3x. How much a host loses depends on its receive buffer ceiling: macOS autotunes to 4 MiB, Ubuntu's default `tcp_rmem` stops at 6 MiB, and hosts tuned past the segment size don't stall.

**Commits**
1. `msg/async/ProtocolV2: crc large rx data segments as they arrive`: read segments larger than `ms_crc_data_rx_chunk_size` (new, default 1 MiB, 0 disables) in chunks, fold each chunk into a running crc32c, and have FrameAssembler check that against the epilogue instead of rescanning. Only crc mode is affected; secure mode and the msgr2.1 first segment are unchanged.
2. A FrameAssembler unit test with a precomputed rx crc (fails if the precomputed value is ignored).
3. **WIP**, replacing 1's extra reads:
   - rx: crc whatever each socket read delivered as it lands (`ms_crc_data_rx_incremental`), and cache the result on the buffer (`buffer::ptr::set_crc32c_cache`), so the OSD's later `list::crc32c()` for the object data digest still hits the cache.
   - tx: while the socket is full, crc the next queued message's data 1 MiB at a time (`ms_crc_data_tx_incremental`), cache-aware, and hand FrameAssembler the precomputed value.
   - Tests: `PrecomputedTxCrcTest`, `BufferPtr.crc32c_cache`.

**Results**, rados bench with 24 MiB objects, 1 memstore OSD over loopback, GB/s (Linux: mean of two interleaved runs), for commit 1:

| | write | rand t=1 | t=4 | t=16 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **macOS 27, Apple M5 Max** (rcvbuf max 4 MiB) | | | | |
| before | 5.9 | 4.0 | 5.2 | ~5.0 |
| chunk size 1 MiB | 6.3 | 6.0 | 10.5 | 10.0 |
| ms_crc_data=false | 12.3 | 6.2 | 13.8 | 11.2 |
| **Ubuntu 24.04, Neoverse-N1, 16 cores** (tcp_rmem max 6 MiB) | | | | |
| before | 1.34 | 0.79 | 0.99 | 1.00 |
| chunk size 1 MiB | 1.33 | 0.81 | 1.09 | 1.09 |
| ms_crc_data=false | 1.65 | 0.89 | 1.12 | 1.10 |
| **Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64, 8 cores** (tcp_rmem max 32 MiB) | | | | |
| before | 2.16 | 1.61 | 1.59 | 1.62 |
| chunk size 1 MiB | 2.04 | 1.41 | 1.59 | 1.65 |
| ms_crc_data=false | 2.51 | 1.76 | 1.81 | 1.76 |

Where the receive buffer is smaller than the segment, chunking recovers most of what crc costs reads. Where it is larger there is no stall to remove, and the extra reads cost ~12% with one read in flight and ~5% on writes (the x86 host).

Commit 3 avoids the extra reads: 2x reads on macOS, neutral on x86.

**Open problems:**
- On N1, commit 3 gives no read gain on memstore, and an unexplained ~10% read loss on BlueStore (a brd RAM disk, where crc off reads the same 1.0 GB/s, so crc isn't the limit there). Next step is perf on N1, and capping the crc work per callback.
- Writes on macOS stay at ~6.2 vs 11.8 GB/s with crc off: the client's sending thread is CPU-bound (52% `sendmsg`, 23% crc), so moving crc into idle time can't halve it. That needs crc off-thread or zero-copy send (related: #70638 MSG_ZEROCOPY, and #66377 for client-supplied crcs through the buffer cache).

**Feedback wanted:** is computing the crc incrementally in the read path (and caching it on the buffer) acceptable in msgr2, or would you rather see the chunked reads (commit 1) alone, off by default? And does anyone see the same stall on production hosts with default `tcp_rmem`?

73462.author: anthonyeleven

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/65424

On the hardware monitoring page, the "For Developers" section shows the docstring of `unittest.mock.Mock` ("Create a new Mock object…") for every `NodeProxyEndpoint` method. The docstrings in `cephadm/agent.py` don't appear.

The `ceph-mgr-commands` directive in `api/mon_command_api.rst` and the `mgr_module` directive import the mgr modules with `cherrypy` and other dependencies replaced by `unittest.mock.Mock`. Afterwards they remove the mocks from `sys.modules`, but the mgr modules stay imported. Sphinx reads `api/` before `hardware-monitoring/`, so autodoc finds `cephadm.agent` already imported. By then each endpoint method is the Mock that the mocked `@cherrypy.expose` returned.

This makes two changes:
- After each mocked import, unload the mgr modules that it imported, so that autodoc imports them again.
- Add `cherrypy` to `admin/doc-requirements.txt`, so that `cephadm.agent` can be imported without the mocks. I first tried `cherrypy` in `autodoc_mock_imports`, but Sphinx's mock unwraps only one of the four stacked decorators, so the methods were dropped from the page.

I tested it with Read the Docs-style builds of main and of this branch:
- Python 3.12, `READTHEDOCS=True`, `dirhtml`, and the packages from `.readthedocs.yml`, including the pybind stubs.
- On this branch, the section shows the endpoint docstrings, with parameters, return types, and the 404 that they raise. No Mock text is left.
- In the full build, 634 of 635 pages are identical, and the warnings are identical. The changed page is the hardware monitoring page. The other autodoc pages that import mgr modules, `mgr/modules` and `mgr/orchestrator_modules`, are unchanged.
- Each change is needed:
  - With `cherrypy` installed but without the unload, the page still shows the Mock text.
  - Without `cherrypy`, a fresh import of `cephadm.agent` fails with `No module named 'cherrypy'`.

It cherry-picks cleanly to umbrella, tentacle, and squid. I've built it only on main.

73463.title: client: keep a snapshot directory's request path while it is open
73463.author: dvanders
73463.body:
A libcephfs readdir of a large snapshot directory can continue in the **live** directory partway through, with no error. The caller gets a mix of snapshot and live names, and an incomplete snapshot listing. https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82652 has the details and a reproducer. It reproduces on main, v21.2.0, v20.2.5 and v19.2.7, each with its own client and MDS. With `client_cache_size = 100`, a 3000-entry snapshot listing returned 1539 snapshot entries and 1485 live ones. ceph-fuse is not affected in testing, because the kernel's lookup reference keeps the dentry pinned.

**Cause.** For each readdir (and readdir_snapdiff) request, the client rebuilds the directory's request path with `Inode::make_nosnap_relative_path()`. For a snapshot inode, that walks the inode's dentries up to the snapdir. The open `dir_result_t` pins the inode, but not those dentries. Once the client cache trims them, the path falls back to `#<ino>`, which the MDS serves as the head directory:

```
readdir #0x10000000000//s1
trim_dentry unlinking dn s1 in dir 0x10000000000
readdir #0x10000000000 arg2='f_03701'      <- the live directory
```

readdir_snapdiff hits the same fallback, but gets -EINVAL, because the MDS rejects a snapdiff on the head. That is how this was found.

**Fix.** Take the request path of a snapshot directory when it is opened, while its dentries are known to be there, and use it for its readdir and snapdiff requests.

**Test.** The new `LibCephFS.SnapReaddirAfterDentryTrim` reads a 3000-entry snapshot directory with `client_cache_size = 100`, statting 2000 other files after the first 50 entries. On a vstart cluster (main):
- passes with this change;
- fails without it, by running the same test binary with an unfixed libcephfs: 1485 live entries;
- the other 30 `LibCephFS.*Snap*`, `*Readdir*` and `*Dir*` tests pass.

Other callers of `make_nosnap_relative_path()` on snapshot inodes (getattr, lookup, open) may hit the same fallback. They are not changed here.

73468.title: client,libcephfs: open snapdiff streams on subdirectories without a path walk
73468.author: dvanders
73468.body:
**Draft.** It depends on #73463: its first two commits are that PR. A walk that opens subdirectories this way keeps a snapshot directory's stream open for a long time, which is exactly what triggers https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82652.

A recursive snapdiff walk, like the one cephfs-mirror does, opens every subdirectory with `ceph_open_snapdiff2()`. That opens the directory by its full path in *both* snapshots, then the first readdir fetches attributes for "." and "..", and every subdirectory entry served from the reply buffer gets a getattr with rstats. That adds up to about **7 MDS requests per directory for 1 snapdiff request**. On a tree of many small directories, those requests, not the diff, are what the MDS spends its time on: about half its CPU goes to the messenger.

- **`ceph_open_snapdiff2_at(parent, name, &out)`** (and `SnapDiffHandle2.openat()` in the Python binding) opens a subdirectory's stream on the inode that the parent's snapdiff reply already put in the client cache. It needs no requests and starts past "." and "..". If the entry is no longer cached it returns -ENOENT, and the caller opens it by path as before.
- **No getattr for snapdiff entries served from the reply buffer.** They are snapshot inodes the MDS just sent.

Same 1M files, 1% changed between two snapshots, vstart (1 MDS, 3 OSDs), one client walking the whole tree:

| tree | before: wall / MDS CPU / requests | after: wall / MDS CPU / requests |
|---|---|---|
| 10,000 dirs x 100 files, warm | 26.8s / 14.7s / ~71,000 | **4.4s / 2.4s / 10,012** |
| 10,000 dirs x 100 files, cold | 49.8s / 29.9s | **25.2s / 16.6s** |
| 100 dirs x 10,000 files, warm | 1.03s / 0.62s / 1,405 | 0.77s / 0.49s / 806 |

The remaining cold cost is the MDS loading directories into its cache, which a separate MDS PR addresses.

**Credit.** https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/75885 raised the same problem: `ceph_open_snapdiff()` resolves the full path for every directory of a large scan. #68229 by @sajibreadd addressed it with `ceph_ll_open_snapdiff()` on inodes, and was closed as stale. This takes the same idea, opening the stream on an inode the client already has, as a call on the parent stream, so a walker needs no inode handles of its own.

**Testing**
- The new `LibCephFS.SnapDiffOpenAt` walks a nested tree after every kind of change snapdiff reports: an attribute change deep down, a file deleted and one created, a directory tree created and one deleted, a directory moved to another parent, a file replaced by a directory. It checks that a walk using `ceph_open_snapdiff2_at()` returns exactly the entries of a walk by path.
- The same comparison on the benchmark trees: identical output for 10,062 and 19,962 entries.
- `ceph_test_libcephfs_snapdiff` on vstart: all tests pass, including `SnapDiffOpenAt` (`SnapDiffHardlinkReplicaInode` is skipped; it needs two active ranks).

73470.title: mds: load only the entries a snapdiff can report when it fetches a directory
73470.author: dvanders
73470.body:
**Draft, for feedback on the approach.**

When a `readdir_snapdiff` finds a dirfrag not in cache, the MDS fetches the whole dirfrag into its cache, like readdir, and then reports only what changed between the two snapshots. On a cold walk of a tree where 1% of 1M files changed, the MDS built **~1.02M cache inodes to report ~10k entries**, and loading the dirfrags (decode, allocation, cache insertion) was **83% of its CPU** for the walk. The diff itself barely shows up in a profile. When the tree doesn't fit in the cache, the walk also evicts its own directories, so even a second walk re-fetches everything, and other clients' metadata goes with them.

- **`CDir::fetch_snapdiff()`** reads the dirfrag like `fetch()`, but loads only the entries `build_snap_diff()` can report, through the partial-load path of `_omap_fetched()`; the dirfrag stays incomplete. It skips:
  - dentries in neither snapshot, or only in between them (decided from the key and the dentry's first snapid alone);
  - primary file dentries that span both snapshots and have no old_inodes. `build_snap_diff()` passes over those as unchanged.
  
  Entries already in the cache are left to `build_snap_diff()` as today (e.g. pending snapflushes need cached inodes). The request pins what was loaded, so trimming can't drop it before the diff runs.
- **`InodeStoreBase::peek_bare()`** reads only the mode and the old_inodes count of a stored inode, and skips everything else by length. It falls back to a full decode for encodings older than inode_t struct_v 6. `unittest_mds_inode_peek` checks it against `decode_bare()` on every combination of the fields it skips.
- **Only under cache pressure.** A dirfrag loaded in part stays incomplete, so the next readdir or snapdiff of it reads it from RADOS again. With room in the cache, a full load is the better deal. So the partial load is used once the cache holds `mds_snapdiff_fetch_changed_only_cache_ratio` (default 0.5) of `mds_cache_memory_limit`. `mds_snapdiff_fetch_changed_only` (default true) turns it off.
- **New perf counters** `dir_fetch_snapdiff` and `dir_fetch_snapdiff_skipped` count these fetches and the dentries they didn't load.

Results: vstart (1 MDS, 3 OSDs), 1M files, 1% changed between two snapshots, one client walking the whole tree. MDS CPU seconds:

| | 100 dirs x 10k files, cold | warm | 10k dirs x 100 files, cold | warm | cache inodes loaded (cold) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| before, 8 GiB cache | 5.83 | 0.49 | 16.49 | 2.47 | 1.02M / 1.03M |
| this PR, 8 GiB cache (below the ratio: full loads) | 6.27 | 0.48 | 12.90 | 2.07 | 1.02M / 1.03M |
| this PR, ratio 0 (always partial) | **1.54** | 1.73 | **5.72** | 5.87 | **34k / 48k** |
| before, 1 GiB cache | 6.23 | 5.98 | 14.95 | 12.77 | 488k / 359k |
| this PR, 1 GiB cache | **2.60** | **1.08** | **5.19** | **3.55** | 222k / 220k |

This is the case `LibCephFS.HugeSnapDiffSmallDelta` exercises (https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82300, #73245), and it may help there.

**Correctness.** The diff of a cold walk, with the option off and with the partial load forced (ratio 0), is identical on three trees:
- a nested tree with every kind of change (47 entries);
- 100 x 10k files (10,062 entries);
- 10k x 100 files (19,962 entries).

The skip rules must stay in step with `build_snap_diff()`; the comment on `snapdiff_skippable()` says so. They are compatible with #71936 (comparing projected inodes): projections only exist for cached inodes, and those are never skipped.

**Open questions**
- Is a partial load into an incomplete dirfrag acceptable here, or should snapdiff build its reply without the cache for the skipped part?
- Is cache use the right gate, and is 0.5 the right default?
- None of the existing snapdiff tests diffs a directory the MDS has to fetch: their directories stay in the cache, so they never reach this code, old or new. The new test below does. Should a qa job also run the whole snapdiff suite with a small cache and ratio 0?

**Testing**
- `unittest_md

73471.title: qa/tasks/mds_thrash: reset the start limit of cephadm MDS units
73471.author: vshankar
73471.body:
With cephadm, stopping and starting an MDS goes through its systemd unit, which allows 5 starts in 30 minutes (StartLimitBurst). Thrashing gets there quickly, as each start counts, manual or not. The MDS then fails to start:

```
17:43:52.409 INFO:tasks.cephadm.mds.c:Restarting mds.c (starting--it wasn't running)...
17:43:52.411 DEBUG:...trial035:> sudo systemctl start ceph-8a88d0f4-d7aa-11f1-a943-d404e6e7d460@mds.c 17:43:52.478 ...stderr:Job for ceph-8a88d0f4-d7aa-11f1-a943-d404e6e7d460@mds.c.service failed.
17:43:52.802 ...systemd[1]: ceph-8a88d0f4-d7aa-11f1-a943-d404e6e7d460@mds.c.service: Start request repeated too quickly.
```
and the thrasher dies with CommandFailedError, about 20 minutes into a job. Nothing fails the job until teardown, so the workload runs on without MDS thrashing in the meantime.

Reset the unit's start limit before reviving an MDS, as is done for OSDs in ceph_manager.revive_osd(). Ignore the exit status: the command fails with "Unit ... not loaded" if systemd has already unloaded the stopped unit, in which case there is no count to reset.

73473.title: qa/multi: test metadata sync update ordering

73474.title: client: preserve cached readdir offsets across snapdiff
73474.author: LiShengG
73474.body:
Snapdiff replies enumerate a delta rather than a complete directory, but insert_readdir_results() stores their positions in shared Dentry objects. This changes offsets in an already complete and ordered readdir cache, causing subsequent ordinary reads to skip entries or repeat them when resuming from a saved cookie.

Compute each reply position locally and copy it into the stream buffer. Only ordinary readdir requests update Dentry::offset, preserving cached full-directory positions without changing snapdiff pagination.

Add regression coverage for colliding names, for same-name deletion and recreation including an active directory stream and a seekdir cookie, and for the entries a reply attributes to the older snapshot, which go to the stream's own directory rather than to the opponent one. The three new tests pass on vstart with the fix and fail without it.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82534

73475.title: rgw/beast: send small responses without waiting for Nagle's algorithm
73475.author: dvanders
73475.body:
With default settings, an S3 GET of a small object from the beast frontend takes **~40 ms**, which caps a keep-alive connection at ~25 small GETs per second. https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82657 has the details.

**Cause.** RGW writes the response headers (`ClientIO::complete_header()` flushes them) and then the body (`send_body()`) as separate writes. Beast sets `TCP_NODELAY` only with `tcp_nodelay=1` in `rgw_frontends`, and the default is 0. With Nagle's algorithm enabled, a body smaller than a segment waits until the client acknowledges the headers, and Linux clients delay that ACK by up to 40 ms. The option was added in #27008 (2019) to match civetweb's, with Nagle on as the default. Neither cephadm nor Rook sets it. The same mechanism added 40 ms to RGW's own requests to Open Policy Agent in https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/52067.

**This PR fixes it twice**, so that a deployment that sets `tcp_nodelay=0` explicitly is fixed too:
1. **`tcp_nodelay` defaults to 1** (doc and PendingReleaseNotes updated); `tcp_nodelay=0` restores Nagle's algorithm.
2. **The headers go out with the start of the body.** `complete_header()` leaves them in the output buffer, and the first `send_body()` writes headers and body as one gathered `async_write`. A response without a body has its headers flushed in `complete_request()`, which every request reaches. This also saves a send per response.

**Results.** vstart, 1 memstore OSD, 1 radosgw (`rgw_thread_pool_size=512`), 16 clients each with one keep-alive connection, anonymous GETs of public-read objects, 20 s per run:

| | 4 KiB GETs/s | p50 | RGW CPU per 4 KiB GET | 64 KiB GETs/s | RGW CPU per 64 KiB GET |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| main, default (`tcp_nodelay=0`) | 381 | 42.0 ms | 1,578 µs* | 9,333 | 855 µs |
| main, `tcp_nodelay=1` | 10,031 | 1.55 ms | 821 µs | 9,116 | 879 µs |
| this PR, default | **10,450** | **1.50 ms** | 746 µs | 9,307 | 813 µs |
| this PR, `tcp_nodelay=0` | **10,491** | **1.49 ms** | 745 µs | 9,310 | 811 µs |

\* RGW's fixed background CPU divided over only 381 requests per second.

**Testing.** Besides the runs above, an S3 check passes with this PR in all three `tcp_nodelay` modes:
- boto3 PUT/GET/HEAD of 0 B, 1 B, 4 KiB, 64 KiB and 5 MiB multipart objects;
- a ranged GET, a listing, and a 404 with its error body;
- 20 raw keep-alive requests and responses on one connection, with each response's framing checked;
- a GET following a HEAD on the same connection.

73498.title: common/options, doc/rados: describe the RDMA messenger options
73498.author: anthonyeleven
73498.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/65537

None of the 16 `ms_async_rdma_*` options had a description, and the docs mentioned `async+rdma` only in the `ms_type` text. This describes each option from what `src/msg/async/rdma` does with it, and adds an RDMA section to the network configuration reference with the setup checks: the TCP handshake, the device, port, and GID, the locked-memory limit, and containers. It also lists `ms_public_type` and `ms_cluster_type`, which were not rendered anywhere.

Points for a messenger developer to check:

- `ms_async_rdma_local_gid` and `ms_async_rdma_roce_ver` are read only under `HAVE_IBV_EXP`, which `cmake/modules/Findverbs.cmake` sets only when `ibv_exp_query_gid_attr()` compiles. Builds against rdma-core use `ms_async_rdma_gid_idx` alone.
- `ms_async_rdma_dscp` is written to the GRH traffic class (`Infiniband.cc`), so the text says to set 4 times the DSCP; the default 96 is DSCP 24.
- The example puts only the cluster network on RDMA (`ms_cluster_type async+rdma`). Is that the setup to show?
- Under cephadm, only NFS daemons with `enable_rdma` get `/dev/infiniband` and `memlock=-1`. The text tells readers to check device access and the memlock limit for other daemons rather than claiming they work.

@tchaikov @dkelson, would you take a look? You reviewed and wrote #69614, the last fix in `msg/async/rdma`.

73499.title: qa: avoid admin socket timeouts after OSD restart
73499.author: kamoltat
73499.body:
Based on @amathuria initial investigations: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/59079#note-51

Problem:
The recovery-preemption test sends admin-socket config changes after
restarting osd.1 without waiting for it to come up. BlueStore can still
be mounting while OSD::init() holds osd_lock, causing the config handler
to block and the admin-socket commands to time out.

Solution:
Set the recovery options after the initial healthy check, before the
restart sequence, to avoid sending config changes during OSD startup.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/59079
Assisted-by: Co-pilot
Signed-off-by: Kamoltat (Junior) Sirivadhna <ksirivad@redhat.com>

73500.title: mgr/cephadm: check for hosts being logged into container registry
73500.author: adk3798
73500.body:
This patch changes a few things in order to handle cases where a host is no longer logged into a registry but nothing triggers cephadm to attempt to log it back in. The triggers for logins prior to this patch are

- New registry login credentials are added (adds all hosts)
- A host is newly added to the cluster (just that host)
- The entire metadata for a host is invalidated (happens when a host's addr is changed or it is taken out of offline/maintenance status)
- mgr failover (adds all hosts)

This patch now checks the login status during gather-facts if the module find login credentials available. If we check and are not logged in that host is added to the registry login queue.

This patch also now has us mark the existence of login credentials at mgr startup or when new credentials are provided. That should cover the only times we'd need to assuming nobody is manually changing the mgr/cephadm/registry_credentials mon db entry.

We also now kick the serve loop after storing new credentials in order to make the login happen quicker in cases where the serve loop was idle.

Signed-off-by: Adam King <adking@redhat.com>

Resolves: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82680

73505.title: doc/cephfs: re-add extra data pools after Monitor store loss
73505.author: anthonyeleven
73505.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/68682

The procedure for recovering a file system after losing every Monitor store recreates it with `ceph fs new --recover` and one data pool, and said only that extra data pools "need to be reapplied later". The reporter couldn't add their erasure-coded data pool back: the rebuilt OSDMap keeps each pool's `cephfs` application tag, and `ceph fs add_data_pool` refuses any pool that has one (it calls `_check_pool()` with `force` false). This adds the steps that worked for the reporter: remove the tag with `ceph osd pool application rm`, then run `ceph fs add_data_pool`, which sets the tag again. The steps come before the MDS daemons join, because `Server::is_valid_layout()` refuses creates in a directory whose layout names a pool that isn't attached. The page now also says that the data pool given to `ceph fs new` is the default data pool.

Question for CephFS: is removing the tag the procedure you want documented, or should `add_data_pool` accept a pool that's tagged for the same file system?

@vshankar @neesingh-rh, would you take a look? Venky assigned the tracker issue to Neeraj in 2024-11.

73506.title: mgr/cephadm: never deploy an agent without listener credentials
73506.author: rkachach
73506.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82701

### Problem

The cephadm agent's listener, which receives mgr → agent messages, needs a TLS certificate and key. The mgr only generates them when the agent spec has `ssl: true` and `certificate_source: cephadm-signed`. `_apply_agent()` sets both, but no other path enforces them:

- An agent spec applied by hand (`ceph orch apply -i agent.yaml`) defaults to `ssl: false`.
- Agent specs stored by older releases (e.g. tentacle) have no `ssl`, because the agent service there always generated a certificate. After an upgrade, any agent deployed or reconfigured from such a spec is affected.

With such a spec, `get_certificates()` returns empty credentials, and `CephadmAgent.generate_config()` writes an empty `listener.crt` and `listener.key`. The cephadm binary only checks that these files exist. The agent then starts in a broken state:

- `MgrListener` sets up TLS outside any `try`, so `load_cert_chain()` fails and only the listener thread dies.
- The agent keeps sending reports, and the systemd unit stays `active`.
- Every mgr → agent message is refused. Each refusal marks the host out of date again, so the mgr retries on every report.
- `ceph orch redeploy agent` doesn't help, because it regenerates the config from the same spec.

### Changes

1. **python-common: agent specs always use cephadm-signed TLS.** A new `AgentSpec` defaults `ssl` to `true` and `certificate_source` to `cephadm-signed`, and rejects any other value. Specs written by hand or stored by older releases are normalized on apply and on load. Stored specs never contain `ssl: false`, because the field is only serialized when it's true, so existing specs keep loading.
2. **mgr/cephadm: refuse to generate agent config with empty TLS credentials.** `generate_config()` raises an `OrchestratorError`, so the deploy or reconfig fails with an error event instead of leaving behind an agent that can't be reached.
3. **mgr/cephadm: migrate stored agent specs and reconfigure agents without listener certs.** Migration 11 → 12 runs after startup, because it needs the cert store. It:
   - saves the normalized agent spec, patching the stored JSON as `migrate_9_10` does;
   - schedules one reconfig over SSH for every agent whose host has no agent listener certificate in the cert store.

   Agents that already have a certificate are left alone.
4. **cephadm: reject an empty agent listener cert or key.** `CephadmAgent.validate()` also rejects an empty `listener.crt`, `listener.key` or `root_cert.pem`. It runs before anything is written, both on deploy/reconfig over SSH and on config push over HTTP.
5. **cephadm: exit the agent if its listener cannot start.**
   - The listener's socket and TLS setup now run in `MgrListener.setup()`, which is called before any agent thread starts. If it fails, the agent exits with a clear error.
   - If the listener thread stops on an unexpected error later, the agent exits too.
   - The agent unit gets bounded restarts (`StartLimitInterval=30min`, `StartLimitBurst=5`), so a broken agent ends up `failed` instead of restarting forever. A reconfig or redeploy already runs `systemctl reset-failed`.

node-proxy is out of scope here and will be handled separately.

### Testing

Each commit includes its own unit tests:

- `python-common`: `AgentSpec` normalization (missing `ssl` / `certificate_source`), and rejection of `ssl: false` or a non-cephadm-signed source.
- `mgr/cephadm`: an agent spec without

73507.title: mgr/cephadm: detect and handle unreachable agents
73507.author: rkachach
73507.body:
## Problem

With `use_agent=true`, the mgr talks to each agent in both directions:

- the agent sends metadata to the mgr's agent endpoint;
- the mgr connects to the agent's listener port to request fresh metadata (ack counter) and to push config changes.

When the first path works but the second doesn't (listener failed to start, firewall, TLS mismatch), cephadm doesn't detect it:

- **No health warning.** `CEPHADM_AGENT_DOWN` only fires when an agent stops reporting.
- **No back-off.** Every processed report with a stale ack starts a new `AgentMessageThread`. Each thread retries with 3 s and 5 s sleeps and then logs an ERROR.
- **Log flooding.** There is one ERROR per report per host, and the message threads contend on the logging lock.
- **Reconciliation stalls.** `_apply_all_services()` applies only the agent spec while any online host's metadata is not up to date. A host whose agent never acknowledges the latest counter is never up to date, so every other spec is held back indefinitely.
- **Silent listener failure.** If the agent's listener fails at startup (for example, `ssl.SSLError: [SSL] PEM lib` with an empty listener cert/key), the agent keeps reporting. The mgr only finds out by failing to connect.
- **No visibility.** No command shows which agents the mgr can reach.

## Changes

1. **`mgr/cephadm: track mgr->agent failures per host and back off`**
   - The mgr keeps an in-memory reachability record per host.
   - After a failed message, the mgr waits before retrying the host: 30 s, doubling up to 10 min. No ack requests or HTTP config pushes are sent to the host until then.
   - A host counts as unreachable after 3 consecutive failures.
   - A successful message clears the back-off. So does an SSH deploy/reconfig, which keeps the failure totals for reporting.

2. **`mgr/cephadm: add CEPHADM_AGENT_UNREACHABLE health warning`**
   - Lists agents that report but can't be reached, with the port, since when, and the last error.
   - Grace period after a deploy: max(120 s, agent-down threshold). After a mgr failover, the daemon's `last_deployed` is used.
   - Skips hosts already in `CEPHADM_AGENT_DOWN`, and offline, maintenance and draining hosts.
   - Only pushed to the mon when its content changes.

3. **`mgr/cephadm: summarize agent message failures once per pass`**
   - Per-message failures and recoveries are logged at DEBUG.
   - The serve loop logs one WARNING summary at most once a minute: failed messages, the hosts with the most failures and their last error, and the unreachable and recovered counts.

4. **`cephadm: report the agent listener state in metadata`**
   - Agent: `MgrListener` tracks `starting`, `listening` or `failed`. A startup failure is caught and logged once. Each report carries `"listener": {"state": ..., "error": ...}`.
   - Mgr: a `failed` listener flags the host as unreachable at once, with no grace period and no message threads. When the agent reports its listener is back, the back-off is cleared.
   - Older agents and older mgrs are still compatible.

5. **`mgr/cephadm: don't hold back service apply for unreachable agents`**
   - Hosts with unreachable agents no longer block non-agent specs.
   - The wait for the other hosts is capped at max(300 s, 5 × agent-down threshold). Once the cap is hit, a single WARNING names the stale hosts.
   - `all_host_metadata_up_to_date()` is unchanged, so the upgrade still waits for every host.

6. **`mgr/cephadm: show agent reachability and ack state per host`**
   - New command `ceph cephadm agent-status [<hostname>] [--format plain|json|json-pretty|yaml]`. It shows the last report, metadata/ack state, listener state, reachability, failures, retry time and last error.
   - `ceph orch ps` shows agent daemons as `running, unreachable` or `running, listener down`. Only the returned copy is changed, not the daemon cache.

7. **`doc/cephadm: troubleshoot unreachable agents`**
   - Adds the health check entry to the operations guide.
   - Adds an "Unreachable C

73510.title: mds: finish resolve when no peer is in the recovery set
73510.author: xiubli
73510.body:
If a rank fails while every other in rank is still `up:creating` (e.g. rank 0
fails right after `max_mds` was raised from 1 to 2), the replacement enters
`up:resolve` with an empty recovery set, because `get_recovery_mds_set()` does
not include `up:creating`. It sends no resolves and receives none. Since
`maybe_resolve_finish()` is only called from `handle_resolve()`, the rank
stays in `up:resolve` forever. The new rank does not send resolves when it
goes active either, because the map was already resolving when it joined.
The daemon keeps beaconing `up:resolve`, so the monitor never replaces it and
the file system stays degraded until the rank is failed by hand.
sending the subtree resolves, finish resolve when the resolve, resolve-ack
and rollback gathers are all empty.

This is the same failover/scale-up race as https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/80402
(#71644), but an earlier window: there the new rank is already active when
the recovering rank enters resolve, here it is still creating. The two
changes are independent.

### Testing

New qa test `tasks.cephfs.test_resolve` (added to `fs:functional`). It keeps
the new rank in `up:creating` with `mds_sleep_rank_change`, fails rank 0, and
checks that rank 0 gets past `up:resolve` while rank 1 is still creating. It
then checks that both daemons are kept and that a directory pinned to rank 1
is exported to it.

Local vstart_runner:
- main without the fix: rank 0 stays in `up:resolve` with an empty
  `resolve_gather` (test fails)
- main with the fix: the test passes; rank 0 logs
  `send_subtree_resolves no peers to wait for` followed by `resolve_done`

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82668

73511.title: build: keep sccache keys stable across shas in CI builds
73511.author: djgalloway
73511.body:
CI builds (ceph-dev-pipeline sets `CEPH_BUILD_NORMALIZE_PATHS=true`) leak the git sha into compiler arguments. rpm's `%autosetup` unpacks into `rpmbuild/BUILD/ceph-<ver>-g<sha>/`, and on noble/resolute Ubuntu's dpkg maps the build dir to `/usr/src/ceph-<ver>-g<sha>-1noble` through `-fdebug-prefix-map`. Both change with every commit, so sccache keys never match an earlier build.

When `CEPH_BUILD_NORMALIZE_PATHS` is set, this unpacks the rpm sources into a version-free `rpmbuild/BUILD/ceph` and sets `DEB_BUILD_DEBUGPATH=/usr/src/ceph` for the deb build. Builds without that variable are unchanged.

Verified in ceph-dev-pipeline: after a cold build of this branch, rebuilding a new sha with identical sources raised the sccache hit rate on centos9, rocky10 and noble from the usual 17% / 17% / 2% to 99%, the same as jammy. The remaining misses are the files that include `ceph_ver.h`.

73512.title: reef: rgw: restrict SSE-KMS key ids to their tenant or bucket owner
73512.author: vupn0712
73512.body:
## Summary

https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82278

Backport of #73225 to reef.

RGW takes the SSE-KMS key id straight from the client's header (or the bucket's `PutBucketEncryption` default) and hands it to whatever KMS backend is configured, without ever checking it actually belongs to the caller's tenant or the bucket owner. Since RGW talks to the KMS backend under one shared, RGW-wide credential rather than the caller's own identity, any tenant who knows another tenant's key id can just use it -- the real owner's key policy never comes into play.

This adds an off-by-default option, `rgw_crypt_s3_kms_key_scope` (`none`/`tenant`/`owner`), that requires the key id to start with an owner prefix before RGW will use it.

On reef, that covers PUT, POST and multipart init -- every write path that actually resolves a key id and encrypts. CopyObject is not covered here: on reef the copy path never encrypts the destination at all, so there's no key id to check in the first place. That's existing reef behavior, unrelated to this change -- see #73513 for the follow-up that makes CopyObject fail loudly instead of silently storing plaintext.

Tested end to end against a real single-node cluster with a real HashiCorp Vault transit backend, both `tenant` and `owner` scope modes, plus a batch of key ids specifically crafted to try to slip past the prefix check.

## Test plan

- [x] Same testing as #73225 -- real Vault 1.15.6, both scope modes, cross-tenant key rejected, unrecognized key id rejected (fail closed).
- [ ] CI

73513.title: reef: rgw: refuse CopyObject that would silently drop encryption
73513.author: vupn0712
73513.body:
## Summary

https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82707

On reef, CopyObject never actually encrypts the destination object -- a separate, pre-existing gap from #73435. Right now a CopyObject request that sends `x-amz-server-side-encryption*` headers, or that targets a bucket with default encryption turned on, still comes back 200, but the copy gets written as plaintext. The client has no way to know that happened; it looks like the copy succeeded and got encrypted when it didn't. Copying *from* an already-encrypted source is already refused with `501 NotImplemented` in `RGWRados::copy_obj()`.

The fix here is just consistency: return that same 501 when the destination would need encryption too, instead of silently dropping it, so the client can fall back to GET + PUT, which does encrypt correctly. Any `x-amz-server-side-encryption*` header triggers it, so does a bucket encryption policy on the destination -- including the case of copying an object onto itself just to update metadata in such a bucket, which used to succeed and quietly leave it unencrypted.

The check sits in `verify_params()`, after `verify_permission()`, so someone without write access to the destination still just gets 403 and can't use this to probe whether a bucket has encryption configured. Swift COPY isn't affected, since Swift PUT doesn't apply S3 bucket default encryption either.

main doesn't need this -- it already encrypts CopyObject destinations properly, so this is reef-only.

## Test plan

- [ ] CI
- [ ] Manual check against a lab cluster that the 501 actually fires in each of the three trigger cases above

73514.title: squid: rgw: apply bucket default encryption to CopyObject
73514.author: vupn0712
73514.body:
## Summary

https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82706

squid is missing main's CopyObject encryption machinery entirely -- no `RGWCopyObjDPF`, no `DataProcessorFactory`, no decrypt/re-encrypt on copy. So before the actual fix (backport of #73435) can even apply, this first backports the 18 existing main commits that build that machinery, then adds the two #73435 commits on top.

End result on squid: copying into a bucket with default encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS) and no explicit SSE headers now gets encrypted with the bucket default, matching PutObject/PostObject/CreateMultipartUpload and AWS. That's the actual bug being fixed -- see #73435 for the full writeup.

Side effect of pulling in main's CopyObject machinery: squid can now also copy *from* an encrypted source (it decrypts and re-encrypts), where it used to just return `501 NotImplemented`.

One thing this does *not* include yet: `rgw_crypt_s3_kms_key_scope` (#73225 / #73512) isn't backported to squid, so CopyObject on squid doesn't get that tenant/owner key check yet. Once that backport exists, it'll cover CopyObject for free -- both PUT and CopyObject go through the same `rgw_s3_prepare_encrypt()`. Tracking that as a separate follow-up rather than bundling it in here.

Conflicts hit while cherry-picking are noted in the individual commit messages -- mostly squid lacking a few things main has since picked up (bucket logging journal records, `x-amz-tagging-directive` handling, checksums on complete()).

## Test plan

- [x] s3-tests included (cherry-picked CopyObject/UploadPart encryption tests, plus the new bucket-default-encryption copy tests).
- [ ] Not deployed/tested against a live lab cluster yet -- only built as RPMs so far.
- [ ] CI

73515.title: rgw: don't log the TOTP code from a malformed x-amz-mfa header
73515.author: vupn0712
73515.body:
## Summary

https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82480

When `x-amz-mfa` doesn't split into exactly `<serial> <code>` on a single space (say, a TAB between them), `verify_mfa()` logs the whole header at level 5 before refusing the request -- TOTP code included. The request gets rejected, but the code itself was never consumed, so it's still valid for the device's window (two 30s steps either side by default), which is plenty of time for whoever can read the log to turn around and replay it in a well-formed header.

`debug_rgw`'s default gather level is 1/5, so the line sits in the in-memory log even at default settings and comes out via `ceph daemon <rgw> log dump` or a crash dump -- both of which tend to travel further than the credential they'd be carrying (support bundles, log shipping, etc).

Fix is just to stop logging the raw header and log the field count instead -- still tells you the header was malformed, without ever putting a live code somewhere a log ends up.

## Test plan

- [ ] Not built or run -- it's a one-line log message change with no behavior change (still returns the same -EINVAL either way).
- [ ] CI

73516.title: client: close-to-open consistency and NFS-style attribute/dentry caching
73516.author: dvanders
73516.body:
A CephFS client keeps file data, attributes and names exactly coherent, which
is what POSIX asks for and what most workloads that share a tree do not need.
They pay for it anyway: as soon as another client writes, the MDS revokes the
shared capabilities and every `stat()`, lookup and read of the affected inodes
becomes a round trip. This series lets a libcephfs client (ceph-fuse,
NFS-Ganesha, other gateways) opt into the consistency NFS gives, per mount:

- `client_close_to_open` (+ `client_close_to_open_timeout`): file data is
  flushed before `close()` returns (on ceph-fuse, at FLUSH, which `close()`
  waits for) and revalidated on `open()` and around advisory locks, and
  caches survive the MIX file lock. `O_DIRECT`, `O_SYNC` and `O_APPEND`
  descriptors keep strict semantics for their own reads, but what they write
  is still flushed at close.
- `client_attr_cache_timeout`, `client_dentry_cache_timeout`: `stat()`,
  lookups and `readdir()` are answered from what the client has for that long
  after losing the capabilities (NFS `acregmax`/`acdirmax`). Only names that
  exist are cached: whether a name does not exist is always asked of the MDS
  (NFS `lookupcache=positive`). The name an operation opens, creates or
  replaces is resolved at the MDS, as NFS does at the server, so a stale
  cached name never opens a file another client removed or replaced, nor makes
  a create fail with `EEXIST`; an open by inode (`ll_open()`, how ceph-fuse
  opens) through such a name fails with `ESTALE`, and the kernel looks the
  name up again. The client's own `unlink()`, `link()` and `rename()` are
  never hidden: the inodes whose link count they change are asked of the MDS
  again.
- ceph-fuse hands the kernel the same intervals as FUSE entry/attr timeouts,
  counted from when the client last knew the answer to be current. Without
  that, every path component of every `stat()` is a FUSE round trip. Under
  close-to-open it also drops the kernel's cached attributes on open, and
  keeps the kernel page cache across an open only if `Fc` protected it
  without a break. With names cached it mounts with `default_permissions`:
  the kernel then resolves cached paths without asking the client, so it has
  to check permissions itself. Before an exclusive create, `mkdir()`,
  `mknod()`, `symlink()`, `link()` or a rename over a name it still caches,
  the kernel looks the name up again; the client recognises such a lookup (a
  name whose kernel timeout has not run out) and resolves it at the MDS, so
  those do not fail with `EEXIST` on a name another client removed.
- libcephfs exports the same answers (`ceph_ll_attr_ttl()`,
  `ceph_ll_dentry_ttl()`, `ceph_ll_keep_page_cache()`,
  `ceph_ll_open_invalidates_attrs()`) and `ceph_ll_flush()`, so a FUSE file
  system written against the C API can do what ceph-fuse does.

All options default off; nothing changes for existing mounts. Two small fixes
come first: `lazyio_synchronize()` could skip invalidation, and opening a file
with LazyIO always cost an MDS round trip.

Feature: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82710; the two LazyIO fixes:
https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82709 (backport candidates on their own).

## Results

vstart (1 MDS, 3 BlueStore OSDs) on one machine, one client machine (Linux
7.0) with four mounts (four sessions), 64k-file tree; "churn" is three other
mounts creating, overwriting and unlinking at 150 ops/s each. ceph-fuse is
built against libfuse 3.14. Mean of two runs; MDS requests per 30 s run.
The fourth column is the series without its last two commits, which hand
the cache timeouts to the kernel: the caches alone, behind FUSE.

| | kernel | ceph-fuse | ceph-fuse, options at 60 s | without the kernel timeouts |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| stat known paths, idle | 227k/s | 11.3k/s | 1.85M/s | 11.5k/s |
| stat known paths, churn | 16.8k/s [542k MDS] | 5.9k/s [240k] | 1.41M/s [102k] | 10.0k/s [76k] |
| `ls -l` walk, churn | 70.7k/s [405k] | 6.7k/s [193k] | 769k/s [37k] | 10.7k/s [37k] |

73518.title: tentacle: rgw: reject a bad port in an [ipv6] endpoint
73518.author: vupn0712
73518.body:
backport tracker: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82599

---

backport of https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/72305
parent tracker: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/81305

`parse_endpoint()` passes the same `error_code` to `parse_port()` and then `make_address_v6()` for an `[ipv6]:port` endpoint. `make_address_v6()` clears that error_code on entry, so a successful address parse wipes out whatever `parse_port()` had just set, and a malformed port like `[::1]:notaport` gets silently accepted instead of rejected. 73520.title: client: make the automatic reconnect interval configurable
73520.author: dvanders
73520.body:
With `client_reconnect_stale`, a client that finds itself blocklisted resets
its sessions and reconnects with a new address, but `Client::tick()` does that
at most once every 30 minutes, a limit that is hard-coded. A client evicted a
second time within that window stays blocklisted, and every request fails until
it is remounted. The kernel client's `recover_session=clean` has no such limit.

- New option `client_reconnect_stale_interval` (secs, default 30 min, as
  before; 0 = no limit). It is read at every tick, so it can be changed at
  runtime.
- The first reconnect is always allowed: `last_auto_reconnect` started at the
  epoch of a monotonic clock, so on a host up for less than 30 minutes even the
  first reconnect was refused.
- Documented in `client-config-ref.rst` and `eviction.rst`.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82713

## Testing

- `ceph_test_libcephfs_reclaim --gtest_filter=LibCephFS.ReconnectStaleInterval`
  (new): a client with `client_reconnect_stale_interval = 0` is evicted twice
  (`client evict id=<its id>` via `ceph_mds_command`) and creates a file after
  each eviction. Passes on vstart (1 MDS, 3 OSDs) in 3.7 s. With the
  interval left at the 30-minute default, the first round passes and the second
  fails (no reconnect within 20 s), which is the bug.
- Every eviction in the test is of the test's own client.
- `PendingReleaseNotes` updated.

73521.title: msg: make invalid compression algorithm warnings visible
73521.author: mayankgongal5
73521.body:
## Summary
Fixes https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/76076 by making invalid compression algorithm warnings visible to users.

## Changes
- Changed `ldout(cct,5)` to `lderr(cct)` in `_parse_method_list()`

## Problem
The `ms_osd_compression_algorithm` option accepted any string, but invalid algorithm names were only logged at debug level 5 (invisible by default). Users could configure garbage values like `"snappyy"` and compression would silently be disabled.

## Solution
Use `lderr(cct)` instead of `ldout(cct,5)` so the warning is always visible. The error message now tells users exactly what went wrong and lists all valid algorithms.

## Testing

- Verified valid algorithms still work correctly

73523.title: tentacle: rgw/rados/rgw_sync: fix unintended uint64_t->int conversion
73523.author: vupn0712
73523.body:
backport tracker: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/78884

---

backport of https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/70483
parent tracker: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/78491

fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/78491

The metadata-sync shard CR (`RGWMetaSyncShardCR`) and the marker-tracking helper keep the full-sync completed-entry count as a plain `int` while the value it's eventually stored into (and the bucket sync status reported to operators) is `uint64_t`. Once the count crosses INT32_MAX, the `int` wraps and shows up downstream as a value close to UINT64_MAX, so `radosgw-admin bucket sync status` prints something like "full sync: 1844674407xxxxxxxx objects completed" instead of the real count. Widening `total_entries` and the `index_pos` parameters in `try_update_high_marker`/`start` to `uint64_t` removes the wraparound.

73525.title: client: discard dirty data when reconnecting after being blocklisted
73525.author: dvanders
73525.body:
With `client_reconnect_stale`, a blocklisted client reconnects on its own
with a new address. It kept the data it had buffered before the eviction,
and wrote it out after the reconnect, overwriting what other clients had
written to the same files in the meantime: the writes the objecter cancelled
with `-EBLOCKLISTED` leave their buffers dirty again in the ObjectCacher, and
a session closed before the client sees its blocklist entry (the usual
order) only releases clean data.

- Before the automatic reconnect in `tick()`, and when the blocklist entry
  goes away in `handle_osd_map()`, discard all dirty and in-flight buffered
  data (`purge_set`) and set `-EIO` on the handles open at the time, so
  `fsync()` and `close()` report the loss. This is what the kernel client
  does with `recover_session=clean`.
- Clients with the default `client_reconnect_stale = false` are not
  affected: they stay blocklisted, and their dirty data is purged when the
  blocklist is noticed.

Related: #73520 makes the reconnect interval configurable, which makes this
path easier to reach (more than one reconnect per 30 minutes).

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82714

## Testing

- `ceph_test_libcephfs_reclaim --gtest_filter=LibCephFS.ReconnectStaleDiscardsDirtyData`
  (new): A (client_reconnect_stale=true) buffers 64 KiB without flushing, is
  evicted, B writes and fsyncs the same range, A reconnects; the test checks

73534.title: mgr, mgr/cephadm: cut mgr CPU and blocking during cephadm upgrades at scale
73534.author: NitzanMordhai
73534.body:
During a cephadm OSD upgrade at scale the mgr spends most of its time on full
PG map scans and full osdmap dumps, much of it with the GIL or the ClusterState
lock held. This PR fixes the issues listed in the tracker:

- `osd ok-to-stop --max` scanned the whole PG map for every candidate OSD.
  It now indexes the PGs by OSD once per call and checks only the candidate's
  PGs, so a call does at most 2 full scans. Answers are unchanged.
- New native `OSDMap` getters (`get_require_osd_release()`, `get_pools()`,
  `get_pools_by_name()`, `get_osd_uuid()`, `exists()`) so callers no longer
  dump the whole map to read one field.
- cephadm no longer dumps the osdmap per OSD deploy, per upgrade pass, per
  queued OSD during removal, or for an empty removal queue, and reuses an
  `osd df` result for up to 2 seconds.
- cephadm parses the SSH identity once instead of on every new connection,
  and stops asyncssh from also loading the default `~/.ssh` keys each time.
- A PG whose pool is being deleted no longer reads a null pool in
  `_check_offlines_pgs()` (found by reading the code).

`_maximize_ok_to_upgrade_set()` (crush bucket upgrades) was reviewed and left
as is: the same index gave about 2x there, a few seconds over a whole
100 OSD bucket upgrade.

## Results

Measured with fake OSDs and the cephadm test harness from #<fake OSD PR>,
debug build, size 3, min_size 2, host failure domain.

Full OSD upgrade, 100 OSDs (20 hosts x 5), 16384 PGs, `test-upgrade --measure`:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| upgrade time | 529s | 475s |
| mgr CPU avg / max during the upgrade | 35% / 146% | 20% / 122% |
| mgr CPU avg before the upgrade | 72% | 17% |
| ok-to-stop, 20 calls: median / total | 1975ms / 39.6s | 56ms / 1.1s |
| py-spy dumps at mgr CPU >= 80% | 93 | 9 |

Before, the top GIL holders in those dumps were asyncssh key parsing and the
osdmap dump per OSD deploy. After, neither shows up. The remaining ones are
pg_autoscaler and balancer osdmap dumps, which are not part of this PR.

ok-to-stop alone, 100 OSDs (20 hosts x 5), 16384 PGs, time inside the mgr,
median of 5 calls:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `osd ok-to-stop 0 --max 16` | 1980ms, 100 full scans | 46ms, 2 full scans |
| `osd ok-to-stop 0 --max 5` | 88ms, 5 full scans | 46ms, 2 full scans |
| `pg stat` during `ok-to-stop --max 16` | 2012ms (467ms alone) | 475ms (453ms alone) |

Removing 20 OSDs:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 100 OSDs, 8192 PGs | 201s, cephadm thread 44%, 2153 `osd df` | 158s, cephadm thread 6%, 64 `osd df` |
| 300 OSDs, 32768 PGs | 6 removed after 612s | all removed in 322s, `orch osd rm` 88s -> 9s |

Tests:
- cephadm unit tests, including new ones for the removal queue, deploy,
  upgrade and SSH key loading
- mgr selftest compares the new getters against the full dump
- `qa/standalone/misc/ok-to-stop.sh`, with a new check for `--max` on a
  degraded PG

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82532

73539.title: mgr: drop an OSD's pool usage when the OSD stops reporting the pool
73539.author: anthonyeleven
73539.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/72754

`ceph df` computes a pool's STORED and USED from the `store_statfs_t` that each OSD sends for every pool it holds a PG of. The mgr keeps the latest one per (pool, OSD) in `PGMap::pool_statfs`. An entry is replaced only when the same OSD reports the pool again, and removed only when the OSD itself is removed. So when an OSD's last PG of a pool moves to other OSDs, the OSD stops reporting the pool and its last report stays in the pool's sum until the active mgr restarts. That's Sam's diagnosis in the tracker. In the tracker's test, moving each pool's only PG to three other OSDs doubles STORED and USED.

On a Reef 18.2.8 lab cluster, we moved one PG of a 16-PG replicated pool (5 objects, 327,680 bytes) with `pg-upmap-items`, so its old OSD held no PG of the pool. The OSD's entry stayed in `pool_statfs`, and the pool's STORED went from 3,276,823 to 3,386,049 bytes with the object count unchanged. After `ceph mgr fail` the new mgr's numbers were back at the baseline.

This drops an OSD's entry for each existing pool that is missing from its report:
- `ClusterState::ingest_pgstats` queues the removal of each such (pool, OSD) entry and cancels any pending update for it. A pool that a later report names again cancels its pending removal.
- `PGMap::Incremental` gets `pool_statfs_rm`, and `PGMap::apply_incremental` subtracts each removed entry from its pool's sum.

Both OSD implementations report every pool they hold a PG of (`OSD::collect_pg_stats`, and crimson's `OSD::get_stats`), including PGs still being deleted. So a stray copy's space still counts until its deletion finishes, and is dropped after that.

The new `pgmap.pool_statfs_rm` test in `src/test/mon/PGMap.cc` applies two OSDs' entries for a pool, removes one, and checks the pool's sum.

@ljflores, one question: are you OK with treating a pool missing from an OSD's report as zero usage, or would you rather the OSD sent explicit zero entries for pools it no longer holds a PG of?

The tracker's second question, why a 4K append grows the fast EC pool by 5K, is separate and isn't addressed here.

73540.title: mgr/cephadm: only scan for stray tuned profiles when a host's set cha…
73540.author: rkachach
73540.body:
…nges

On every serve loop pass, _write_all_tuned_profiles() runs "cephadm _orch sysctl-dir --list" on every reachable host, one host after the other, to look for profile files that no longer apply. It does this even when no tuned profile has ever been defined and nothing has changed since the previous pass.

This used to be a plain "ls" over the existing SSH connection. Since the listing moved behind the cephadm binary, every call starts the cephadm binary on the host, so the scan now costs seconds per host per pass. The cost grows with the number of hosts, and the rest of the serve loop waits behind it.

A stray file can only appear when a profile stops applying to a host: the profile is removed, or its placement no longer includes the host. Both change the set of profile names the host should have. So record, per host, the set of names last reconciled there, and only list /etc/sysctl.d when the expected set differs from it. Hosts with no record (new hosts, or the first pass after an upgrade) are scanned once. Settings changes keep using the existing timestamp check in _write_tuned_profiles().

The set is recorded only after the scan and the writes succeed, so a failure is retried on the next pass, and is not recorded for unreachable hosts. It is saved with the host cache entry when it changes, so a mgr failover doesn't rescan every host, and it is dropped when the host is removed.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82672

73543.title: crimson/osd: avoid throttle deadlocks with dependency level
73543.author: tchaikov
73543.body:
before this change, client writes and recovery could deadlock when crimson_osd_scheduler_concurrency was set: they held every throttle slot while waiting for ops that needed a slot themselves. a client op waits for replica writes and pushes, recovery waits for pull responses, scrub waits for its local scan. the same issue reports a BudgetBlocked loop in pg_recovery: a retry round already holding a slot still saw itself as out of budget.

this series assigns ops three levels: foreground, recovery, and leaf. foreground ops may wait on recovery or leaf ops; recovery waits on leaf ops; leaf ops only do local work. each level leaves capacity for the levels below it, so the ops being waited on can run. mClock still chooses the order.

a request whose level is full never enters the scheduler. it waits in a staged queue in the throttler, ordered by message priority, then round robin over owners, then arrival, and moves into the scheduler when a release frees capacity for its level. the scheduler never has to dequeue past blocked work, so mClock does not charge a blocked class for service it never got, and wpq does not lose a blocked owner's turn. WeightedPriorityQueue and both scheduler implementations are unchanged.

one tradeoff: a staged request joins mClock when it is admitted, not when it arrives, so its tag does not account for the time spent waiting for a slot.

the total concurrency limit stays shared, with nonzero values below 3 raised to 3. unit tests in test_operation_throttler.cc cover the deadlock, the staged queue order, and the limit changes.
