73548.title: rgw: Deprecate bash rgw-gap-list, add new python script
73548.author: linuxkidd
73548.body:
## The bash rgw-gap-list has many shortcomings.
To name a few:
- Very slow on large clusters, sometimes measuring in many months
- Practically no results until almost the end of the run
- Likely to produce false positive results due to time between listing and comparison
- Single run, no ability to break up the check across multiple processes or hosts

## The Python version provides the following benefits:
- True multi-process / multi-host execution coordination
- Multi-threaded RADOS stat / response checking
- Scans occur per bucket, providing near real time results
- Results are stored in RADOS and can be dumped from any host
- A status dashboard that can be output from any host
- A prometheus exporter for statistics and status
- The ability to verify the gap results
- Ability to scan a specific subset of buckets
- Ability to exclude a subset of buckets
- Ability to scan based on S3 object prefix

These improvements allow scaling of the gap list scan so execution can take hours or days where the bash version could take months.  It also provides mechanisms for rescan of specific buckets, objects, etc as desired by the storage administrator.

## Scan operation process:
- Determine a count of buckets requiring scan
- Check for / populate RADOS objects for scan state synchronization
- Add host / process id to active process list in RADOS
- Dump a list of buckets ( or use a provided list )
- Per bucket:
  - Check scan state / skip if scan is alreaady active or if previously scanned recently
  - Lock the bucket as being scanned by this host/process id
  - Issue `radosgw-admin bucket radoslist` command and iterate the response
  - Spawn 2nd thread monitoring the RADOS stat response queue
  - For each RADOS object, issue an async RADOS stat command to the cluster against the first pool in the pools list
  - If the stat rails, issue subsequent async RADOS stat commands to all other pools in the pools list
  - Once all responses received, log any missing objects as a gap
  - If the gap results grow to 4mb, or at the end of the bucket, dump the gap list results to a RADOS object
  - Once the entire bucket is scanned and all results received, release the lock
- When the process has exhausted the bucket list, remove itself from the active process list

## Report output options
- `-r` ( with or without `-j` ) produce a report of running processes and scan status for all buckets scanned or being scanned so far
- `-g` ( with or without `-j` ) produce a gap list output
- `-x` ( with or without `-j` ) produce a verified gap list output - this option performs a new async stat against all RADOS pools provided in the pools list.
- `--promexport` generate a Prometheus Export to stdout

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/76474

73551.title: cephadm: describe NVMe namespaces and allow a mgr module to constrain OSD sizing
73551.author: vmackie
73551.body:
## What this does

Adds a way for cephadm to describe a local NVMe namespace, and an optional hook that
lets a mgr module constrain how an OSD is sized before it is created.

Three commits:

1. **`cephadm: ask fcm_ad for device constraints before creating OSDs`** — before
   `ceph-volume lvm batch` runs, cephadm asks the optional `fcm_ad` mgr module whether a
   data device needs space left unallocated, and passes the answer through as
   `data_allocate_fraction`. The module is optional: if it is not present or not
   enabled, `mgr.remote()` raises and the OSD is created exactly as it is today. No
   behaviour changes for any existing deployment.

2. **`cephadm: add nvme-info to describe a local NVMe namespace`** — a new
   `cephadm nvme-info --device /dev/nvmeXnY` subcommand. It validates the device path,
   reads the PCI IDs and `nsid` from sysfs, issues Identify Controller (CNS 1) and
   Identify Namespace (CNS 0) via `NVME_IOCTL_ADMIN_CMD`, and prints one JSON object
   with both structures as raw hex.

   It deliberately **parses nothing out of the Identify data** — not even `nsze`. Every
   field a caller might want is already in the blob, so new requirements become changes
   in the caller rather than repeat trips through this code. It resolves multipath-style
   node names (`nvme0c0n1`) when locating the controller in sysfs.

   Also adds `CephadmOrchestrator.get_nvme_device_info(host, device_path)`, a thin
   `@handle_orch_error` wrapper that runs the subcommand on a host via
   `_run_cephadm_json`.

3. **`cephadm: report an absent NVMe namespace rather than failing`** — a namespace with
   no sysfs entry returns `{"device": ..., "present": false}` and exits 0 instead of
   raising. A caller reads an error as "the probe is broken" and aborts OSD creation; an
   OSD spec naming an explicit path that no longer exists was taking the whole spec down
   with it. Nothing can be provisioned on a device that is not there, so there is nothing
   to abort. Every other failure still raises, so a broken probe cannot be mistaken for a
   negative answer.

## Why

Some NVMe devices need a region of the namespace left unallocated by BlueStore, for a
consumer that writes to it directly. Deciding that requires reading Identify data from
the drive, and the policy for interpreting it does not belong in Ceph.

The split here keeps all of that outside the tree: `nvme-info` describes the hardware
and interprets none of it, and the sizing decision is delegated to a mgr module that
Ceph does not ship. What lands here is a device-description subcommand and an optional
integration point.

## Testing

`src/cephadm/tests/test_nvme.py` (33 tests) covers device-path validation, the ioctl
passthru struct layout and command encoding, the output contract, absent and
unreadable namespaces, and the subcommand wiring, with the ioctl faked.
`src/pybind/mgr/cephadm/tests/test_cephadm.py` covers the constraints hook, including
the module-absent path.

The subcommand has also been exercised against real hardware: both Identify structures
come back byte-identical to `nvme id-ctrl -b` / `nvme id-ns -b` on the same device.

73559.title: doc/cephfs: explain caps that cover every file system
73559.author: anthonyeleven
73559.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/74356

The tracker issue asks what `fsname=*` means in an MDS capability, and how `allow rw fsname=*` differs from `allow rw`. The File System Information Restriction section of the client capabilities page shows only caps for a single file system. In the code there is no `fsname=*`: the MDS and Monitor cap grammars accept only `[a-zA-Z0-9_.-]` in an `fsname` value (`src/mds/MDSAuthCaps.cc`, `src/mon/MonCap.cc`), and the Monitor parses MDS caps when they're set (`AuthMonitor::valid_caps()`). A cap without `fsname` matches every file system (`MDSCapMatch::match_fs()`), and `ceph fs authorize '*'` writes exactly that: MDS and Monitor caps with no `fsname`, and the OSD cap `allow rw tag cephfs data=*`. This adds that to the section, with an example.

Tested on a one-Monitor Tentacle 20.2.5 cluster (the `fsname` grammar is the same on main):

- `ceph auth get-or-create client.star mds 'allow rw fsname=*' mon 'allow r'` fails with `Error EINVAL: mds capability parse failed, stopped at 'fsname=*' of 'allow rw fsname=*'`.
- `mon 'allow r fsname=*'` fails the same way (`mon capability parse failed`), and so does `fsname="*"`.
- `ceph fs authorize '*' client.alluser / rw` writes `mds "allow rw"`, `mon "allow r"`, and `osd "allow rw tag cephfs data=*"`, as in the new example.

@rishabh-d-dave @batrick, would you take a look? Patrick opened the tracker issue in 2026-01, and it was assigned to Rishabh.

73560.title: doc/rados: add C++ API reference for librados

73566.title: umbrella: doc/rados: add object size, I/O rate, and omap guidance
73566.author: anthonyeleven

parent tracker: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/20215

The tracker asks for librados guidance on the trade-offs of object size, I/O rate, and omap versus regular data. Introduction to librados has none, so this adds an Object Size, I/O Rate, and Omap section at the end of the page.

- Object size: the `osd_max_object_size` limit and its scrub check, the 4 MiB objects that RBD, CephFS, and RGW use, the `min_alloc_size` cost of very small objects, and EC optimizations removing small-object padding in Tentacle and later.

- Omap: stored in RocksDB, supported on replicated pools and, since Umbrella, on erasure-coded pools with EC optimizations (#66726); the `LARGE_OMAP_OBJECTS` thresholds.

73568.title: umbrella: mds: introduce standby anti-affinity scoring matrix
73568.author: anthonyeleven
73568.body:

---

backport of https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/69801
parent tracker: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/75892

This PR introduces a multi-tiered standby selection scoring matrix to the MDS Monitor to dynamically prioritise anti-affinity over software rules, protecting the cluster's failure domains.

* **Score-Based Selection Matrix**:  Implements a graded scoring matrix (Scores 1 to 6) across FSMap and MDSMonitor,  that ensures both primary replacements and standby-replay followers are strictly barred from co-locating on the same physical host as an active or failing rank. * **Documentation**: Updates PendingReleaseNotes and standby.rst to accurately map out the new selection grid, score tiers, and state recovery behaviours.

73570.title: common/PriorityCache: credit grants made at the last priority
73570.author: ming1
73570.body:
`balance_priority()` grants each cache's request at `Priority::LAST` with `add_cache_bytes()`, then splits the remainder by ratio with `set_cache_bytes(LAST, share)`, which overwrites the grant. The bytes left the pool, but no cache is committed them. BlueStore's caches ask at `LAST` for content older than their last age bin (720 s), so the grant is lost on every balance and the OSD runs below `osd_memory_target`: 170 to 270 MiB of a 1484 MiB pool with 2 M small objects, about 1 % on a small hot set.

The fix adds the share on top of the grant, and skips a zero share because rbd-mirror's `PriCache::add_cache_bytes()` asserts at a priority it did not ask at. With nothing asked at `LAST` the result is byte-identical to today; the ratios still split only the memory nobody asked for.

4-OSD vstart, 2 GiB target, same load (osd.1): onode cache commit 368 -> 792 MiB, 371k -> 510k onodes, 93 -> 99 % hit rate, OSD mapped 1546 -> 1745 MiB of 2048. The RocksDB block cache goes 288 -> 184 MiB because it loses its 24 MiB share of the unspent memory and asks for less; its request was granted in full in both runs.

Harmful since Cache Age Binning (`56351838337`, v17.1.0) made the caches ask at `LAST`. The second commit adds a gtest driving the real `Manager::balance()` with fake caches: four cases, two fail without the fix and the zero-ratio case fails without the `fair_share > 0` guard.

PendingReleaseNotes: OSDs holding cache content older than the last age bin now use that memory, so their RSS moves closer to `osd_memory_target` after the upgrade.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82836

73572.title: common/TrackedOp: do not let the age of a new op wrap around
73572.author: xiubli
73572.body:
`dump_ops_in_flight()` samples `"now"` once and then walks the in-flight shards under their locks.  Ops registered on other threads while it walks have an `initiated_at` later than that `"now"`, and the unsigned `utime_t` subtraction now - initiated_at wraps around to about `2^32` seconds.  On a busy MDS or OSD a good share of the ops in a dump then show an `"age"` of `4294967296`, `dump_blocked_ops` lists ops that have just arrived as blocked, and `get_age_ms_histogram()` counts them in its largest bin.

Add `TrackedOp::get_age(now)`, which returns 0 for an op initiated after now, and use it in these three places.  The slow request checks compare `initiated_at` with now - `complaint_time` and are not affected.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82837

73574.title: doc/rados: say which librados io context calls are thread-safe
73574.author: anthonyeleven
73574.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/74489

The tracker issue asks which operations on a `rados_ioctx_t` are safe to call from several threads at once. The reporter is writing Rust bindings and needs to know whether an io context can be marked `Sync`. The [`rados_ioctx_t` docs](https://docs.ceph.com/en/latest/rados/api/librados/#c.rados_ioctx_t) say only that changing the io context's settings is not thread-safe. This adds a Thread safety section to that page, before the API reference, with what is safe and the exceptions. It changes only `doc/rados/api/librados.rst`.

**This comes from reading the code and from the sandbox test below, not from a statement by the RADOS developers, so please check it.** What the code shows:

- Reads, writes, and object operations, sync and async, pass the io context's settings to `Objecter::prepare_*_op()` and then call `Objecter::op_submit()`, which takes the Objecter's `rwlock` (`src/librados/IoCtxImpl.cc`, `src/osdc/Objecter.cc`). Async writes are tracked under `aio_write_list_lock`.
- `snap_seq`, `snapc`, `oloc` (locator key and namespace), and `extra_op_flags` (the full-try flag) are plain members that every operation reads without a lock (`src/librados/IoCtxImpl.h`).
- Every synchronous operation writes `last_objver`, and `set_sync_op_version()` marks that race with `ANNOTATE_BENIGN_RACE_SIZED`. So concurrent operations on one io context are expected, and `rados_get_last_version()` is not meaningful when threads share an io context.
- `TestLibRBD.ConcurrentCreatesUnvalidatedPool` (`src/test/librbd/test_librbd.cc`) shares one `rados_ioctx_t` between four threads.
- Async writes hold a reference on the io context until they complete, but async reads do not, and the completion of a read that has a callback uses `c->io->client`. So the text says to call `rados_ioctx_destroy()` only after every async operation has completed, not just after `rados_aio_flush()`.

The issue also asks about librbd's `rbd_image_t`. That isn't covered here: no test in `src/test/librbd` shares one image handle between threads, so the code is less conclusive.

### Sandbox test

I ran a test program against a throwaway cluster (one Monitor and one memstore OSD in a `quay.io/ceph/ceph:v20` container, 20.2.5). In each mode, 8 threads shared one handle:

- **One `rados_ioctx_t`, 120 seconds:** 429,731 operations of 7 kinds, with 1,166,780 completion callbacks. The kinds were sync and async reads and writes; write and read operations with data, an xattr, and omap; writes to each thread's own region of shared objects; 16 async writes followed by `rados_aio_flush()`; sync and async stat; and listing with a list context per thread. Every read was checked against what its thread wrote. There were no errors, no mismatches, and no crash or hang.
- **Changing the namespace, 20 seconds:** one thread called `rados_ioctx_set_namespace()` with `"elsewhere"` and then `NULL`, 1.68 billion times, while 7 threads each rewrote 64 objects of their own. The 433,093 writes landed in three namespaces: the default (448 objects), `elsewhere` (448), and a 9-byte namespace `\x00lsewhere` (287) that no thread ever set. That namespace is the first byte of the empty string followed by the rest of `elsewhere`.
- **One `rbd_image_t`, 120 seconds:** 274,591 operations of 5 kinds, with no errors or mismatches. The kinds were sync and async reads and writes, 8 async writes followed by `rbd_aio_flush()`, stat and flush, and image metadata set and get. This change still doesn't cover the image handle.

A passing test doesn't prove that there are no races, so this backs up the code reading rather than replacing it.

@cbodley @rzarzynski, would you check whether this matches what librados guarantees?

73576.author: vshankar
73576.body:
snaptest-git-ceph.sh and ffsb.sh retry a failed or slow clone from an EXIT trap. A trap on EXIT runs while the shell is already exiting: it cannot resume the script, and without an explicit exit, the script keeps the status it was exiting with. This is seen with the MDS thrasher, where the clone of ceph.git stalled during a failover, then ended with:

The retry cloned successfully, but the workunit still exited with status 128 without running any of the snapshot tests.

Retry inline instead. If the second clone fails too, set -e still fails the test.

73587.title: tools/contrib: sync upmap-remapped.py with cernceph/ceph-scripts
73587.author: FredNass
73587.body:
This syncs the in-tree copy of `src/tools/contrib/upmap-remapped.py` with the version maintained at [cernceph/ceph-scripts](https://github.com/cernceph/ceph-scripts), as of commit cernceph/ceph-scripts@6a83fb45d0089a21ce966b057c7824707b1e239c, after cernceph/ceph-scripts#51 and cernceph/ceph-scripts#52 were merged.

The file is a verbatim copy of `tools/upmap/upmap-remapped.py` from that repository, which is what #67886 asked for when it added the tool here.

### What changed upstream

- argparse command line; the cluster work now runs from `main()`, so the functions can be tested
- a remapped pg which already carries pg-upmap-items gets its mapping recomputed instead of having its items removed (running the script twice now produces no commands the second time)
- it never maps a pg onto an osd which is down
- **when a crush rule changes failure domain** (`host` -> `rack`, `rack` -> `row`): it keeps the acting osds the new rule still allows and replaces only the ones that violate it, so it no longer lets the whole pool backfill. On a production map (1600 osds, ec 6+2, 16384 pgs, `rack` -> `row`), a plain rule change moves 84.5% of the shards when the floor is 26.5%
- it breaks the shard rotations this can leave behind on ec pgs, because pg-upmap-items cannot express them

When the acting set already satisfies the rule, which covers every case the script was used for before, the output is unchanged.

The tests (`tools/upmap/test_upmap-remapped.py`) stay in cernceph/ceph-scripts and are not copied here, since `src/tools/contrib` has no test harness.

Related: #70441 (tracker [#78569](https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/78569)), the mon-side counterpart for `ceph osd pool set <pool> crush_rule <rule>`.

@dvanders, could you review this and merge it if you have the permissions? Thanks!

73594.title: rgw: fix HEAD responses for ACL requests
73594.author: mheler
73594.body:
Bucket and object HEAD ?acl requests returned an ACL body with a Content-Length different from GET's, leaving bytes that a client reusing the connection reads as the next response.

These responses now omit the body per [RFC 9110 9.3.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.3.2) and use GET's Content-Length per [8.6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-8.6).

73596.title: cls/lock: lock requests respond with expiration timestamp
73596.author: cbodley
73596.body:
allow clients to use the librados::OPERATION_RETURNVEC flag to request a cls_lock_lock_reply response that encodes the osd's expiration timestamp

use of this timestamp is subject to clock skew between the client and osd

motivated by an [rgw design](https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/73291) that uses these osd expiration timestamps to guard write operations on other rados objects using a new librados api [assert_before()](https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/73599). the idea is that osd clocks are more likely to be synchronized than the rados clients

73597.title: mds: gather Fc/Fb before moving the file lock from LOCK to MIX
73597.author: anthonyeleven
73597.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82875

A client can read zeros from a file another client has just written with buffered I/O. We hit it in production with kernel clients and an 18.2.8 MDS: a build tool's download cache handed back zero-filled files after one worker replaced a cached file and another updated its timestamps and reopened it.

A timestamp update xlocks the inode's filelock. The way there goes through LOCK, and LOCK and the xlock states let any client keep Fc and Fb, so the writer keeps its unflushed data. When the xlock ends with one client wanting Fw and another wanting Fr, `file_eval()` calls `scatter_mix()`, which moved LOCK straight to MIX: `issue_caps()` revoked the writer's Fc and Fb and granted Fr in the same pass, without waiting for the revokes. A reader with Fr and no Fc reads from the OSDs, so objects the writer hadn't written back yet came back as zeros. Every other transition into MIX gathers caps first.

For regular files, `scatter_mix()` now uses `LOCK_LOCK_MIX`, which has been in `locks.h` since 2009 without a table entry or a user, to gather the caps MIX doesn't allow before moving to MIX. Like LOCK, it lets the auth MDS take wrlocks meanwhile. A file with nothing to gather still goes straight to MIX, so the common case doesn't change. Directories keep the direct path: there these bits are async dirop caps, and returning them can wait on requests that need the lock.

`_finish_xlock()` had the same gap: when the xlocker is the target loner it set EXCL directly, so the loner got Fr and Fw while other clients could still hold Fc and Fb. It now takes that shortcut only when no other client holds caps EXCL doesn't allow it, and otherwise goes through the normal gather.

The new test in `qa/tasks/cephfs/test_filelock_mix.py`, run in fs:functional, follows the tracker's deterministic reproducer. A writer keeps a 64 MiB buffered file open, with its flush slowed by `wsize=4096` on the kernel client or a small `objecter_inflight_op_bytes` on ceph-fuse; another client touches it, then touches it again with `mds_log_pause` set and opens it for reading while the setattr still holds the xlock; a third client reads after the journal resumes. It has not run under teuthology yet.

Tested on 18.2.8 with three kernel clients and the same steps by hand. Stock: the reader got zeros in 8 of 8 runs, 859 to 5,192 of 16,384 4 KiB blocks each, and in 0 of 3 controls without the second touch. With this change: 0 of 8 and 0 of 3, and the MDS log shows the lock held in `lock->mix` until the writer's cap update after its flush. On main, `ceph-mds` and the MDS unit tests build, and the unit tests pass.

@vshankar @batrick @xiubli

73599.title: librados: add assert_time_range operation
73599.author: cbodley
73599.body:
allow rados operations to assert that they happen before/after a given time with respect to the osd's clock

motivated by an [rgw design](https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/73291) that relies on [cls_lock](https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/73596) to return its expiration timestamp so that write operations on other rados objects (without access to that lock state) can assert that they're applied before that lock expiration

the presence of clock skew between clients and osds may make this feature unreliable. but rados requests may be delayed for an arbitrarily long time, so it's useful to put some bound on time-sensitive operations

the assert_after() operation was not motivated by the rgw design, but may be useful for clients that want to test for clock skew

<details>

73600.title: rgw: rgw_s3_auth_disable_signature_url only denies presigned urls
73600.author: mheler
73600.body:
rgw_s3_auth_disable_signature_url threw for any signed request without looking at how it was signed, so turning it on to stop presigned urls returned 403 to every client that signs in the Authorization header too.

Deny a request only when its signature is in the query string, or when the query carries X-Amz-Algorithm. The second case catches a presigned v4 url whose signature is replayed in the Authorization header, where a route check alone would miss it. Presigned v2 and v4 urls are still refused.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82341

Also ensure `include/ceph_assert.h` is properly included where needed and remove redundant inclusions.

73602.title: [WIP] mds: migrate a file's data to another pool
73602.author: dvanders
73602.body:
**WIP, not ready to merge.** Posted early for design review, starting with
Andras, who asked for this in https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/40285.

## What

Change the pool of an existing CephFS file or tree, moving its data:

    setfattr -n ceph.file.migrate.pool -v <pool> <file>
    setfattr -n ceph.dir.migrate.pool  -v <pool> <dir>

A file migration copies every object, including the clones that hold its
snapshot versions, to the new pool, then switches the layout of the file and
of its snapshotted inodes in place. The old pool keeps no data for the file
afterwards, so the space is freed even when snapshots exist. A directory
migration is a background job, journaled per rank, that walks the tree across
ranks and is watched and steered with
`ceph tell mds.<x> migrate status|pause|resume|abort`. New files created in
the directory after the job starts go to the new pool too.

## How

- **Locking:** the filelock is xlocked so that clients lose Fb, with snapshot
  versions flushed as for a snapshot (`LOCK_XLOCKSNAP`). Files of 64 MiB or more
  (`mds_file_migrate_precopy_min`) with no writers are first copied unlocked,
  then checked under the lock (change_attr, mtime, size) and copied again if they
  changed.
- **Snapshots:** each object's clones are replayed oldest first with copy-from
  at the clone's snapid and the snap context of the previous clone, so the new
  pool gets the same clone history.
- **Old objects become RADOS redirects** to the copies, so a client still
  holding the old layout of a snapshot inode (snap caps cannot be revoked) reads
  the right data. A new OSD op, `remove-clones`, drops the old clones of a
  redirect. **This op is the part that most needs RADOS review.** The inode is
  flagged, and the redirects are purged with the file.
- **Moving back** into a pool that still holds redirects uses a fresh namespace
  (`ceph_migrate_<gen>`), so nothing collides with them.
- **Crash safety:** the layout switch is journaled together with the old
  layout, and after a failover the new rank finishes clearing the old pool. The
  client gets its reply once the new layout is durable.
- **Guard:** `fs rm_data_pool` refuses a pool that still holds objects, unless
  given `--yes-i-really-mean-it`.

## Status and testing

Tested on vstart (3 OSDs, replicated and EC 2+1 pools, 1 to 3 active MDS), with
scripts that check every snapshot version byte for byte against the original:

- functional suite (83 checks)
- MDS kills at each of the 5 kill points of `mds_kill_file_migrate_at` (37 checks)
- multi-rank jobs with ranks failing and stopping
- a concurrent-reader stress run: 10,676 reads, 0 wrong
- unmodified kernel client (6.8) readers during migration
- librados tests for `remove-clones`, including degraded clones

Not done yet: anything at scale (largest test 6 GB and a few thousand files),
teuthology runs of the new qa task, cephfs-data-scan with redirects, and hard
links or files whose snapshots span renames (those fall back to moving only the
head version).

Questions for reviewers:
1. Is a redirect plus `remove-clones` acceptable to RADOS, or is there a better
   primitive? Pool migration (#69112) may have one.
2. The inode format change (`migrating_from`, `migrate_gen`, a new flag).
3. Is the background directory job worth having in the MDS, or should it be a
   tool driving `ceph.file.migrate.pool`?

Related: #69112 (Pool Migration).

73604.title: doc/dev: design for extended features and clean rejection of clients
73604.author: aainscow
73604.body:
Design for the W release: a set of extended features with no fixed limit, carried in the msgr2 banner, and a clean refusal at the monitor for clients that lack a required feature. Vampire gets a first step that changes no wire format (see "Phasing" in the doc).

## Summary

- **Extended features:** a peer that sets msgr2 banner bit 2 appends its 64-bit feature word and a variable-length set of extended features to the banner (each release keeps up to 4,096 of them; the cap rises without a wire change). Peers that don't set the bit see nothing new, and a new client against an older cluster is admitted as today.
- **Clean rejection:** the monitor refuses a client that lacks a required feature during authentication, with `-EPROTONOSUPPORT` and a reason. Every client, kernel or userspace, already treats that as final, so it fails in under a second instead of retrying until `client_mount_timeout`. Clients are refused only for a feature an operator has explicitly required, with a command that first checks the connected clients; a feature that needs a requirement cannot be used before that. A cluster whose operator requires nothing admits the same clients as today.
- **Kernels:** unmodified kernels need nothing and are refused cleanly. Taking part needs 12 lines of kernel code, all in `prepare_banner()`.
- **msgr1:** keeps working while no extended feature is required. A cluster that requires one effectively requires msgr2 of its clients for as long as it does.
- **Phasing:** Vampire gets `ceph osd set-require-min-compat-client` accepting feature names (bit 54 with its marker for pool migration) and the MonClient fix, neither of which changes the wire. The extended set and the clean rejection are W work. The kernel's part in bit 54 is described for what it requires.
- **MonClient:** three existing bugs need fixing first: a false success from `authenticate()`, no recovery after a failed re-authentication, and hunting on after a refusal.

The doc also covers prior art, the options considered (including why the spare msgr2 banner bits aren't used directly), cephx, compatibility and upgrades, what bounds the data a peer sends before authentication (Security), risks and an implementation plan.

## Notes for reviewers

- The last section, "Testing so far (temporary)", records what the prototype and the draft implementation, https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/73605, have been tested with. It will be removed before this merges.
- Open questions are at the end of "Risks and open questions".

73605.title: msg, mon: extended features in the msgr2 banner and clean rejection of clients
73605.author: aainscow
73605.body:
Draft implementation of the design in https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/73604 (steps 1 to 3 of its implementation plan): a clean refusal at the monitor for clients that lack a required feature, and extended features in the msgr2 banner. This targets the W release; Vampire gets only the MonClient fix (https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/73638) and a separate change teaching `ceph osd set-require-min-compat-client` feature names, which this branch's `osd require-client-features` command stands in for until the two are folded together.

## Summary

The commits follow the design's plan, so the first eight change no wire format and can be backported.

- **Step 1, a MonClient bug since Nautilus:** `authenticate()` no longer reports success when the mon refuses the session. A client refused at identification took 210 s and then "succeeded" with `client_mount_timeout` 10; it now fails after 10 s. These first two commits, the fix and its recreate test, are also https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/73638 (https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82890), which should merge first.
- **Step 2, refusal at authentication without a wire change:**
  - `AUTH_BAD_METHOD` carries Linux errno values, so Windows clients read the mon's errors correctly.
  - The authenticator can turn away peers that lack required features (`AuthServer::handle_peer_missing_features()`, `Policy::features_checked_by_auth`).
  - The mon refuses such clients with `-EPROTONOSUPPORT` and a reason: msgr1 clients in their first `MAuth`, older msgr2 clients by a second strike on their proven `global_id`. Only mons in the quorum refuse. The decision and the strikes live in `PeerFeatureGate`, which has unit tests. The cluster log gets one line a minute; each attempt is logged at `debug_mon` 10.
  - MonClient stops hunting at that refusal, and a running client turned away for features keeps retrying with backoff (3 to 30 s), but not after other auth errors.
- **Opt-in requirements (review feedback):** an operator turns a requirement on explicitly and once, with `ceph osd require-client-features <feature>...`. The command refuses while a connected client lacks the features or cannot exchange extended features at all (those clients would hang once their tickets expire) unless `--yes-i-really-mean-it` is given. The requirement is kept in the mon store, so it needs no map change and outlives mon restarts; `unrequire-client-features` lifts it and `ceph features extended` shows it. Nothing derives a requirement from what the cluster is doing.
- **Step 3, extended features:** `feature_set_t` and `ceph_features_ext.h`; the banner trailer, the reason trailers and `Policy` requirements in msgr2 (spec in `doc/dev/msgr2.rst`); the mon's refusal for missing extended features; `ceph features extended`.

## Not done yet

- No real extended feature exists yet: numbers 0 and 1 are for tests. Of the design's "Turning a requirement on" the connected-client check is done; still missing: blocklisting lacking clients when forced, an admin-socket escape, the OSDs checking the banner's extended set too, and a gate that stops a feature being used before it is required (there is no such feature yet). Turning a real requirement on needs the checks in the design's new section "Turning a requirement on": refuse while connected clients lack it, unless forced; gate on `min_mon_release` and mgr versions; a mon admin-socket escape.
- The health check that names refused clients.
- Clearer client output. Over msgr2 the mon's reason follows a long connection dump in the messenger's log line, and MonClient then adds "failed to auth with my available methods", which is misleading for a feature refusal. Over msgr1 the line is already clean (`monclient(hunting): <mon> refused this client: <reason>`). Clients older than this branch get no reason at all and see only "(93) Protocol not supported".
- The kernel patches come after the wire format is agreed.

## Testing

- Full build including `tests` (gcc 14). Every commit's changed fil

73606.title: doc/mgr: document how to access the dashboard API documentation
73606.author: abrahamperz

The Ceph Dashboard ships an interactive Swagger UI page for the Ceph REST API (Help menu > **API**, i.e. `/#/api-docs`) and serves the raw OpenAPI specification at `/docs/openapi.json`, but neither is mentioned anywhere in the documentation.

This adds an "Accessing the API Documentation" section to `doc/mgr/ceph_api/index.rst` that explains:

The dashboard overview in `doc/mgr/dashboard.rst` now links to the Ceph API page and to the new section.

The paths come from `src/pybind/mgr/dashboard/controllers/docs.py` (`@Router('/docs', secure=False)`, `openapi.json` endpoint) and the frontend `api-docs` route / help menu entry.

Validation: the edited files parse without warnings with docutils; the `docs` check / ReadTheDocs build is the final validation.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/24755

73608.title: test: fix uninitialised memory reads in unittest_ipaddr
73608.author: abrahamperz
73608.body:
Running `unittest_ipaddr` under valgrind (`ctest -R unittest_ipaddr -T memcheck`) reports many *"Conditional jump or move depends on uninitialised value(s)"* errors (tracker #64892).

Root cause: the tests build their own fixtures on the stack and leave fields uninitialised.

- The `struct ifaddrs` fixtures are never zero-initialised, so `ifa_flags` is read uninitialised in `grade_addr()` (a few tests even did `ifa_flags &= ~IFF_UP` on an uninitialised value).
- The `ipv4()` / `ipv6()` helpers only set the address family and address, leaving `sin_port` / `sin_zero` and `sin6_port` / `sin6_flowinfo` / `sin6_scope_id` uninitialised; those are later read when the addresses are formatted (`getnameinfo`).

Fix: value-initialise every `struct ifaddrs` fixture and `memset()` the sockaddr in the `ipv4()` / `ipv6()` helpers.

Before this change valgrind reported 64 errors from 7 contexts; after it, `ERROR SUMMARY: 0 errors from 0 contexts` and all 47 tests still pass.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/64892

73610.title: tentacle: client: advance the iterator in _kick_stale_sessions
73610.author: anthonyeleven
73610.body:
backport tracker: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82876

---

backport of https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/73383
parent tracker: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82547

`Client::_kick_stale_sessions()` never advances its iterator. Commit 730dd8a87a3 "client: switch to use shared_ptr for mds_sessions" replaced `mds_sessions.erase(it++)` with `mds_sessions.erase(it->first)` and dropped the `++it` before the STALE check. Since then:

- The loop never ends while `mds_sessions` holds a session that is not REJECTED. Both callers hold `client_lock`, so the client hangs. One caller is the `kick_stale_sessions` admin socket command. The other is `Client::tick()`, when a blocklisted client reconnects because `client_reconnect_stale` is true.
- A REJECTED session is erased by key, and the loop then reads the erased iterator. A STALE session is erased inside `_closed_mds_session()`, which also leaves the iterator dangling.

The first commit erases through the iterator and steps past a session before closing it, as the loop did before that commit. I modeled the old and new loops in a standalone program with the same map, session states, and erase calls, built with AddressSanitizer. The old loop spins forever, and the fixed loop finishes with no errors.

The second commit adds `test_client_kick_stale_sessions` to `qa/tasks/cephfs/test_misc.py`. It runs the command against a ceph-fuse mount that has an open session, then checks that the mount still works. Without the fix, the command hangs and the test fails. I have not run it in teuthology.

Both commits cherry-pick cleanly to umbrella, tentacle, and squid with the same line counts. No open PR touches these lines.

73613.title: umbrella: doc/rados: modernize PG Calc and add FD Calc
73613.author: anthonyeleven
73613.body:
backport tracker: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82880

---

backport of https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/73356
parent tracker: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82513

Two commits: a rewrite of PG Calc, and a new FD Calc page beside it.

### PG Calc

The PG Calc page restored in eaaf7225312 loads the old ceph.com WordPress theme stylesheets, jQuery, and jQuery UI from web.archive.org and Google, and `pgcalc.js` is the Wayback Machine's rewritten copy of the old script. The theme stylesheets restyle the docs page around the calculator, its table runs past the content column, and **Generate Commands** navigates to a `data:` URL, which current browsers block, so it does nothing.

This rewrites `pgcalc.js` in plain JavaScript with its own CSS and nothing loaded from other sites. The suggested PG count is unchanged for a given size: 200,000 random inputs give the same count as the previous code.

- Each pool has an application and is replicated or erasure coded, with its own *k* (at least 2) and *m* (at least 1). An erasure-coded pool counts *k+m* shards.
- **Generate Commands** creates a replicated CRUSH rule, and an erasure-code profile and CRUSH rule for each *k* and *m*, with a chosen failure domain and CRUSH root; then each pool with its rule, its size or profile, `allow_ec_overwrites` for erasure-coded RBD and CephFS pools, and its application (`rbd pool init` for replicated RBD pools). It shows them with Copy and Download buttons and leaves out removed pools.
- A pool is marked red, and left out of the commands, when OSD # is less than its size or *k+m*, so its PGs can't be placed. A pool is marked amber when it has fewer than three replicas or *m=1*. Erasure coding for an RGW index or metadata pool or a CephFS metadata pool draws a warning that a future release may support it but most deployments should stick with replication, and *k* above 8 draws one that writes and rebuilds slow down for diminishing savings in space, linking the EC overhead table in the latest docs.
- A column heading opens a native dialog to set that value for every pool, and **Add pool** adds a row directly.
- The RGW presets use the pools that RGW creates today (`.rgw.root`, `default.rgw.{control,meta,log}`, `default.rgw.buckets.{index,non-ec,data}`), the Infernalis-era presets are gone, CephFS and erasure-coded RGW presets are added, and All-in-One puts 100% of the data in `rbd` rather than 200%.
- The calculator renders into `pgcalc-root`, because Sphinx gives the anchor for the page's `pgcalc` label the id `pgcalc`, ahead of the calculator.

The instructions, field descriptions, and formula move out of raw HTML into RST, so the docs theme styles them and `:confval:` links work, and a new section describes the generated commands. The Target PGs per OSD guidance now cites `mon_target_pg_per_osd` and `mon_max_pg_per_osd`, which d34fa3316f0 raised to 200 and 500 for Umbrella, and says so in words that read right on tentacle, where they are 100 and 250. 73614.title: umbrella: doc/cephfs: describe pinning the subvolume trash folder
73614.author: anthonyeleven
73614.body:
backport tracker: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82882

---

backport of https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/73424
parent tracker: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/61902

61902 began as a code change: put `/volumes/_deleting` on rank 1 by default, so that large recursive deletes stay off rank 0. In the tracker discussion, the code change was dropped because of the per-subvolume trash and distributed ephemeral pins, and documenting it under recommended settings was suggested instead. This adds a "Pinning the Trash Folder" section after "Removing a Subvolume" in `doc/cephfs/fs-volumes.rst`, written from the code on main:

- **Where the load goes.** A removal with no retained snapshots renames the whole subvolume into `/volumes/_deleting` (`SubvolumeBase.trash_base_dir` and `Trash.dump`), and the purge threads `rmtree` it there (`Trash.purge`). So the unlinks go to the rank that holds `_deleting`, which is the rank that holds `/volumes`.
- **Subvolumes with their own pin.** `ceph fs subvolume pin` sets the pin on the subvolume's base directory (`SubvolumeBase.pin`), which is the directory that gets renamed, so that pin goes along and the subvolume is purged by its own rank.
- **Retained snapshots.** `SubvolumeV2.trash_incarnation_dir` moves the data to the subvolume's own `.trash` and puts only a symlink in `_deleting`. The purge follows the link (`purge_queue.py`), so the subvolume's rank does the work.
- **Empty folder.** `MDCache::trim` calls `Migrator::export_empty_import` on an empty imported subtree, which doesn't check the export pin, so the empty `_deleting` goes back to the rank that holds `/volumes`. `MDBalancer::handle_export_pins` exports a pinned directory only once it isn't empty, so the next removal moves it to the pinned rank again. This is the behavior that the description wanted to avoid with a placeholder file. The section doesn't suggest one, because the purge threads would delete it.

Clean cherry-pick of 1 commit, with the same line changes as on main.

73624.title: tentacle: mds: do not replicate an xlocked dentry whose linkage is projected
73624.author: anthonyeleven
73624.body:
backport tracker: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82861

---

backport of https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/72790
parent tracker: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/81730

`handle_discover` lets a `path_locked` discover replicate an xlocked dentry. The exception is meant for the xlocker's own witnesses, but `MDiscover` carries no request id, so a peer working on another request gets it too, for example `handle_peer_rename_prep` opening a remote dentry's inode. If the dentry belongs to a rename that has already projected its new linkage, such as an early-replied rename waiting on its journal entry, the new replica gets the old linkage and is not a witness. When the rename commits, `_rename_finish` sends `MDentryLink` to that replica, and the peer fails `ceph_assert(dnl->is_null())` in `MDCache::handle_dentry_link`.

This change allows the exception only while the dentry has no projected linkage. Otherwise the discover blocks on the xlock as a normal discover does, and the log is nudged so an early-replied xlocker does not hold it until the next tick. The xlocker's own witnesses all traverse before it projects, so they are unaffected.

Testing: reproduced deterministically on v18.2.7 with two active ranks, one kernel client and `mds_log_pause` on the rename leader. The reproducer script, debug_mds 20 logs from both ranks and the sequence are on the tracker. Without this change the peer rank aborted in 2 of 2 runs. With it, cherry-picked onto v18.2.7, it aborted in 0 of 2: the auth rank logs `handle_discover blocking on xlocked`, and the second rename completes once the first commits. The diff is identical on main.

73626.title: mgr/dashboard: avoid decoding URL parameters twice
73626.author: tchaikov
73626.body:
Commit f21d0da5a3e19e3f9bbde084e71b4a09f8dcb0a1 added URL decoding for tracker #24621, where editing an image named "foo/bar" returned 404: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/24621

73627.title: mon,crush: add osd crush rule set-device-class
73627.author: anthonyeleven
73627.body:
Refs: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/71891

Adds `ceph osd crush rule set-device-class <rule> <class> [--yes-i-really-mean-it]`, which adjusts existing CRUSH rules to place data only on one device class. This is the first of three pieces in tracker 71891, which also absorbed https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/75832 ("CRUSH rules should specify a device class"), closed as its duplicate. The other two are a default device class for new pools and a health warning for pools on a rule that names no class. They will come together in one later PR, so that the warning never lands without the default.

Why: a rule that takes a root without a class spans every class under it, and once any other rule names a class, the roots overlap. Today the fix is a new rule plus `osd pool set crush_rule` for every pool, or an offline `crushtool --reclassify-root`, which refuses as soon as any rule already names a class.

What it does:
- **No data movement when possible.** If the rule's only take is a root whose devices are all of that class, no bucket under that root also sits in another bucket, and no rule takes a shadow bucket under that root, it renumbers the buckets the way `CrushWrapper::reclassify()` does, so the class's shadow tree keeps the original bucket IDs. It copies each original bucket's weight sets onto its shadow, because `device_class_clone()` recomputes them and can get a different answer, for example for a host added after `weight-set create-compat`. It then compares every bucket that any rule can reach, by ID, with the map from before, and keeps the renumbering only if nothing differs. Every classless rule under that root then names the class, the output lists them, and group flags set with `ceph osd set-group` move to the renumbered buckets. This covers the usual legacy cluster: one class, every pool on `replicated_rule`.
- **Otherwise, this rule only.** Its take steps point at the class's shadow buckets. If any pool uses the rule, its data moves, so the command then requires `--yes-i-really-mean-it`, and the reply says why the buckets could not be renumbered (for example, "default holds osd.11, which is of class ssd").
- It refuses a take with no device of the class under it, a take that already names a different class, a take of a device, a rule with no take step, a class that doesn't exist, and stretch mode (https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/78741: under a device class the dividing bucket is a shadow, so PGs go inactive when a site is lost; see also #70600).
- Running it again is a no-op ("already uses device class"). If the change is still pending, the reply waits for the commit, as `create-replicated` does.

Tests: fourteen `unittest_crush_wrapper` cases. The renumber cases check that the mappings stay identical for 1024 inputs: plain, with a compat weight set, with a bucket-level reweight-compat (the root's entry for a host no longer equals the host's own total), with a straw (v1) host under a straw2 root, with a rule that takes a host, and with an erasure-coded (indep) rule. The others cover the fall-back when the check finds a difference (a host whose weight in the root isn't the sum of its OSDs), a host with two parents, a host also linked under another root, mixed classes, a rule beside a class rule, two take steps, no take step, and a class with no devices under the take. Each fall-back case also checks the reason it reports. `qa/workunits/mon/crush_ops.sh` covers the command line, including a renumber on a single-class root with a group flag that has to follow, and the fall-back once that root's hosts are linked under a second root. Built on CentOS Stream 9 / GCC: `unittest_crush_wrapper` 40/40 passed, and the mon and mgr objects compile. Removing the weight-set copy makes the bucket-level reweight-compat and straw-host tests fail, and forcing the placement check to pass makes the fall-back test fail.

@kamoltat, your plan of action on 71891 (a class-specific rule for .mgr by default, with the class picked by a heuristic)

73628.title: crimson: fix invalid prv_shard assertion in ms_handle_connect
73628.author: zchaffee1
73628.body:
Because cluster_msgr handles lossless peer connections which can migrate across
reactor cores (--smp >= 2), crimson::mgr::Client receives connect and reset
notifications for nonMGR connections. When an OSD peer reconnects after migrating
shards, prv_shard != this_shard_id(), causing an immediate abort.

Moreover, both ms_handle_connect() and ms_handle_reset() would dispatch
background tasks into foreign shard gates, accessing mgr::Client's shard-local
state across cores.

Fix this by filtering out non-MGR connections in both ms_handle_connect() and
ms_handle_reset().

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/74085
Signed-off-by: Zack Chaffee <zachaffee@gmail.com>

73632.title: cephadm: let set-spec-affinity move adopted OSDs
73632.author: anthonyeleven
73632.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/57991

`ceph orch osd set-spec-affinity` runs `cephadm update-osd-service` on the host. That writes the new service name into the `unit.meta` file of each OSD and sets the `osdspec_affinity` BlueStore label. `update_meta_file` only updates keys that the file already has, and `cephadm adopt` writes no `service_name`. On an adopted OSD that cephadm has not redeployed, the command therefore sets the label, reports success, and leaves the OSD in the bare `osd` service.

This lets `update_meta_file` add missing keys when asked, and has `update-osd-service` add `service_name`. The other caller keeps the old behavior. It also sets the label before writing `unit.meta`, so that an OSD whose label update fails stays in its old service.

Tested on a Tentacle 20.2.5 cluster adopted as `doc/cephadm/adoption.rst` describes:

- With stock cephadm, `ceph orch osd set-spec-affinity osd.moved 10` printed success and changed the label, but `ceph orch ps` still listed osd.10 under `osd`.
- With this change, `cephadm update-osd-service --service-name osd.again --osd-ids 10`, the host command that set-spec-affinity runs, moved the adopted osd.10 to `osd.again`. The label, `unit.meta`, and `ceph orch ps` agreed.

https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/72640 documents how to bring adopted OSDs under a service.

Backports: tentacle, umbrella.

73633.title: common/LogClient: count cluster log entries awaiting an ack; test acks through a peon
73633.author: dvanders
73633.body:
Follow-up to #72555 (https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/81604), so that the next regression of this kind is caught by a test, and so that operators can see it coming.

When the monitors lose the acknowledgements of a daemon's cluster log entries, as daemons connected to a peon did from v18.2.8, v19.2.3 and v20.2.0 until #72555, the daemon's log queue grows for as long as it runs. Nothing shows it until a monitor restart: then every daemon connected to that monitor sends its whole queue again, 1000 entries per message, and the leader commits it all again. On large clusters that has meant months of old entries, high monitor CPU and tens of thousands of slow ops.

**common/LogClient: count the cluster log entries awaiting an ack.** A `clog` perf counter set in every daemon: `queue_len` (entries waiting for an acknowledgement, PRIO_USEFUL so exporters pick it up), plus `sent`, `resent` (queued again for a new monitor session) and `acked`. A growing `queue_len` is the early warning, and `ceph daemon <daemon> perf dump clog` the check before a monitor restart. PendingReleaseNotes entry included.

**qa/standalone/mon: check that daemons on a peon get log acks** (`mon-log-ack.sh`). Two monitors and an OSD; the monitor the OSD is connected to is made a peon with `mon add disallowed_leader` (the OSD keeps its session; pinning its `mon_host` is not enough, it moves on the next session reopen). Scrubs make the OSD log; the test checks that `clog.queue_len` drains to 0 for the OSD and for the peon's own log client.

## Testing

On a main-based build (2026-11-06, with #72555):

| | `mon-log-ack.sh` |
|---|---|
| main | passes |
| main with #72555 reverted | fails: osd.0 sent 10, acked 2, `queue_len` stays at 8 |

Not yet run in teuthology (`rados/standalone`).

73634.title: mgr/cephadm: preserve host state across SSH connection resets
73634.author: tchaikov
73634.body:
An SSH connection to a host's old address can fail after set-addr has succeeded, marking the host offline again. A late success can replace the new connection, and an old command failure can close it. 

Invalidate pending connection attempts when resetting a host and only let current attempts update its connection cache or offline state. Only close the connection a failed command used. After validating and saving a new address, clear the previous offline state.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82886

73635.title: crimson/osd: drop MPing quietly
73635.author: ronen-fr
73635.body:
Clients (the Objecter) ping the connections of their laggy ops, to detect a reset of a lossy connection; the message itself carries nothing. The crimson OSD did not handle it, and each one was logged as an error ("ms_dispatch unhandled message ping"), on every connection with laggy ops.

Handle it as the classic OSD does: by dropping it.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82887

73636.title: include/encoding: add a features-aware encode() for optional<>
73636.author: ronen-fr
73636.body:
Every other container with a feature-dependent encoding - pair, list, vector, the maps and the sets - offers both encode(x, bl) and encode(x, bl, features). std::optional and boost::optional offer only the first.

For a denc-supported T, encode(optional<T>, bl, features) still resolves: denc_traits<optional<T>> exists, and the generic denc entry point takes the features and ignores them. For a legacy featured class - one declared with WRITE_CLASS_ENCODER_FEATURES, which has no denc traits - there is no candidate at all, and neither spelling compiles. The three-argument form finds no matching overload. The two-argument form matches, then fails one level down in encode_optional(), which calls encode(*p, bl) on a type whose only encode() takes features.

Add the missing overloads, and the encode_optional() that passes the features down to the contained value. Where a call previously reached denc's generic encode(), the new overload is the more specialised candidate and wins, emitting the same bytes.

73638.title: mon/MonClient: don't report success when the session is refused
73638.author: aainscow
73638.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82890

Over msgr2 a client authenticates before the session handshake, so MonClient sets `active_con` at `AUTH_DONE`. If the mon then refuses the session at identification, for example because the client lacks a feature the OSDMap requires (`CRUSH_MSR` once an MSR rule exists), `authenticate()` can time out with `active_con` set and return 1 ("in progress"). `rados_connect()` then returns +1, which C callers take as success, after 11 to 21 times `client_mount_timeout` (about 55 and 105 minutes by default).

`authenticate()` now also waits for `_finish_auth()`, and succeeds only when it reports no error. With `client_mount_timeout` 10, a client refused at identification took 210 s (`rados`) and 110 s (`ceph -s`) and then reported "Operation not permitted"; with the fix both fail after 10 s with `ETIMEDOUT`.

This is step 1 of the plan in https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/73604. https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/73605 builds on these two commits and makes the mon refuse such clients at once.

https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/69318 also changes `authenticate()`, to start a fresh hunt when it is retried after a failure. The two change different lines and apply together cleanly.

## Testing

- New recreate test `unittest_mon_client_authenticate` (`MonClientAuthenticate.SessionNeverCompletes`): a mon that authenticates the client and then ignores it, so the session never completes, which is the state a refusal at identification leaves the client in. On main `authenticate()` returns 1 (3 runs out of 3); with the fix it returns `-ETIMEDOUT` (3 out of 3). `unittest_mon_client_shutdown` still passes.
- Each commit compiles on its own with gcc and clang-19 `-Werror`. Also built and tested with the rest of https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/73605 (gcc 14).
- The measurement above, on a vstart cluster where the mon refuses clients at identification.

73643.title: doc/cephfs: describe O_APPEND across hosts and file locks
73643.author: anthonyeleven
73643.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/44503

posix.rst says nothing about O_APPEND or file locks. This adds two sections after "fsync() and error reporting":

- Appending from more than one host: a client that waits for the caps to extend a file can append at a stale end of file and overwrite another host's append (https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/7333). Kernel clients fix this in Linux 7.3 (d2a8d446a09c); ceph-fuse and libcephfs don't yet (#70279 is in review), so the section gives the flock(2) workaround. When #70279 merges, the ceph-fuse line needs the release that has the fix.
- File locks: kernel clients (fs/ceph/file.c .lock/.flock), ceph-fuse (fuse_ll_setlk, fuse_ll_flock), and libcephfs (ceph_ll_setlk, ceph_flock) support fcntl(2) and flock(2) advisory locks. The MDS keeps separate fcntl and flock lock states per inode, so locks are seen across hosts and the two kinds don't conflict.

The new sections are at the end of the file, so they don't overlap #73312, #69754, or #73516, which also touch posix.rst.

@xiubli, could you check the O_APPEND description against #70279 and the kernel fix?

73646.title: rgw: throw boost::system::system_error instead of a bare int
73646.author: abrahamperz
73646.body:
This is a first step toward https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/81903: RGW auth paths report errors by throwing a bare `int` (e.g. `throw -EACCES;`). A bare `int` escapes `catch (const std::exception&)`, so any generic code that wraps these paths has to remember to catch `int`, and the compiler never warns if it forgets. That is what left `call_once()` waiters blocked in #81105 / #71896.

Per review, the bare-`int` throws now throw `boost::system::system_error`, built with `ceph::to_error_code()`, and the catch sites recover the value with `ceph::from_error_code()`. For negative values the conversion round-trips exactly, so the S3/Swift error codes (including the rgw `ERR_*` values) and the engine/applier fall-through behaviour are unchanged.

### What changed

- `rgw::auth::Exception` (in `rgw_auth.h`) now aliases `boost::system::system_error`.
- Converted the bare-`int` throws in `rgw_auth.cc`, `rgw_auth_filters.h`, `rgw_auth_keystone.cc`, `rgw_auth_s3.cc`, `rgw_rest_s3.cc`, `rgw_rest_sts.cc`, `rgw_rest_swift.cc` and `rgw_swift_auth.cc`.
- Updated the matching catch sites (`catch (const int)` / `catch (int)`) in `rgw_auth.cc`, `rgw_rest_client.cc` and `rgw_loadgen.cc`. In `Strategy::apply()` the new handler stays before the existing `catch (const std::exception&)` sibling, so genuinely unexpected exceptions still hit that fallback as before.
- `WebTokenEngine::get_cert_url()` no longer throws a bare `-EINVAL`: it runs inside `validate_signature()`'s `catch (std::exception&)`, which the int escaped.

### Scope

The larger questions from the tracker (which throw sites could return the error as a value instead of throwing, and whether `call_once()` can go back to catching only `std::exception`) are out of scope for this first step.

### Verification

- The changed `rgw_common` translation units build cleanly, and the rgw auth unit tests pass.
- Runtime behaviour (each path still returns the same HTTP error code) is exercised by the S3/Swift/STS integration suites, which need `ci-approved` to run here.

73648.title: rgw/beast: answer 431 and send Date for oversized request headers
73648.author: RaminNietzsche
73648.body:
When the request header section is larger than the beast frontend's `max_header_size` (16 KiB by default), `handle_connection()` answers the failed header parse with a bare `400 Bad Request`: no explanation and no `Date`. RFC 6585 [section 5](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585.html#section-5) defines `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` for this case, which tells the client what to fix (usually an oversized cookie or token), and RFC 9110 [6.6.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-6.6.1) requires an origin server with a clock to send `Date` on 4xx responses. This answer is written before the REST layer that normally adds `Date`.

When the parse error is `http::error::header_limit` this answers 431; other header parse errors stay 400. Both early responses now carry an IMF-fixdate `Date`. The log line reports the status that was sent instead of a fixed 400.

Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82899

## Testing

On a single-host vstart cluster built from this branch:

| Request | Answer |
|---------|--------|
| `X-Big` header of 70000 bytes | 431, `Date: ... GMT`, `Content-Length: 0` |
| malformed request line | 400, `Date: ... GMT`, `Content-Length: 0` |
| normal `GET /` | 200 |

`qa/workunits/rgw/test-header-too-large.py` (added here) passes.

73650.title: crush: fill every position of shadow bucket weight sets
73650.author: anthonyeleven
73650.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82900

`CrushWrapper::device_class_clone()` declared the per-position totals for a shadow bucket inside its per-position loop and stored them on every pass, so only the last position survived. With a positional weight set (`ceph osd crush weight-set create <pool> positional`), every rebuild of the shadow trees left each shadow bucket's entries for its child buckets at 0 at all but the last position. A rule with a device class then always took the first child there: replicated pools of size 3 or more and erasure-coded pools mapped each PG to a single OSD, and size-2 pools put every PG's first OSD on the same host. Compat weight sets have one position and are not affected.

This totals every position before storing them. A child with fewer positions uses its last one, as CRUSH does when it picks weights. A child with no weight set, such as a straw (v1) bucket, gets 0 as before.

Tests: a new `unittest_crush_wrapper` case, `device_class_clone_weight_set_positions`. It builds three straw2 hosts and a straw (v1) host, a three-position weight set with one host cut to a single position, and a replicated rule on class `hdd`, then rebuilds the shadow trees. It checks that all 1024 inputs map to three OSDs and that every position of the shadow root's entry for each host equals that host's total, taking the last position for the one-position host. With every host at three positions, the old code maps all 1024 inputs to a single OSD and leaves the position-0 entries at 0. With the empty check removed, the straw host makes it crash. With the clamp removed, the one-position host's entries are garbage and 518 of 1024 inputs map short. Built on CentOS Stream 9 / GCC: `unittest_crush_wrapper` 27/27 passed.

73651.title: osdc/Objecter: don't abort a listing seek when the pool is gone
73651.author: abrahamperz
73651.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82436

Seeking an object listing after its pool has been deleted aborts the client. `Objecter::list_nobjects_seek()` (both the `uint32_t` and the `hobject_t` overload) maps the new position with `osdmap->raw_pg_to_pg(pg_t(..., list_context->pool_id))` without checking that the pool is still in the client's OSD map. `OSDMap::raw_pg_to_pg()` asserts `p != pools.end()`, so the seek kills the process instead of returning. The same listing *without* a seek already handles the gone pool gracefully: `list_nobjects()` checks `get_pg_pool()` and completes the next step with `-ENOENT`.

`list_nobjects_get_cursor()` has the matching defect: when the listing still holds a fetched entry it calls `osdmap->get_pg_pool(pool_id)->hash_key(...)`, which dereferences the null the deleted pool now returns (SIGSEGV).

### What changed (`src/osdc/Objecter.cc`)

- Both `list_nobjects_seek()` overloads now check `osdmap->have_pg_pool()` before mapping the position. If the pool is gone they skip `raw_pg_to_pg()` and set `at_end_of_pool`, so the listing simply ends: the next `list_nobjects_next()` returns `-ENOENT` (exactly what an unsought listing returns), and the C++ `NObjectIterator` compares equal to `end()` instead of spinning. The seek return value is unchanged on the normal path.
- `list_nobjects_get_cursor()` fetches the pool once and falls back to the last known position (`list_context->pos`) when the pool is gone, the same value it already returns for an empty buffer, instead of hashing through a null pool.

Behaviour on a live pool is unchanged; this only affects the window after the pool has been removed from the client's map.

### Verification

- Builds cleanly (the `osdc` object and `librados` link).
- The fix mirrors the existing `-ENOENT` guard in `list_nobjects()` and covers every seek-path site that reaches the asserting `raw_pg_to_pg()` / null-deref: the two `list_nobjects_seek()` overloads and `list_nobjects_get_cursor()`. The C/C++ API wrappers (`rados_nobjects_list_seek{,_cursor}`, `rados_nobjects_list_get_cursor`, `IoCtxImpl::nlist_seek`/`nlist_get_cursor`) only forward to these.
- Reproducing the original abort and confirming the `-ENOENT` result end to end needs a live cluster (create a pool, start a listing, delete the pool, then seek), which runs under the rados API integration suite rather than locally; that is left for the gated CI here.

73653.title: crush: give a shadow bucket no weight set when its bucket has none
73653.author: anthonyeleven
73653.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/82903

`CrushWrapper::device_class_clone()` gave the shadow of a straw2 bucket that has no weight set, in a map that has one, 0 positions but a `weight_set` from `calloc(0, ...)`, which glibc returns as a pointer that is not NULL. `get_choose_arg_weights()` then clamps the position to -1 and reads `weight_set[-1]`. Such a bucket arises when a straw bucket is converted with `ceph osd crush set-all-straw-buckets-to-straw2` after a weight set was created. Encoding skips entries with no positions, so decoded maps are not affected, only a process that rebuilds the shadow trees and maps in the same process, such as `crushtool --rebuild-class-roots --test`.

This leaves the weight set NULL when there are no positions, as it is for the bucket itself.

Tests: a new `unittest_crush_wrapper` case, `device_class_clone_empty_weight_set`. It builds a straw root with three straw2 hosts, a compat weight set and a replicated rule on class `hdd`, converts the straw root to straw2 and rebuilds the shadow trees. It checks that the shadow root has no weight set and that all 1024 inputs map to three OSDs on three hosts. On the old code the shadow root's weight set is not NULL, and with that check removed, mapping crashes with a segmentation fault. Built on CentOS Stream 9 / GCC: `unittest_crush_wrapper` 27/27 passed.

This changes the same function as https://github.com/ceph/ceph/pull/73650, in a different hunk, and the two merge cleanly.

73654.title: doc/radosgw: describe moving the persistent notification queues
73654.author: anthonyeleven
73654.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/71326

notifications.rst doesn't say where the queues of persistent topics are kept or how to move them to another pool. This adds a section, "Moving the Persistent Notification Queues to Another Pool", before "Topic Management via CLI", and a pointer to it from the tip about putting the log pool on fast media.

- The queues are in the zone's `notif_pool`, by default `<zone>.rgw.log:notif`.
- Every RGW in the zone must be stopped for the move: an RGW opens `notif_pool` only when it starts (`RGWRados::open_notif_pool_ctx()`), and a running RGW can change a queue object while it is being copied.
- The new pool must be replicated, because the list of queues (`queues_list_object`) is kept in omap.

The steps follow @yuvalif's flow on the tracker, with two changes:
- `radosgw-admin zone modify` has no `--notif-pool` option, so the zone is changed with `zone get` and `zone set`.
- `rados export` ignores `-N` and exports every namespace in the pool (`PoolDump::dump()` sets `all_nspaces`), so the objects are copied one at a time with `rados cp --target-pool --target-nspace`, which copies data, xattrs, and omap.

Tested on a one-node 20.2.5 cluster with one RGW and a persistent HTTP topic whose endpoint was down, so 5 notifications were queued. Following the steps moved the queue to the new pool; once the endpoint came up, the 5 notifications were delivered from the new pool, and the old queue object was left untouched. New notifications were delivered both after the move and after the old copies were removed. On the same cluster, `rados -p default.rgw.log -N notif export` exported every namespace in the log pool (default, gc, lc, notif, reshard, and restore), and `radosgw-admin zone modify --notif-pool` failed with `ERROR: invalid flag --notif-pool`.

@yuvalif, could you check the steps?

73655.title: (DONT REVIEW. STILL TESTING) rgw: external authorizer for AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
73655.author: billyridgway
73655.body:
## Summary

Adds an optional external authorization step to STS `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`.
After RGW has validated the OIDC token and the role's trust policy has allowed the
request, RGW asks an external authorizer for an explicit Allow before issuing
credentials. The first provider is IBM IAM (PEP), behind a generic provider
interface.

Nothing changes when no authorizer is configured.

## Behaviour

- **Hook point:** the end of `RGWREST_STS::verify_permission`, after the native
  trust-policy check.
- **Fail closed:** a Deny, timeout, transport error, non-2xx reply, malformed
  reply, or invalid or unreadable config denies the request.
- **Configuration:** zone-wide metadata (section `ext_authz`, key `default`), so it
  replicates through metadata sync. Managed with `radosgw-admin ext-authz
  set|get|rm` and the Admin Ops endpoint `/admin/ext-authz` (new `ext-authz` cap).
  The service credential is redacted on `get`.
- **Role to action mapping (IBM):** roles named by `readonly_role_name` and
  `readwrite_role_name` use `action_readonly` and `action_readwrite`. Any other role
  uses `action_assume_role` and sends the role ARN as `objectRole`. Action names are
  configurable.
- **Subject:** only the payload segment of the JWT is sent as
  `subject.accessTokenBody`. IBM IAM rejects the whole signed token with HTTP 400.
- **Service token:** fetched with an API key and cached. On a 401 for a cached
  token, RGW fetches a new token and retries once.
- **Role binding:** a role tagged `rgw:ext-authz=<provider>` is denied unless that
  provider is the configured, enabled authorizer. Removing or disabling the
  authorizer, or naming a different provider, does not leave the role open to its
  trust policy. The tag is RGW control metadata, so it is not copied into the
  session as `aws:PrincipalTag/...` and does not require `sts:TagSession`.
- **Observability:** `ext_authz_*` perf counters, one audit log line per decision,
  and the start of a failed reply body at level 1. Tokens and keys are never logged.

## Supporting change

`RGWHTTPClient` gains `set_ca_blob()` for a PEM CA bundle. On libcurl older than
7.77 it falls back to an `SSL_CTX` callback.

## Docs and tests

- `doc/radosgw/ext_authz.rst`, `PendingReleaseNotes`.
- Unit tests: `src/test/rgw/test_rgw_ext_authz.cc`.
- QA: mock IAM and mock OIDC issuer, a config-lifecycle workunit, a
  `qa/suites/rgw/ext-authz` suite, and a multisite replication test.

## Testing done

- Unit tests pass on the v20.2.4 backport build.
- Run on an OpenShift cluster (Ceph 20.2.4) against the IBM IAM test environment:
  allow for a read-only and a read-write role, fail closed when the IAM call
  is rejected, and the role tag binding with the authorizer on and removed.
- Run against mock services: allow, deny, HTTP 500, malformed reply and timeout all
  fail closed; TLS with a private CA bundle.

## Not tested

- A real Deny from IBM IAM, and a custom role (IAM has no `s3.assume-role` action yet).
- The 401 retry, and the Admin Ops endpoint.
- Replication of the config to a second zone, and `service_credential_file`.
- This `main` branch has not been built. Only the v20.2.4 backport has.
- Keycloak-driven STS tests and the new workunit.

## Open questions for the IAM owners

Attribute names `objectAccount` and `objectRole`, the final `s3` action names, and
whether the PEP host differs from the IAM host.

73657.title: doc: explain the reclaim race and the NFS-Ganesha grace database
73657.author: anthonyeleven
73657.body:
Fixes: https://tracker.ceph.com/issues/76793

This expands `doc/dev/cephfs-reclaim.rst`, the developer page on the libcephfs reclaim interface, as the tracker issue asks:

- A new section, Racing the MDS Session Timeout, explains why an NFS server that exports a CephFS mount races its MDS session timeout. The MDS marks a silent session stale after `session_timeout` and evicts it after `session_autoclose`. If it releases the session's capabilities and locks before every NFS server is enforcing the grace period, another client can take state that an NFS client is about to reclaim. The section then explains how `ceph_set_session_timeout()` and `ceph_start_reclaim()` with `CEPH_RECLAIM_RESET` close that gap.
- A new section, Coordinating the Grace Period Across NFS Servers, describes the NFS-Ganesha `rados_cluster` recovery backend: the grace database with its epochs and per-server flags, the order in which a restarted server starts the grace period, waits for every server to enforce it, and resets its old session, and the `ganesha-rados-grace` tool.

The MDS behavior comes from `find_idle_sessions()` and `reclaim_session()` in `src/mds/Server.cc`. The NFS-Ganesha behavior comes from its `next` branch: `src/support/rados_grace.c`, `src/SAL/recovery/recovery_rados_cluster.c`, `src/MainNFSD/nfs_main.c`, and `src/FSAL/FSAL_CEPH/main.c`.
